en: *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara-ṭippaṇī*. Oṃ! Homage to Vajraḍāka!
Having paid homage, this commentary on the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* is being written.
The detailed exposition from the Guru is for the sake of the perfect recollection of something else.

"Within the spaces," and so forth. "Space" (*ākāśa*) is the *dharmodayā*. "Inert" (*jaḍa*) is earth. "Transparent" (*svaccha*) is water. "Without room" (*anavakāśa*) is wind. "Luminous" (*prakāśinī*) is fire. "The universe" (*viśva*) is the universal lotus situated within the *dharmodayā*. "Abode of the Vajra" (*vajrālaya*) is the universal vajra above the universal lotus. "The eye" (*nayana*) is the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), produced by the transformation of the four great elements—which have been moistened by the stream of nectar born from the meditative union with Vairocana arising from the *bhrūṃ*-wheel seen above the four mandalas. "In the realm of beings" (*sattvadhātāv*) means that very [realm] is the "realm of beings" (*sattvadhātu*) because it is the support for the *ḍākas* and *ḍākinīs*. Likewise, it is "delightful" (*manorama*) because it consists of the five jewels. This is what is meant: the connection with the subsequent phrase is "situated in the peaked pavilion within the *dharmodayā*. Because its nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it pervades all things; thus he says it is "situated even among beings and non-beings," beginning with "beings" (*sattva*). "He" (*sa*) refers to mobile things. "Vessel" (*bhājana*) refers to immobile things. "World" (*loka*) is an epithet for these two. To explain "beings," he says "earth," and so forth, in their respective order: those situated in heaven, the mortal world, and the underworld. "In between" (*antara*) refers to others besides the vessel-world. "In the mind," and so forth, refers to the mind, body, and speech of these very [beings]. "In one" (*ekasmin*) refers to their purified form, which is the nature of great bliss, in the aspect of the subject (*grāhaka*). "Or two" (*dve vā*) refers to the bodhicitta in which emptiness and compassion are inseparable, consisting of wisdom and method. "In space and delight" (*khe ratāv*) refers to the aspect of the object (*grāhya*) whose nature is emptiness. "Sixfold" (*ṣaḍdhā*) refers to the six sense-bases (*āyatana*) beginning with form. "In the five" (*pañcasu*) refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*). "In the twelve-sixes" (*dviṣaṭkeṣu*) refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the twenty-four great elements. "Even in nineteen" (*ekonaviṃśatsu*) should be applied here as well, meaning "in the eighteen elements together with the person" (*pudgala*). Then follows the description of the vessel-world: "in the worlds" (*jagatsu*). This is a further specification of the same: "in the entirety of the three realms" (*traidhātukamaśeṣeṣu*). "In the father," and so forth—this should be connected immediately after "in the four. The meaning is: "in the father and so forth, as they are known in the world. "External," and so forth—by the designation of external and internal, he describes beings and non-beings. "In all women" (*sarvayoṣitsu*) means that because she is the basis of pleasure for all types, he is situated there. "And in phenomena" (*dharme ca*) refers to blue, yellow, and so on. "And in all actions" (*sarvakarmasu ca*) refers to the characteristics of the activities such as coloring belonging to these very [phenomena] like blue. "In the selfless" (*anātmani*) refers to the body of the deity, which is empty of intrinsic being, unlike the ordinary self. "In the fruit" (*phale*) refers to the resultant Hevajra. "In the cause" (*hetau*) refers to the causal Hevajra. "Called the effect" (*kāryākhya*) is an epithet for these two. He states these two as "the Vajrin of the goal and the means" (*sādhyasādhanavajriṇī*). Alternatively, the "goal" (*sādhya*) is great bliss; the "means" (*sādhana*) is the method for that very [bliss]. Now, pointing out the Mother, in order to show the two states of the goal itself—consisting of the stained and the stainless—he says "For instance," and so forth. "In the storehouse-consciousness" (*ālayavijñāne*) refers to that characterized as the abode of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). "In the realm of phenomena" (*dharmadhātāv*) refers to when it has attained the state of non-abode. "Non-arising" (*anudbhava*) means devoid of production from any other cause than the moment of the appropriating mind (*upādānacitta*). "In the realm of beings" (*sattvadhātāv*) means in the support, because it is the support for the seed of that which is called the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*). "In the space-element" (*khadhātau*) means in the aspect of emptiness, because it nourishes practitioners; and "in the selfless" (*anātmani*) because of the discernment of the nature of the aspects of subject and object. "In that which is designated as self" (*ātmasaṃjñini*) because it exists with a self that is devoid of both [subject and object]. "In the selfless" (*anātmani*) is explained as "in the manifestations" (*vibhāveṣu*). "Manifestations" (*vibhāva*) means that in this [state], entities such as the grasped and so forth have departed; the plural is used because it is worthy of worship. "In that which is designated as self" (*ātmasaṃjñini*) is explained as "not non-existence" (*nābhāva*).

Because it exists in the form of the disappearance of the grasped and the grasper, it is not non-existent (*abhāva*). Because it protects the limb characterized by the object of knowledge (*jñeya-lakṣaṇa*) which is bliss, it is in *Sukhāvatī*. Because it has the form of a triangle and the nature of the earth, it is in the triangle (*trikoṇaka*). Because passion (*rāga*) and the rest are absent therein, it is *Araja* (the dustless). These very [terms] are the primary and secondary designations; thus there are such expressions as "in those free from defects" (*vigatadoṣeṣu*), and so forth. Because it is devoid of all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is "waveless" (*nistaraṅga*). Because its essence is one-pointedness of mind in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is "in absorption" (*samādhau*). Because its nature consists of the experience of the bliss of the limb that is the object of grasping, it is "internally experiencing great bliss" (*antaḥsutsukhavedini*). Because it must be hidden from those who are unworthy vessels, it is "secret" (*rahasye*). Because it is supreme, it is "supreme" (*parame*). Because it is delightful, it is "delightful" (*ramye*). Because this very self is the self of all, it is "the self of all" (*sarvātmani*). Because it is eternally continuous, it is "always" (*sadā*). The connection is with the word "abides" (*sthita*). To the question "Who is he?", he says: "consisting of all Buddhas," and so forth. Because his nature is that of all Buddhas, the meaning is that he is "composed of them," namely Mahāvajradhara. And because he is constantly engaged for the sake of sentient beings (*sattva*), he is a "being" (*sattva*). Because he prevents the *ḍākinīs*, such as Nairātmyā and others, from going outside, he is like a "vajra-fence" (*vajrapañjara*), thus a "vajra-fence. Having abided, what did he do? He says: "this one," and so forth. "This one" refers to the *ḍākinī-vajrapañjara*; in the ultimate sense, due to the absence of a cause, he is "self-arisen" (*svayambhū*). Because he possesses the six qualities such as sovereignty, he is "Bhagavān. By way of being the *dharmakāya*, he is "one" (*eka*), without a second. Because he has the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, he is the "presiding deity" (*adhidaivata*). The connection is with the word "spoke" (*uktavān*). "The five mandalas" means the pentad of mandalas; this is the sense. He states that very thing with the words beginning "of the Vajrin," which is easy to understand. With the words beginning "Gaurī," he speaks of the deities of the retinue (*māṇḍaleyadevatā*): "Puṣpā and the rest" means Puṣpā, Dhūpā, Dīpā, and Gandhā. "Lāsyā and the rest" means Lāsyā, Gītā, Nṛtyā, and Hāsyā. "Vaṃśā and the rest" means Vaṃśā, Vīṇā, Mardalā, and Murajā. "Locanā and the rest" means Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā. "Of various colors" means endowed with white and other colors. Their colors are to be understood according to the *saṃhāramaṇḍala*. "Atimoha," and so forth: the excessive delusion of sentient beings is "Atimoha," which is the confusion of the mind. For the removal of that, there is "Mahāmoha," which is great enthusiasm (*mahotsāha*). Therefore, the meaning is that they have that as their nature. "Atiteja" means the excessive brilliance of sentient beings. For the removal of that, there is "Mahādīpti," which is radiance. "By power" means by that very nature. "Atirāga" is attachment to sense objects. For the removal of that, there is "Mahārāga," which is great attachment or intentness. Therefore, the meaning is that they have that as their form. "Maherṣyā" is a mental state that prevents others from engaging with one's own possessions. One covers, conceals, or prohibits that with great effort; thus it is "Mahāvaraṇa," which is great enthusiasm. Therefore, the meaning is that they have that as their nature. "Anyayāna" is the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and others. "Vajrasattva" refers to Akṣobhya; "born from the unshakeable wisdom" (*akṣobhyajñānasambhava*) means that from which the unshakeable wisdom of emptiness arises in the Supreme, such is the sense. "Jagat," and so forth: of the world, the mass of sentient beings. "In the inexhaustible wisdom of emptiness. "For the purpose of invitation" means for the sake of making [them] face [it]. "Destroyer of the five obscurations" means the destroyer or slayer of the five obscurations of the wisdom of emptiness regarding the five: self, sentient beings, objects, conceptual constructions, and the activity of the five wisdoms. "Matsariṇaḥ" means the envious. "In many ways" means fivefold. "Of those attached to extreme emptiness" means of those thinking "everything does not exist. "The state of perfect Buddhahood" (*sambuddhatā*) means the form of Vairocana. He describes the practice with the words beginning "whatever...": "Whatever" refers to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. "Should go to the path of the senses" means one sees, hears, smells, tastes, or touches. "Each of those" means all of them. "By nature" means by way of their original form, not by modification—this is the sense. "By the yoga of supreme concentration" means with a mind that is completely concentrated. "Consisting of all Buddhas" means one should perceive them as being composed of the five *ḍākas* as appropriate. To the question "How is one able to perform this? he says: "by whatever... and so forth, which is easy to understand. He speaks of the benefit for sentient beings with the words beginning "by whatever...". Regarding the lack of awakening to the teaching, he shows the form with the words beginning "Cittavajra... and so forth.

"Of various natures" means belonging to various lineages (*gotra*). "By the conceptualization of a self" means by means of views such as a [real] self. "Bliss" refers to the nature of that which is to be accomplished, the maṇḍala-circle whose essence is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "Because of non-difference" means because of similarity. "Having the form of the Teacher" means the Teacher, adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*), together with those belonging to the maṇḍala. Thus ends the first chapter.

"Attained by the three worlds" means a teacher of benefit to the three realms. "The worship of the *samaya*" refers to the materials for worship appropriate to each, according to the divisions of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*). "By the transformations of the Vajra-worship" refers to the specific types of worship mentioned immediately above. "Scent, *hūṃ*, born of the Vajra": the scent is produced from the transformation of the seed-syllable and the emblem. It should be given specifically to the King of Horses; this is the meaning. "The self of the seed-syllable Samantabhadra" means it is born from the syllable *hūṃ*. "Seized by the application of the mudrā with the two index fingers": having formed the Vajra-bind, one links the two ring fingers like a chain, presses the middle and little fingers with the thumbs, and bending the two index fingers, holds them at the heart—this is the mudrā. "Nāginīs and Yakṣiṇīs": having visualized the syllable *kṣīṃ* on the golden seat and so forth, one attracts the Yakṣiṇī with its rays, causes her to enter there, and meditates upon the Yakṣiṇī as yellow in color, holding a white parasol, with her head trampled by Bhūtaḍāmara; thus she is accomplished. Likewise, the Nāginī is [summoned] by the syllable *naṃ*. For a human woman or a celestial maiden, however, the seed-syllable is the first letter of their name. "The lotus" is an eight-petaled lotus, colored according to the Nāga of its own direction. "The eight Nāgas": in the East is blue Ananta; in the South, white Vāsuki; in the West, red Takṣaka; in the North, red Karkoṭaka; in the petals of the Southeast and Southwest, pale-white Padma and Mahāpadma; in the Northwest, yellow Śaṅkhapāla; and in the Northeast, multicolored Kulika. "The throne made of Garuḍa and the Vajra" means the Garuḍa-throne born from the syllable *gaṃ*. "Interwoven with two *hūṃ*s" means that at the end of the garland-mantra, the syllable *phuḥ* is placed between two *hūṃ*s; the sense is: *hūṃ phuḥ hūṃ phaṭ*. In words such as "kissed" (*cumbita*), the suffix *-kta* denotes the state of being. In words such as "Vajra-lotus," the nominative case is to be understood in the sense of the genitive. "Because of great affection" means because of a great longing for accomplishment. "The Vajra of the Bursting" means by means of a chain whose nature is as indestructible as a vajra. "Then, by the four Ḍākinīs" refers to the four [deities] beginning with Sūrya mentioned immediately above. Here is the sequence: for those who have turned away from granting accomplishment, in the first six months, one should perform recitation preceded by worship; in the second, striking with the heart-hook; in the third, performing the ritual of pinning (*kīlana*) preceded by forceful summoning and so forth. Now, regarding "then it issues forth" and so on, "the Vajrin" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); from the withdrawal of the arms and so forth, one should understand the [withdrawal] of the Cakrin, Ratnī, and others. "The Vajra-añjali" and so on: in the hollow of the hands is a moon-maṇḍala; therein, by the syllable *hūṃ*, is a white vajra. One should visualize the fingers as having the form of vajras, and from the head, offer a handful of flowers. "Homage to all Tathāgatas": the meaning is that while bowing, one should offer oneself. Here, in the maṇḍala of withdrawal, Acala is the withdrawal of the four gatekeepers. Locanā is the withdrawal of the Maṇḍala-deities and Yoginīs of Śāśvata. Māmakī is the withdrawal of the Yoginīs of Vajrasattva. Likewise, Pāṇḍarā and Tārā are the [withdrawal] of the Yoginīs of Lokeśvara, and [the withdrawal] of the Yoginīs of Sūrya and Vajrasūrya. The intention is that the dance should be understood as performed by all the Maṇḍala-deities. This concludes the Second Chapter.

"Abiding in the Vajrapañjara-samādhi" means abiding in the Hevajra-samādhi. "Situated in the center of the space-element" means situated in the center of the *dharmodayā*. "The eight lotuses" refers to a red eight-petalled lotus. "Abiding in the samādhi named Vajra" means that, having bestowed names upon the Buddhas according to their respective families, one remains there in the restraint of the mind; this is the intended meaning. Passion is Amitābha; hatred is Akṣobhya; delusion is Vairocana; commitment (*samaya*) is Amoghasiddhi; the being (*sattva*) is Vajrasattva; and the jewel (*maṇi*) is Ratnasaṃbhava. "Accomplishers of desire and liberation" means they are the accomplishers of liberation through the five types of desire. The third chapter.

"HŪṂ-syllable" refers to Vajrahūṃkāra. Regarding "mudrā" and so forth: it is to be explained immediately after the [description of] the mudrās. Through that, "victory" means the overcoming of others. One is "established" in that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is one-pointedness of mind. A "mudrā-sign" (*mudrācihna*) is simply a sign, a seal. As for the body, there should be the hand-mudrā; thus, by means of the HŪṂ-vajra, the vajra, wheel, and so forth [are produced] from the hands and other limbs that have been purified. By this same extension, the foot-mudrās, gaze-mudrās, and so forth are also included. Regarding "speech-mudrā" and so forth: on the tongue, there is a white vajra with a white HŪṂ-syllable. "Recitation of mantra" refers to the recitation of the Nirodha-krodha. Regarding the mind, "sign-mudrā" means that having mentally transformed and fashioned it, signs such as pincers and so forth are also present in the meditation mandala. He says "that very same" [to mean] "that indeed. "The pincer is in the right," and so forth—all is easy to understand. This is a partial commitment (*samaya*). "Dākinī" is the speech that exists. Because the bodies of the deities and so forth have been made manifest, there is no [obscuration]; the sense is that the nature of emptiness is difficult to fathom. One is established in the meditative absorption of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

Thus, because it is the cause of supreme bliss for the disciple. "Supreme bliss" refers to the five empowerments (*pañcābhiṣeka*). In that state, one is established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is one-pointedness of mind. "The empowerment of knowledge" (*vidyāseka*) refers to the five empowerments. Regarding the phrase "one's own knowledge" (*svavidyā*) and so forth, the meaning is: by means of the eight vases produced from the *bodhicitta* generated through the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). It should be understood here that the all-purpose vase (*sārvakarmika-kalaśa*) and the victory vase (*vijaya-kalaśa*) are also included. "The Vajra-holder" (*vajrin*) refers to Akṣobhya. "By means of generating the Vajra-mind" (*vajracittaprabhāvana*) means by means of the cultivation of the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*). "Everything" (*sarvam*) refers to the songs, dances, and ritual implements being cultivated. "By the application of Vajra-verses" (*vajragāthāprayogataḥ*) means by reciting the passage beginning with "The empowerment is the great Vajra. To explain the nature of the water and other empowerments, he says: "Whatever appears," and so forth. Although whatever [appears], such as water and so on, has been said to be the form of Akṣobhya and others, the underlying sense is that its nature is Heruka in the form of bliss. "Phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) refers either to external Buddha-qualities or to [the objects] themselves. "Because" (*yat*) means because of Heruka. "By the method of all-encompassing utility" (*sarvopayikavidhānena*) means the arrangement of all the necessary mandala implements; the meaning is their presentation according to rule through the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) that they are like an illusion (*māyopama*). "With all unsurpassed worship" (*sarvānuttarapūjayā*) means by means of outer, secret, and essential (*tattva*) worship. "From hand to hand" (*karātkara*) means from the hand of the preceptor (*ācārya*) into the hand of the disciple. "Having taken up all reassurance" (*sarvāśvāsaṃ samādāya*) means having expressed reassurance to the disciple with verses beginning with "Having seen, having entered," and so forth. "Teacher of the Samādhi-Vajra" (*samādhivajradeśaka*) means the teacher of the samādhis beginning with the Initial Yoga (*ādiyoga*). "Having brought forth" (*niścārya*) means having placed them in the mind; "called the Vajra-Samaya" (*vajrasamayākhyam*) refers to the three samādhis. "One should perform the seven purifications" (*viśuddhīḥ sapta kārayet*) refers to: confession of sins, the vow not to commit sins, rejoicing in merit, dedication of merit, taking refuge in the Three Jewels, the generation of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*), and relying upon the path. "Having generated the awakening mind" (*bodhicittaṃ samutpādya*) is an elliptical expression for having performed the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatābhāvanā*).

Having also meditated upon this [mandala] such as the *Vajrapañjara* and so forth, "the visualization of the *dharmodaya*" means that one should perform the meditation on the *dharmodaya*—which has arisen from the transformation of the *vajra-hūṃ-kāra* and other syllables—within the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*). "Therein" means within the *dharmodaya*, upon a double lotus (*viśvapadma*) and a double vajra (*viśvavajra*). "The fivefold form" refers to the meditation on the moon, sun, and so forth. "The primordial person" refers to those who have become the cause. "The circle of *ḍākinīs*" refers to the host of deities beginning with Gaurī. Regarding "in the Gandharva," it means within the three syllables situated between two red *hoḥ* syllables. Regarding "the leader of the circle," it should be understood that he "arises. "One should place the term 'trivajrā'": at the heart, throat, and head, one should visualize the three syllables *hūṃ*, *āḥ*, and *oṃ*, representing the Sky-farer (*khacarī*), Earth-farer (*bhūcarī*), and Subterranean-dweller (*pātālavāsinī*). "The passion of the Vajra" means that for the sake of manifesting the circle of *ḍākinīs*, one must effect the gratification of the two vajras—the Wisdom and Means—in every maṇḍala; this is the intended meaning. "The six limbs" refers to the blue, yellow, and other colors. Regarding "self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth: in the *Karmarāja-śrī-samādhi*, one's own meditative absorption is one's own gnosis (*svajñāna*). Through that, there is the consecration of others, which is the application of them to one's own gnosis. "The sign" refers to the five signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*). "In the form of a cloud" means that because the subtle rays of light, like mustard seeds, appear as a single dense mass, the Hevajra [vision] takes the form of a cloud. "Resembling smoke" means his breath resembles a fragment of smoky clouds. "Firefly" (is the next stage).

"Like the light of a firefly" refers to the sun; "a brilliant lamp" refers to the form of a blazing lamp-flame for the lotus; "always luminous" and so forth refers to a clear light in the form of the sky for the vase. It should be understood that within all five signs, in sequence, the very form of the Buddha appears in the manner of a mirage and so forth. "Afterwards" means when success has been achieved. "Vajra-bodied ones" refers to the Bodhisattvas. "Of the mass of gnosis" refers to the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*. "Born from a womb" refers to those born from a womb, egg, moisture, or spontaneously (*aupapāduka*). "By the practice of Mahāmudrā" refers to the nature of the *nirmāṇakāya*. "One should enjoy" means by way of the unsurpassed teaching of the Dharma. "The Vajra-givers of gifts have acted" means they have uttered the words "Excellent! Excellent! The phrase "and indeed body, speech, and mind" means even the body, speech, and mind. "Abiding in the Great Vajra Samādhi" means that Hevajra, who has ascended to the intellect of the body and mind as the Great Vajra, is the object of that; "samādhi" is one-pointedness of mind, and the meaning is that he abides therein. "For women are of various forms": therein, Mohavajrā is white, Dveṣavajrā is blue, Piśunavajrā is yellow, Rāgavajrā is red, Īrṣyāvajrā is green, and Nairātmyayoginī is blue. "With life departed, standing above" means they stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a solar disc on top of a corpse. "By this very method" means the solar seat is due to its being produced from the sun. Among them, Bhūcarī is red at the throat, Khecarī is black at the heart, and Pātālavāsinī is white at the body. He states their seed-syllables with the words beginning with "Oṃ": Oṃ is the Vajra of the mind of Pātālavāsinī, Hūṃ is that of Khecarī, and Āḥ is that of Bhūcarī. "In the form of a cow" means they are white. "Vajra," etc., means the yoga of the door-keepers of Vajra Heruka. "One should visualize the Goddesses in the corners" means the four deities, Pukkasī and the others, are to be seen in the corners. The four items, such as the Bodhicitta-bell, are their respective symbols in order. Regarding "the excellent four elements," etc.: therein, the Bodhicitta-vessel is the element [water]; Meru is the earth element; the fire-pit is the fire element; and the great banner is the wind element—this is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning is that the four, Pukkasī and the others, are of the nature of earth and so forth, and this is their meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "Abiding in the samādhi of all forms" means that all forms of the wrathful deities, such as their arms and so forth, are "all forms"; the samādhi therein is one-pointedness of mind, and he abides in that. "This sound" refers to the speech consisting of mantra which is about to be described. "Of women," etc.: having taken an auspicious skull-cup, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp on its back using saffron, *gorocanā*, and blood from a woman. Having written the image of the person to be acted upon in the pericarp, and the *mālā-mantra* ending in "jaḥ" in his heart, saying "Summon so-and-so!", and having visualized oneself in the form of Yamārivajra, with the four deities Gaurī and the others brought through the practice of summoning and so forth, and having filled [the space] with all Buddhas in the form of Hevajra and the rest down to every single atom, one should step upon the heart of the image drawn in the skull-cup with the foot marked by a vajra-hook born from the syllable Hūṃ situated on a solar disc—using the *ālīḍha* posture for attracting a maiden, or the *pratyālīḍha* posture for attracting a man—and recite that Yamāri mantra together with the incitement. This is the collective meaning.

He states the second application with the words beginning "foot-dust" (*pāda*) and so forth. "Foot-dust" (*pādapāṃśu*) refers to the dust from the feet of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). Its "preparation" (*vidhāna*) consists of making an image of the *sādhya* together with earth from both banks of a river. Then, having inserted the mantra written on birch bark or similar material into its heart, one should step upon it as before with the foot and recite that mantra. Regarding "consisting of the three bodies" (*trikāya*) and so forth: the meaning is through the meditation on the generation [of the deity] by means of the transformation of the seed-syllable of the sign of Yamāri, who is of the nature of the three bodies. "Of those who are sealed" (*mudritānām*) means of those who have been seized. "Having performed the *hūṃ*-act" (*hūṃ-kṛtātopa*) means being oneself engaged in the yoga of Aparājita while uttering the mantra accompanied by the syllable *hūṃ*. "Vajra-pressing" (*vajrapīḍana*) means pressing with the two vajras produced from the *hūṃ* seen in both hands along with their rays; or, "vajra-pressing" is striking with mustard seeds that have been turned into blazing vajras by the syllable *hūṃ*. From that, there is "well-being" (*sukham*), that is, health. Regarding "he draws in" (*ākarṣayati*) and so forth: having taken oneself as the support in the form of Padmāntaka, and seeing oneself on the back of Garuḍa situated upon the sun, one [draws in] that which has gone throughout the three worlds by means of the rays from the syllable *hūṃ* situated on the sun in one's own heart.

While reciting the poison-mantra (*viṣamantra*), one effects an attraction. "Awakening the sleeping" is likewise. Having visualized oneself as before, one should see the poison residing within the body of the target being driven out from the head down to the soles of the feet by its rays, turning black. "Shaken up by the wind," and so forth. "At the sole of Gaṇapati's foot" means that one should write the purpose at the end of the foot. Here is the collective meaning: [one should take] charcoal from a cremation ground (not wood-charcoal, *haritāla*, or poison), mixed with the juice of *ariṣṭa* leaves and the blood from the ring toe of the left foot; using a stylus made of a large crow’s wing, one should draw a sword-wheel (*khaḍgacakra*) in the center of a wind-circle on a cloth or similar surface blown by the wind. In its hub, one should place an image and, in its heart, the name of the target interspersed with seed-syllables (*vidarbha*). After writing the *mālāmantra* preceded by an incitement (*sañcodanā*), one should fashion an image from clay from a potter’s wheel, clay from a crossroads, and dust from the feet of the target, and insert it into the heart of that [wind-circle]. Then, having placed it in a skull-casket and performed the invocation, one should conceal the yantra—consecrated eight hundred times with the mantra beginning "To the Yogins who end sleep and obstacles, to Samantabuddha," etc.—in a temple of the Mothers (*mātṛgṛha*), a cremation ground, or a crossroads. Visualizing the target mounted upon the back of a camel situated in a wind-circle, being led toward the southern direction by a man holding a staff in his hand, one certainly causes him to be expelled (*uccāṭana*). Regarding "the procedure for the application": according to the instructions, one should fashion an image from charcoal, anthill-clay, husks, raw meat, and dust from the feet of the target; then, on a cloth from a cremation ground, using a human bone as a stylus, one should write the *mālāmantra* interspersed with the target’s name in the middle of a fire-circle situated within a universal vajra, using poison, blood, indigo, *trikūṭa*, and the juice of *ariṣṭa* leaves. Having inserted this into the heart of the image and placed it between two skull-halves, one should step upon it with the left foot while angry for the sake of killing, chewing stones and bones as if they were betel leaves, and at midday or midnight, recite the mantra accompanied by the incitement "Kill so-and-so! HŪṂ PHAṬ! with a wrathful voice; he dies within seven days. "Poison-faced" refers to the eight serpents previously mentioned. One who possesses the yoga of the eight-armed, four-faced Mahābala should write on a baked earthenware bowl, using indigo juice, an eight-spoked sword-wheel, and in the middle of an eight-petaled lotus: "OṂ NAṂ NAṂ NAṂ NAṂ NAṂ NAṂ NAṂ NAṂ, deliver the wielder of the trident quickly! Having enclosed it with another bowl, wrapped it with blue thread, and having invoked and worshipped Śūlinī and the Nāgas with the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*), and having given the command, one should throw the bowl-casket into a pond or similar place inhabited by Nāgas while reciting the mantra; the Nāgas will certainly rain. "Mounted on a lion," and so forth: the yogin possessing the yoga of Acala-krodha should visualize the target mounted on a wind-circle born from the syllable YAṂ, being drawn by a deity standing on a lion born from SIṂ, holding a noose and a goad, and fallen at his feet; thus he effects an attraction. "One should attract all maidens"—this is the specific distinction regarding the deity-yoga in the same previous sequence. "The person of ignorance" (*avidyāpuruṣa*): having visualized one of the five Ḍākas as possessing consciousness. "By the application of the goad, etc. means by the application of Gaurī, who holds a noose and goad emerging from the heart-seed syllable. "The maiden" means one mounted on a wind-circle. "By the application of the vajra-goad" means having formed the shape of a goad. "It assumes the state of attraction" explains attraction in another way. "Just explained immediately after" means it has not been elaborated upon here; such is the sense. "Having made it into a knowledge-armlet" means having written an eight-spoked wheel on birch bark or similar material, with Sumbha and Niṣumbha in the center, the *Sitātapatra* mantra on the rim, and the mantras of the eight Wrathful Ones on the spokes in their proper places; having thus made it a *vidyā*, one should wear it on the arm or the neck.
The Fourth Chapter.

"Omniscient one" (*sarvajña*) means the omniscient one. "The image of the Buddha" (*buddhabimba*) refers to Vajrasattva, who is accomplished through the sequence of the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*). "Vajrasattva" refers to Śrī Heruka; this should be understood similarly in other instances as well. "From the maṇḍalas produced from the manifold images of the Buddhas" means from the deities of the maṇḍala produced from the fivefold causal Vajradhara. "Of the mantras" refers to the mantra-deities. "The locus of gnosis" (*jñānapada*) refers to the Gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*). "Equal to oneself and marked with symbols and seed-syllables" [is explained as follows]: by the application of the being and gnosis, that is, within the pledge-maṇḍala (*samayamaṇḍala*) of the Gnosis-being.

By means of entry. "The awakening of the Buddha" (*buddhabodhi*) refers to the oneness of the two, like milk and water; this is how one should contemplate. Regarding "by one's own mantra," etc.: the sense is that one should contemplate the arising of the deities by observing the signs such as the vajra through the transformation of one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*), and then performing the radiation and reabsorption (*spharaṇasaṃharaṇa*). Regarding "sound," etc.: it is threefold, distinguished as excellent, inferior, and middling. "Protection situated in the midst of the pledge" (*samaya*) means situated within the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*). "The mandala fivefold" refers to the dissolution mandala (*saṃhāramaṇḍala*), which consists of five mandalas. Regarding "consisting of five-fives," etc.: the meaning is that Śrī Heruka and the others each consist of five, because their nature is the five wisdoms beginning with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Regarding "also in the powder" (*rajasi*): from the word "also" (*api*), it includes the lines (*sūtra*) as well. Therein, there are twenty-five divisions: for Śāśvata, blue, yellow, red, green, and white; for Rūpa, white, blue, red, green, and yellow; for Narteśvara, white, yellow, blue, green, and red; for Aśva, white, yellow, red, blue, and green; for Hevajra, white, yellow, red, green, and blue—this is by way of clockwise rotation. The sense is according to the rule for the inner region. Regarding "of whichever," etc.: the sense is that whichever [deity], such as Hevajra, has a mandala in the center of the dissolution mandala, that very one holds the position of the leader (*nāyaka*) therein. Alternatively, "dissolution mandala" refers to the fifth mandala located in the center of the great mandala (*mahāmaṇḍala*). "Situated in the middle of eight-eights" means that in which there are eight times eight squares—that is the dissolution. It is "situated in the middle of eight-eights" because it stands in the form of that which is both the eight-eights and the center relative to the great mandala. Regarding "again in the twenty-five": it is characterized by twenty-five powders. "Gate-keepers" refers to the female gate-keepers (*dvārapālī*). "Hook" refers to the female hook-holder (*aṅkuśī*); the same applies elsewhere. "Or the king of fish" refers to the Rohita. Regarding "even among the states of existence, the best," etc.: among the five states of existence (*gati*), the human state is the best, because it is precisely there that the three types of awakening (*bodhi*) are attained—this is the sense. "And she" refers to those elephants and so forth, along with the diseases. "She runs" (*dadhau*): the diseases reside in the right skull-cup; the medicines reside in the left skull-cup—this is the sense for all of them. The Fifth Chapter.

"Recollection of mind" (*cittānusmṛti*), and so forth. The meaning is that at the time of emanation for the sake of sentient beings, one should perform the recollection of Hevajra and others through the sequence of radiating and reabsorbing. "The jewel of mind" (*cittaratna*) refers to Ratnasambhava, who is inseparable from the mind. "The great wheel" (*mahācakra*) is the mandala of withdrawal. "Vajrasattva" is Hevajra. "By the four wheels" refers to the four wheels beginning with the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*). The same applies to Śāśvata and the others. The instruction on the recollections is stated by the passage ending with "one should visualize the King of Hatred" (*dveṣarāja*) and so forth. "By the yoga of radiating" means that one should likewise command the withdrawal [of the deities] through the cloud of the mantra-drop (*mantrabindu*), the cloud of one's own body, or the cloud of the symbols (*cihna*). This applies to other cases as well. "The syllable of mind" is the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) of Hevajra; thus, elsewhere too, the word "syllable" refers specifically to the seed-syllable. "The clear mandala" is the moon-mandala. "The red mandala" is the sun-mandala. "The dharma-mandala" is the sun-mandala. "The karma-mandala" is the sun-mandala. "Indestructible," and so forth: the sequence is that the symbols such as the vajra should be understood to be located on the heads of Hevajra and the others within the mandala to be visualized. "Extending for ten million leagues" means immeasurable. "Situated in the middle of the space-element": having brought [the deity] from the seed-syllable in the heart, one establishes them in the space in front. "By the application of the goddesses of the corners" is a metaphorical expression for being in the vicinity of the goddesses of the corners. "Goddesses of the corners" refers to the goddesses such as Gaurī and the others, by means of the ritual of summoning and so forth. "Non-duality" (*advaita*) is the unification with the pledge-mandala (*samayamaṇḍala*). "The arrival of the Buddhas" (*buddhāgama*): the remainder of the sense is that they remain under the pretext of the Buddhas' arrival, using it as a guise. Therefore he says "together with," and so forth. "Having taken hold of the pride of a Buddha" means having resolved oneself into the form of a Buddha; since they visualize the *dharmadhātu*, they are therefore Buddhas—this is the summarized meaning. "From the impelling of the jewel of mind" means from the realization of the jewel of mind according to its true nature. "The great sovereignty over the three realms" occurs precisely through the practice of the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "By the king of mantras": "king of mantras" is an elliptical expression; it should be understood to include the deities as well. The Sixth Chapter.

"Vajra" refers to the state of being established in the *yogotpattisamādhi* because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the *dharmakāya*. "Yoga" is deity-yoga; its "arising" (*utpatti*) is the concentration (*samādhi*) therein, which is one-pointedness, and he is "established" (*sthita*) in that. "Self-yoga" (*ātmayoga*) means the practitioner’s own yoga with the deity. "In the accomplishment of the Buddha-abode" (*buddhālayaniṣpattau*) means in the accomplishment of the celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*). "The practice of the maṇḍala-form in five stages" refers to the meditation on the moon, sun, seed-syllable, mark, radiation, reabsorption, and the arising of the deity—this is the intended meaning. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The true nature of Samantabhadra. This refers to the accomplishment of the Causal Vajradhara within each maṇḍala. The practice of one's own presiding deity (*svādhidaivatasādhana*) serves as the cause for the accomplishment of the leaders and the retinue (*māṇḍaleya*) in each maṇḍala. For this very reason, he says: "Likewise, the arrangement of the maṇḍalas. Showing the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), he says: "Oṃ, the consecration of all Tathāgatas," and so forth. "The maṇḍala consisting of the four elements" refers to the maṇḍalas of earth and the other elements. "The Buddha above that" means having meditated on Vairocana through the transformation of the syllable *Bhrūṃ*. "One should arrange the radiating celestial palace" means one should visualize the celestial palace by completely subduing everything, according to the oral instruction. "Indestructible," etc., is easy to understand. Regarding "the speech of the *vidyās*," etc.: the *vidyās* are the five consecrations (*pañcābhiṣeka*). The "vajra of their speech" is the name of the samādhi in which they reside; such is the meaning. "The vase consecration" (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) refers to the master consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*). "Just as that is not so," etc., means that just as the knowledge of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇajñāna*) is, so the characterized object (*lakṣya*) does not exist, because it is contrary [to that]. "The supreme maṇḍala is drawn" indicates the master consecration. "By the procedure of the seminal fluid of the pledge" (*samayaretavidhānena*) indicates the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*). "Having performed the fire-offering (*homa*) or that born of meditation" indicates the wisdom-knowledge consecration (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*). "Then one should emit the breath" refers to the fourth consecration. Likewise, the verse beginning with "endowed with the five *ḍākas*" indicates the master consecration. "In the application of the vajra-seed," etc.: having visualized oneself in the form of the Sovereign (*adhipati*) arising from the melting of the bodhicitta of the pledge of all Tathāgatas, and having meditated on the disciple in the form of Vairocana, one should consecrate him—this is the remainder [of the sense]. "Hold" means by holding the mantra of consecration, i.e., by its recitation.
The meaning of "kulanāmayā" is that it is by a name corresponding to the family.

Now he speaks of the indication of the secret initiation with the words beginning with "Locanā" and so forth, and "Vajrānuttaram" and so forth. The meaning is that the *bodhicitta* which has arisen through service (*sevā*) is of the nature of the unsurpassed reality (*anuttaratattva*). He states this very point with the words beginning with "Anuttaram. Regarding the words beginning with "Nirāvaraṇa": the sense is that it is the samādhi in which the stainless purification of things is accomplished as the unobscured vajra by means of its production as the nature of nectar (*amṛta*). "By the rite" (*vidhinā*) means by way of producing the state of being nectar. "In the abode of vajra-nectar" (*vajrāmṛtāspada*) means having become the abode of liberation, whose nature is indivisible through service; that is to say, when it has attained the status of a cause. "Born from the limbs of the vajra-creature" (*vajraprāṇyaṅgasambhava*) means that one desires flesh and acts according to one's will. The Seventh Chapter.

"Regarding *sarvakṛtya*": those for whom every duty (*sarvaṃ kṛtyaṃ*) has been performed are the "All-Duty-Performers," namely the Tathāgatas; the meaning is that this is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for their arousal. With the words *oṃ sarvatathāgata* and so forth, he states the empowering mantras (*adhiṣṭhānamantra*) for Khecarī and the others. The passage beginning with *kāyavākcitta* is easy to understand. Regarding *mahāmudrā* and so forth: *Mahāmudrā* is the body of the deity; its "application" (*prayoga*) is its imposition upon one's own body. By means of that, one should purify the body. "Meditative absorption-vajra" (*dhyānavajra*) refers to the visualization (*bhāvana*) of the form of a deity or something else by means of the mind. The sense is that by means of that, [one purifies] the mind, and by the recitation of mantra, the speech. The passage beginning with *mohavajra* is easy to understand. Regarding *yadyapi* and so forth: *virudhyati* means "is contradicted. As for *tadyadyapi*: "of the Victors" (*jinānām*) means "by the Victors" (*jinaiḥ*). He asks, "Why is this so? and answers with the passage beginning with *saṃvṛti*. The "wheel" (*cakra*) is the maṇḍala-wheel. Just as it exists from the perspective of conventional usage (*saṃvyavahārataḥ*), so too its purification is merely from the perspective of conventional usage. Because it is "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*): the sense is that by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatayā*), there is merely the non-conceptualization of form and merely the self-awareness of its own nature; nothing else exists. "The nature of phenomena is the reality" (*vastu*): in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), neither the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) nor the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) exists. "From the discernment of reality" (*bhūtavivekāt*): because of the discernment—that is, the thorough knowledge—of reality, which is empty of duality. He says exactly this with the passage beginning with *sarva*. Since the entire world is devoid of the nature of an apprehending subject and so forth, such as the person (*pudgala*), therefore the "course of the world"—that is, the cognition of things as they truly are—cannot be conceived by the foolish through doubt, precisely because it is so.

Therefore: "By means of the forms of *dharmatā*," and so forth; the meaning is that everything is indeed purified by way of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). He provides an illustration with the words "of those that have been burnt," and so on: medicine is like poison, [in that it produces] poison-eruptions and the like. For one whose body is afflicted—that is, whose body is impaired—[the medicine acts]. "Other poison" refers to that which is directly denoted by the word "poison. "Destruction" (*kṣaya*) refers to the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*); the meaning is the perfect awakening of one free from passion (*vītarāgābhisambodhi*). "From the thorough knowledge of vajra-passion" means from the purification of passion through the form of a deity and so forth. "The four faces": the eastern [face] is yellow; the southern is blue; the western is red; the northern is white. "Fierce seed" (*caṇḍabīja*) refers to *rājikā* (black mustard). "She is not a limb of awakening" means that she is certainly not a constituent part of awakening. The Eighth Chapter.

"Hidden by sound" (*dhvaninigūḍha*) means in a place free from the clamor of people and the like. "Loincloth" refers to yellow cloth. "Jewels" refers to the five jewels; "medicines" refers to the five medicines. This is also indicative of the five grains. Regarding "Oṃ deva... and so forth: the meaning is that one should recite the mantra beginning with "Oṃ" after having attracted the deity Hevajra and others—along with Gaurī and the rest together with their mantras—by means of the seed-syllable in one's own heart through a mass of rays, caused them to enter the vases, bound them, and brought them under control. The mantras such as "Oṃ Moharati... and so forth are to be understood as those for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the vases for Locanā and the other goddesses. However, "Oṃ Vajragaurī... and so forth are for the purpose of attracting the deities of the mantras, Gaurī and the others. Furthermore, regarding "again by that very [means]" and so forth, the meaning is that at the time of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), everything should be performed as previously described.

Now, in order to show the deities established in the locations of the eyes and so forth, he says: "In the eyes and so forth," etc. "One should begin with worship and so forth in sequence" is the brief statement (*uddeśa*). "The state of gnosis" (*jñānapada*) refers to the Gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*). "The Buddhas" refers to those who are established. "The supreme bodhicitta" refers to the forms of the Ḍākinīs and others. From "all phenomena" up to "Heramba-vajra" is the hymn of praise. Regarding "the snapping of the vajra-fingers" (*vajrācchaṭā*) and so forth: having formed the *vajrabandha* with the two arms, one makes a hook with the index fingers while reciting the mantra "Vajrasamāja Jaḥ 3. Then, by snapping the middle and ring fingers, one performs the meditation on the vajra-abode (*vajrabhavanabhāvanā*). This means that through the snapping accompanied by the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should see the mandala of the support and the supported (*ādhārādheya-maṇḍala*), as if it were being beheld. "The vajra-syllable" is the syllable *YAṂ*; the "vajra-maṇḍala" is the wind-maṇḍala; the "vajra-heap" is the fire-maṇḍala. "Vajra-cooking" refers to the purification of substances according to the sequence of blazing, heating, and so forth. "Having caused the vajra-Buddhas to enter" requires the ellipsis "into the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) and so forth. "By binding with the five-pronged [vajra]" means having produced one's own *kuliśa* (thunderbolt) in the form of a five-pronged vajra, one forms a bond by entering through the door of the lotus of Wisdom (*prajñā*). "Situated in the midst of the space-element" means having seen the Buddhas facing outward in the sky, they are cast down into the interior of the lotus of Wisdom by the mouth. "By the application of the vajra-fingers" refers to the application of the eight stakes in the form of Vajrayamāri. "Red" means colored by passion for the welfare of sentient beings. The "body of the deity" should be understood by the term *mahāmudrā*.

"Having observed" means one should look. "With a mind intent on the propitiation of vigor" means with an intention for propitiation preceded by vigor. Chapter Nine. "The vajra-mudrā" refers to the wheel, earrings, and so forth. "With the eye-vajra" means with an eye that is unimpeded and incapable of being obstructed. "The great mind of all sentient beings"—here the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. Chapter Ten.

"One should begin the consecration" means that one joined with the yoga of a white deity such as Vairocana and so forth, having consecrated the object of practice—who is situated within a water-mandala in one's own heart, or who resides within a water-mandala upon the lotus of the consort (prajñā)—and whose diseases have been struck away in the form of monkeys, should visualize him as consisting of the atoms of the white deities. "With a nourishing mind" means with an exceedingly expansive mental state; one possessing the yoga of Vajrasūrya should, as before, meditate on the object of practice situated within a Mahendra-mandala, consecrate him with the nectar from yellow vases, meditate on him as consisting of the atoms of the yellow deities, and visualize a rain of various jewels falling upon his house. "The yogin of Vajradharma, with a passionate mind, should attract and enjoy a maiden" means that, having attracted her in the proper manner, [one should consecrate her] with red vases—

Having consecrated the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and brought them under control, one should fulfill the desired aim. With a "seen mind"—that is, with a cruel mind—through the yoga of the deity Nīla, one should cause a rain of fire to fall upon the *sādhya* and perform the act of killing. This is the eleventh chapter.

Thus [ends] the section of Vādhuni (?). To the question "What did he say?", the compiler says "He said... and so forth. He demonstrates that very point with the words beginning with "On the mountain" (*girau*). "The support of the *bodhicitta*" means that one should perform the meditation on ultimate *bodhicitta*, which is the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*); this is the meaning. "By the yoga of the wrathful deity" (*krodhayogena*) means by means of the pride (*ahaṃkāra*) of the wrathful deity. "By the yoga of the nectar" (*amṛtayogena*): they do not die, thus they are "nectars," namely Vajrahūṃkāra and the others; their "yoga" is making them the central leader in the middle; by that, is the meaning. Alternatively, the "yoga of the nectar" is the radiation of Amṛtakuṇḍalī; by that, one should dispel obstacles—this is the connection. "Situated in the center of the space-element" (*ākāśadhātumadhyastham*) means situated in the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*). The "vajra-maṇḍala" is the wind-maṇḍala. The "radiance-maṇḍala" is the fire-maṇḍala. "Arisen from the five wisdoms" (*pañcajñānasamudbhūtam*) means arisen with the nature of the five wisdoms. "The image of the being" (*sattvabimbam*) is the body of Vajrasattva. From what did it arise? He says: "Arisen from Vajrasattva. "Vajra" is the emblem (*cihna*), and "Sattva" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); the meaning is that it is produced from those two. "In the maṇḍala of the Ḍāka": like a Ḍāka, he is a Ḍāka; [it refers to] Nairātmā, in her maṇḍala. This is the twelfth chapter.

"In one's own self" means from one's own body. "One's own" (*ātmīya*) means belonging to each individual self; it signifies that which pertains to every single self. "They attained" (*āpeduḥ*) means they produced [it]. This is the thirteenth chapter.

"Bhadracaritam" means the conduct or activity of the "bhadras"—that is to say, the means of accomplishment for the *siddhis* such as the magic pill (*guḍikā*) and so forth. "Of Vajra" refers to Hevajra. "Five scents" refers to the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five substances. "The five lamps wrapped in three metals": having wrapped them with three sheets of gold, silver, and copper, one should place them in the mouth; this is the remainder [of the sense]. The phrase "assuming the form of Vajra" also applies here. "Sun-Vidyādhara" means by means of the pride (*ahaṃkāra*) of Vajrasūrya. "Combined with the five meats" means accompanied by the five lamps. "Nandagopa" is a specific type of living being. "Horse-Vidyādhara" means by means of the pride of Paramāśva. "Lokanātha" refers to Padmanarteśvara. "Nāgarāja" refers to the serpent-king Dvivadana. "Añjana-Vidyādhara" means by applying collyrium to the eyes. "Seed" means semen. Regarding "Śārdūla" and so forth: having smeared both feet with tiger-skin oil together with realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and seed, the practitioner of the Vairocana-yoga becomes accomplished through the application to the feet; this is the meaning. Regarding "Anaṅgamaṇḍala" and so forth, this is the collective meaning here: in the middle of a cave on Mount Indraśaila, having drawn the maṇḍala called the Protection Wheel with colored powders (*rajas*) with Vajrānaṅga as the central leader, one should resolve that oneself is the leader situated in its center, and give the command to Sumbharāja who stands below with the mantra beginning "Oṃ sumbha... and so forth. Sumbha, for his part, having established a second emanation of himself in his own place and entered the underworld (*pātāla*), draws forth a maiden from the underworld and presents her to the practitioner. Thus, meditating during the three junctions of the day for seven days, one should accomplish the desired goal. Regarding "Āḍradeśa" and so forth: here too, the procedure is the same as before. Regarding "Vajrasattva" and so forth: by this, he shows the meditation on another deity for the sake of accomplishing the *siddhi*. To show the actual form of the dispatched Sumbharāja, he says "Sumbharājasya" and so forth. "Vajrakoṣa" means a vajra-mace. "By the impelling of the mantra Phaṭkāra" means one should impel him with the mantra beginning "Oṃ sumbha... characterized by the syllable *phaṭ*. In the reading beginning with "Phuḥkāramantre," [it refers to] the mantra of the Horse-King.

"By the mantra of Aśvarāja alone," according to the scripture beginning with "of Vajrapātālaka. "In all phenomena being empty" refers to medicinal substances and the like. "Of all beings" refers to living creatures. "All phenomena" refers to blue, yellow, and so forth. Here, the two words "as" and "so" (*yathā* and *tathā*) are to be supplied.

Now he speaks of the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*) with the words beginning "cāruvaktrām" [the beautiful-faced one]. "Vajrāṅguli" refers to the trunk of an elephant and so forth. "Vajrabhuvanam" is the *dharmodayā*, the mind-vajra. "By the vajra-tongue" means by the tongue marked with a vajra. "In Sukhāvatī" means in the *dharmodayā*. "Vajrasattva" is the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*). "One should take" (*haret*) means one should consume. "Joined with flowers" (*puṣpasamāyuktam*) means suitable for arising from flowers. "With a red lotus" (*raktapadmena*) means by means of service; "with a lotus accompanied by blood" means by the lotus alone. "By the application of the five perfumes" (*pañcagandhaprayogeṇa*) means by consuming the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*); "worship the banner-sandalwood" (*dhvajakarpūraṁ pūjaya*) means either by the consumption of the single *bodhicitta* itself. To state the method for subduing the wicked, he says "triratnam" and so forth. "The vajra-self should summon" (*vajrātmā samāhvayet*) means the yogin, the vajra-self, should summon—that is, bring—the object of practice (*sādhya*). "He should crush" (*nisumbhayet*) means he should kill. "He would go to the realm of the Vajrin" means that the object of practice, having been deceived, through the power of meditation as it truly is, is reborn in the Akṣobhya world-system; this is the meaning. Having shown the power of a yogin who has attained capability, he states the activity of another with the words beginning "aśaktāv". This is the meaning here: when the yogin does not possess attained capability, then, having made the Tathāgatas hear [of the intent], and having fashioned the object of practice (*sādhya*) and the hook (*aṅkuśa*) etc. out of flour, one should rescue the object of practice before those Buddhas using the fashioned hooks and so forth. The phrase "he would go to the realm of the Vajrin" should also be applied here. "Situated in the center of the vajra-maṇḍala" means situated in the center of the protection-wheel (*rakṣācakra*). "Vajrasūrya" is the solar disc. "In the heart" (*hṛd*) means the unstruck (*anāhata*) syllable *HŪṂ* in the center of the lotus-thunderbolt. "With the mouth, Nairātmya-Ḍākinī" means she who is characterized by the vajra. "Nairātmyā, impelled by *bodhicitta*" means within the interior of both apertures. "The object of desire" (*abhilāṣakam*) is the *dharmodayā*, because it is the object of desire. "Non-self" (*anātma*) refers to the other; "self" (*ātma*) refers to oneself. "There is no sensation" (*na vedanam*) means there is only the sensation of bliss; "just as" is the remainder of the sense. "At the end, in the middle. By the words beginning with "svayam," he shows the fruit of meditation. "Free from the five obscurations" (*pañcāvaraṇavarjitam*) means devoid of the five hindrances characterized by sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, regret-and-doubt. "Not afflicted by conditioned things" (*saṁskṛtatvairna bādhyata*) means it is not afflicted by the nature of the conditioned, because this body has the nature of Heruka, which is unconditioned (*asaṁskṛta*). "May it be awakened" (*vibuddhyatām*) means may it become manifest. "Meditation is not meditation" (*bhāvanā na ca bhāvanā*): the meditation that is a deity is not to be performed as meditation; the point is, once the form of the deity is accomplished, what is the use of that? "By a dissimilar cause" (*visadṛśena kāraṇena*) means by that which is empty of form. "Awakening is formless" (*nirākārā bodhiḥ*) means it is indeed formless; moreover, even though it is formless, he shows that very thing with the words beginning "I am existence" (*bhāvo'ham*). "Profound" (*gambhīra*) means in the form of emptiness. "Lofty" (*udāra*) means in a form adorned with the marks and so forth. "Unstruck" (*anāhata*) is the syllable *HAṂ*. "Having the nature of pleasure and pain" means because it is all-pervasive. "Muccuṭī" is the contraction of all fingers, specifically the contraction of the index and middle fingers in the "lion's ear" gesture. "Śāyaka" is an arrow. "One should speak at length" (*vakṣyavistaratām*) means an extreme swelling due to arrogance. "Cakṣuḥ" means the eye. "Kāminī" is *priyaṅgu*. "Kaccoram" is *śaṭī*. The word "keśa" means hair. "Bolaka" is *gandharasa*. "Śālijam" is *khaṭtāsa*. "In every way, the forceful practice" (*sarvathā haṭhasādhana*) means that in the forceful practice, one should repeatedly give all the various perfumes. "All those" (*sarve te*) means by all of them. "He, with agitation" (*sa saṁbhrama*) means respectfully. "At the forefront of play" (*vilāsāgre*) means... (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the final phrase.)

"Moving with grace" means proceeding with playful, rhythmic movements. "With eight steps" means up to eight paces. "Eyes and hands" refers to turning the hand and holding it above the ear like a *patākā* (banner) mudrā using the index and middle fingers. "Hips and hands" refers to [the movement] with the *patākā* hand and the foot. "Circumambulating clockwise" means rotating counter-clockwise (to the left). "Caitya" refers to the left hand held downward while the right hand forms a fist with the thumb extended. "By Vajrasattva" means by the syllable *HŪṂ*. "Meditation on the lotus-vajra" is the manifestation of the lotus and the thunderbolt. "By its nose-tip" means by the filament of that lotus, [visualized] with the syllable *ĀḤ*. "By the *praṇavas*" means by the syllable *OṂ*. "Cintāmaṇi" is the wish-fulfilling jewel-thunderbolt. This is the fourteenth chapter.

"Like at the time of childbirth" means that, as if she were herself present during the time of birth to alleviate the suffering of those afflicted by the pains of delivery; "desiring a lotus" refers to a longing for an ordinary lotus; "having placed the wielder of the thunderbolt" means having introduced the *vajra*; "and indeed the Fully Awakened One" means that the Flower Consecration (*puṣpābhiṣeka*) is called "the Fully Awakened One" because it is accepted by the Fully Awakened Ones; "one should avoid the binding of mudrās," and so forth—this has been stated for practitioners of the Stage of Generation (*utpannakrama*); "without a teacher" means without a preceptor (*ācārya*); "he should prescribe the consecration" means by means of liberation from delusion. This is the fifteenth chapter.
The *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara-ṭippaṇī* is completed.
By whatever merit has been acquired through composing this excellent commentary on the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*, may all people become holders of the vajra.
The first instruction in the *Vasantatilakā*.
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!

Abiding in the nature of the thirty-seven factors conducive to great enlightenment, which consist of the equal and unequal aspects of great bliss; established as the primary four wheels within the channels of one's own body; adorned with the thirty-four consonants along with the five vowels and twelve measures; the Lord of the ten stages beginning with the *pīṭhas*, residing in the divisions of body, speech, and mind; omnipresent, dwelling in the center of the hearts of all living beings, having the form of space, supreme, and profoundly peaceful. ||1||
The Commentary *Rahasyadīpikā*.
Oṃ! Homage to the venerable Vajraḍāka!
To the Lord Heruka, whose intrinsic nature is non-different from the thirty-six consciousnesses (*saṃvid*).
Having prostrated, I shall explain the Vasantatilaka in due order.

Having attained the fourth great mudrā-siddhi, he was firmly committed to accomplishing the welfare of both himself and others; through the display of his extraordinary conduct as taught in the diverse and wondrous Yoginītantras, he captivated those to be trained, causing the mundane and supramundane wonders of his own [realization] to blossom.

The great master named Śrī Kṛṣṇapāda—who, like a second Śrī Heruka, was directly visible with various instructions appearing within his own intellect; who, desiring to reveal a specific oral tradition (āmnāya) manifesting of its own accord to those seeking it, exerted himself in that endeavor; and who now intends to compose this manual for the means of accomplishment (*sādhanopāyikā*) of the Blessed Śrī Heruka according to the internal sequence (*adhyātmakrama*), titled *Vasantatilakā*—has composed this prologue to the manual with the verse beginning "Equal and unequal," in order to pay homage to that very [deity] who is inseparable from his own nature and endowed with his own majesty, for the sake of recollecting his own nature.

In this regard, first the title and so forth are stated: "Vasantatilaka" is the title; the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the *niṣpannakrama* (the stage of completion); the relationship (*sambandha*) between the word and its meaning is characterized by the signifier and the signified; the purpose (*prayojana*) is easy comprehension by way of general characteristics. To state it briefly: the ultimate purpose is the accomplishment of the welfare of the entire world, preceded by the attainment of the *mahāmudrā*, which is itself preceded by perfect knowledge.

The connection [of the verse] is: "Having bowed to that *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, I shall explain the *Vasantatilakā*. Of what nature is it? It is described as "the even and the uneven," and so forth. "Even" (*sama*) refers to those things whose nature is skillful means (*upāya*); "uneven" (*viṣama*) refers to those whose nature is wisdom (*prajñā*). These thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), which are subsumed within the five paths and range from the application of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*) up to right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), constitute its essential nature (*svabhāva*). He is the Blessed One who abides in that very form. In this context, there are twenty-two "even" phenomena because they are subsumed within the mundane path (*laukikamārga*). There are fifteen "uneven" phenomena because they are subsumed within the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*). Alternatively, the "even" are the consciousnesses arising from the right channel (*savyanāḍī*), and the "uneven" are those arising from the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*). Furthermore, there are twenty-four joys (*ānanda*) consisting of the fourfold divisions—beginning with joy—applied to each of the six consciousnesses, such as sight. Within the four wheels (*cakra*), there are twelve joys based on the threefold division of joy and so forth, according to the sequence of entering, abiding, and arising. And there is one joy resulting from the dissolution of all limbs. Thus, the Blessed One, whose single form is the innate (*sahaja*), abides in the nature of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening. Even externally, he is joined by an equal number of ḍākinīs.

To demonstrate that very state of being the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvaratva*), he says: "One's own channels" (*svāṅganāḍī*) and so forth. Within one's own eight limbs—the gates of the body—there are these channels (*nāḍīs*) which have the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, and take the forms of Kākāsyā and the others. Likewise, there are the four wheels (*cakras*), beginning with the Emanation wheel, located respectively at the navel, heart, throat, and crown; these have the nature of the Emanation, Dharma, Enjoyment, and Svābhāvika bodies. Within these—which consist of the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body—he is the sovereign lord by virtue of being the Heart, whose nature is Awakening (*bodhi*) inseparable from the conventional and ultimate truths.

He describes its nature also as the embodiment of mantra: "The consonants are adorned with the five vowels, the twelve mātrās, and the thirty-four [consonants]. Because of the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation from the term "five-vowels," ten [vowels] are obtained. Therein, by the placement of the seed-syllables of the Tathāgatas—marked by the vowels *hūṃ*, *oṃ*, *āḥ*, *hrīṃ*, and *khaṃ*—respectively in the center of the wheel of Dharma and upon the four petals of the directions.

There is the purification of the aggregates (*skandha*). In the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhogacakra*) as well, there is the purification of the five elements through the placement of the five seed-syllables *oṃ*, *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, and *ai*. Likewise, the twelve vowels—excluding the four neuter ones—are downward-facing in the left channel; these same vowels are upward-facing in the right channel, surrounded by the twenty-four consonants beginning with *ka*, which face upward and downward and are colored by the anusvāra whose nature is the letter *ma*. Similarly, those same vowels, together with the neuters, doubled to sixteen, are present in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), excluding the letters at the top and bottom. The thirty-two consonants beginning with *ka*, doubled, are in the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*). According to the system of placing the twenty-four channels, the sibilants (*ūṣman*) are located in the corners of the dharma wheel, situated outside that in the form of the vessel. In the center of all four wheels are the vowels and so forth, the thunderous sound (*meghanāda*), Brahma, and the unstruck syllable (*anāhatanāda*). The letter *ra* is in Jālandhara, and the letter *kṣa* is at the tip of the lower door. Adorned with these, it takes the form of the mantra-line.

In order to demonstrate his sovereignty over the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), he says: "The Lord of the ten stages, such as the *pīṭhas* and so forth, which abide in the divisions of body, speech, and mind. Furthermore, having prostrated to whom shall I speak the *Vasantatilaka*: to him who is the Lord, the Master, of those ten Bodhisattva stages—such as the Joyous (*pramuditā*) and the rest—which are the very nature of these [stages], and which abide in the wheels of body and so forth through their reverse divisions as the *pīṭhas* and so forth; that is, the channels (*nāḍī*) in the locations of the head and so forth, whose forms are indivisible and so on. Here, there are ten Bodhisattva stages, upon which the Bodhisattva, having burned away the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, perceives the Truth. Through the direct realization of the non-conceptual realm, enlightenment is attained after three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

This production of the thought [of awakening] is considered to be: first, that which consists of resolute conviction; second, that which arises from pure high resolve; third, that which is the maturation on the stages; and likewise, that which is free from obscurations.

Because of this statement, there is a distinction here [in the *Guhyasamāja*] from the vision of the *Prajñāpāramitā*: here, the direct realization of the state of Śrī Heruka—which is the form of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), synonymous with the glorious great bliss (*śrīmahāsukha*) that is primarily self-cognizable and consists of the realization of the three bodies (*kāya*) whose nature is the dissolution (*laya*) and so forth accomplished by traversing the ten stages (*bhūmi*) designated by conventions such as Pullīra—is more swiftly accomplished in this very life. Therefore, because the innate (*sahaja*) itself holds sovereignty over the *pīṭhas*, *kṣetras*, *chandohas*, and *melāpakas* in the form of the *dharmakāya* and so forth, the Lord’s status as the master of the ten stages is established. The etymological derivation and the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the *pīṭhas*, etc., and the *bhūmis*, will be explained later.
Śrī Heruka, whose form is the reality of supreme nirvāṇa, possesses a radiance blazing with the emanations of the arising Vasantatilakā.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*). Since all things, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, abide therein by way of their true nature (*dharmatā*), he is the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

"Residing in the center of the hearts of all living beings. All living beings refer to animals, birds, reptiles, humans, and so forth. Residing in the center of their own hearts means situated within the pericarp enclosed by the lotus-calyx of the heart. Its nature consists of the four elements—earth and the rest—arranged in a square. It resides between the solar and lunar mandalas above and below, having the nature of the extremely subtle *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena), subtler than even a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair. It exists in a form inseparable from all the *cakras*, *ḍākinīs*, *vīras*, and others. And it is said: "In the heart, there eternally abides the single, imperishable *bindu*."
"And for those men who cultivate that, supreme knowledge arises"—so it is said;
and from the statement: "In the state of union (*saṃpuṭībhāva*), the single *bindu* shines forth as a union;
having become free from union, the *bindu* proceeds to the state of being beyond *bindu* (*nirbindutā*)."

And what else is it like? It is of the nature of space (*vyomarūpa*) because it is the *dharmakāya*. Alternatively, it is of the nature of the five spaces (*pañcavyomarūpa*), because it is accessible through the touch of the channels such as the *trivṛtā* and others. And it has been said: "The space in the center of the *bhaga*, adorned with the five spaces, joined with the pericarp and filaments, and embellished by eight petals," and so forth.
"Supreme peace," and so forth: it is "supreme" because its nature is ultimate bodhicitta, and it is "peaceful" because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). ||1||

With the words beginning "Śrī Heruka," he speaks in order to correctly demonstrate the nature of *bodhicitta* as consisting of both the absolute (*vivṛti*) and the relative (*saṃvṛti*): "Śrī Heruka. He is the one whose nature is that of the supreme reality of perfect bliss (*paramanirvṛtitattva*), the *sahaja* single *dharmakāya*, and who is identical with it. Likewise, she who arises—that is, emerges from emanation—is this Vārāhī by nature. Through the union with Heruka, who is the springtime in which the flowers of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth blossom, she is like a *tilaka* (mark); she is the flame of the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgnijvālā*), consisting of light, which consumes the fuel of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). Her radiation (*spharaṇa*) is the upward movement through the three wheels (*cakras*) via the central channel (*madhyamārga*); she is radiant (*ujjvalā*) because of that, and her splendor (*bhā*) is shimmering with its shadow-like radiance.

Having prostrated before the Lord of the Primordial Wheel, who has accumulated [merit] through the expansion of the three bodies, for the sake of the happiness of the self and others in the world; ||2||

To him who possesses that: likewise, the "expansion" (*prasara*) of the three channels—Rasanā and the others—which constitute the three families of body, speech, and mind, is the expansion in the places such as Pullīra, namely in the Nirmāṇa [chakra] and so forth. The "accumulation" (*saṃcaya*) of that [expansion] consists of the numbers twenty-four, one hundred and twenty-four, twenty-one thousand, and seventy-two thousand; by that number is defined this wheel of channels whose nature is Anantavīrīṇī. Therein resides the Lord (*nātha*), the Master, in the form of the conventional *bodhicitta*. And it is said:
[The Lord] moves through the spheres of the elements at the feet, the secret place, the anus, the heart, and the head, and reaches the back of Mount Meru.
I bow to you, the Heruka of both minds, who resides within the vajra-lotus of the channels and moments.
I bow to you, Sahaja-Ātma-Heruka, the non-dual and indivisible Tilaka of the Dharmadhātu, who abides within the great sky of the five spaces situated inside the pericarp of the secret lotus.

I bow to you, Herukī, Mother of the World, whose brilliance exceeds the fierce mass of lightning flashing from within the layers of dark clouds, and who simultaneously consumes both the world of sentient beings and their physical environment.

I bow to you, who possess the brilliance of the submarine fire, who are born from the union of the vajra and the lotus within the hollow of the ocean of the navel-cakra, and who are greedy for drinking the essence-nectar of the celestial mansion. Thus, and so forth.

Having paid homage to the nature of the *dharmakāya*, he speaks with the other two [kāyas] in order to pay homage as well, saying: "The bliss of the world’s own and others’ welfare. The bliss of the world—the three realms—that is personally experienced is one's own bliss (*svasaukhya*); this is the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya* during the state of non-emission from the mouth of the *vajra*. In its other state, it is the bliss for the sake of others (*parārthasaukhya*), which has the *nirmāṇakāya* as its essence. This very arising of the world is the arising of the Tathāgata, because the world has that as its nature. And it is said in the *Saṃpuṭatilaka*: "I shall explain the *Vasantatilakā*, which has emerged from the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*)."
In both external and internal forms, according to the sequence of the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara. ||3||
Consisting of all ḍākinīs, red in color, and arisen from all vajras,
he is known as Padmanarteśvara through his yoga with the radiance of the lotus.
He is further known as Vajrasūrya, possessing a supreme, shimmering, upward-shining light.
Also in the *Śrīvajraḍāka*:
"That which shines and blazes is the Sage Mahāvairocana;
he is at the end of the cessation (*viramānta*) and the supreme horse (*paramāśva*), because of the universal arising of the winds."
For this very reason, his body is embraced by Vārāhī; the phrase "by the very same principle previously stated" is the completion of the sentence. ||2||

[Regarding the phrase *śrīherukābhidhānam*: although the Blessed One is nameless, he is conventionally established by the designation "Śrī Heruka. He is delightful and captivating through the sound of the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is like an echo. Since that very sound is the *vasantatilakā* (the "spring ornament"), the Bindu is revealed by that resonance; thus, the Blessed One is the union of Nāda and Bindu. Their meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) is their arising, and because it transcends sequence, its nature is the Utterly Perfected Stage (*utpannakrama*). Having prostrated—this connects with what precedes. ||2||

What kind of *Vasantatilakā* shall I describe? It is that which has emerged from the *yogapīṭhas*. There are four *yogapīṭhas*, known as the *ātmapīṭha*, *parapīṭha*, *mantrapīṭha*, and *tattvapīṭha*, which correspond respectively to the navel, heart, throat, and head. From these it has emerged, proceeding by way of coming and going. That which expresses this, being a means for practice (*sādhanopāyikā*), is also called *Vasantatilakā*, just like the epic poem *Sītāharaṇa*. He asks: "From where has this been extracted? He says: "The tantra named *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*; therein I shall describe, according to their essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), the sequence (*krama*)—known as both 'arisen' (*utpanna*) and 'un-arisen' (*anutpanna*)—which consists of the external and internal characteristics. This is the connection with what precedes. For instance, in the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), there is the mandala-circle consisting of thirty-seven [deities]; in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), however, within great bliss (*mahāsukha*), there is the channel-wheel (*nāḍīcakra*) numbering the same. In this manner, other points should also be inferred. (3)
