The accomplished Śrī Vajraḍākinī resides within one's own body; [this work is composed] for the sake of clear understanding by those who have very little inclination [for extensive texts]. (4)
Having abandoned the artificial mandala and the artificial fire-offering ritual (homa), as well as artificial meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) and artificial recitation (japa). ||5||
"All is artificial," and so forth, [is said] by way of the application of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The external ritual procedure (*prakriyā*) is artificial for the purpose of realizing one's own true nature (*svarūpa*).

He states the purpose [of the work] with the words "The illustrious Vajraḍākinī," and so forth. This Blessed Lady Vajraḍākinī—[she who is called "Vajraḍākinī"] because she "flies" (*ḍayati*) or moves, her limbs illuminated like thousands of flashes of lightning, the Blessed Lady Jñānāgniprabhā Vārāhī; she is "perfected" (*siddhā*) because she is the nature of *dharmatā*, being by her very nature spontaneously accomplished (*niṣpanna*), and because she is to be known by all. Is she situated outside? No, he says: she "is established" (*vyavasthitā*) within one's own body, the physical form consisting of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth, according to the sequence previously mentioned, for it is from that very source that she is perceived. Therefore, for the sake of those individuals who are unable to penetrate the extensive tantra and whose inclination is for what is extremely brief, I shall speak so that there may be a clear understanding—that is, a realization—of her. The meaning is: for the sake of realizing the complete *niṣpannakrama* (the stage of completion) through a very short text. ||4||

In this context, what should the lord of yogins who has ascended to the stage of the perfected process (*niṣpannakrama*) perform—mandalas, fire offerings, meditations, or recitations? He says "no," beginning with the words "artificial" (*kṛtrima*) and so forth. These things, such as images and the like, which exist externally in the generation process (*utpattikrama*), are all "artificial"—that is, fabricated—because they are conceptual constructs and because they are accomplished by means of external implements. Like a jar or similar objects, they possess the nature of perishing due to the destruction of their constituent causes. Therefore, the point is: what is the use of performing or meditating upon those things which are merely causes of vain distraction? If this is so, why then is the ritual procedure not at all the cause for realizing one's own true nature?
Just as a raft is well-employed by certain people seeking the further shore, and then abandoned upon reaching that shore, so too is this systematic method. //7//

Fearing that one might suspect this was taught by the Blessed One [only as a provisional means], he says: "The ritual procedure is artificial," and so forth. Although the previously mentioned ritual procedures, such as those concerning the mandala, are artificial, they were taught for the sake of realizing—that is, understanding—the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the mandala and other elements which are established by their own essence (*svabhāvasiddha*). They are not themselves the form of the fruit. Therefore, relying on the yoga of that which is to be described—the mandala and so forth which are of the nature of essence and spontaneously established—everything external is indeed merely artificial. By that [means], the intention is that the mandala should be meditated upon within the body.

Those who are inclined toward the mandala and so forth should first engage in the meditation on their causes; subsequently, by means of that very path, they will realize that these [elements] are established by their own nature. Thus, having caused them to abandon attachment to external things by showing that "those [elements] exist as established by their own nature," they are introduced to the internal [reality]. Therefore, even that teaching is purposeful. (5–6)

He provides an illustration with the words beginning, "Just as by those seeking the other shore," and so forth. Just as those desiring to reach the far shore of the ocean and the like first diligently rely upon a boat or raft as a vehicle, but having reached the shore, they discard it like a blade of grass; in the very same way, having attained the external sphere, when they obtain that which is internal, they discard the external. This is the meaning, according to the saying: "When the goal is attained, those things which are to be abandoned are called 'means'."

Those jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*) who have previously practiced the non-artificial maṇḍalas and so forth attain the conviction in the non-artificial maṇḍala instantaneously and indeed reach the non-artificial state; this is the distinction. Such a spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is extremely rare. In the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), that lineage is recognized through the gateway of difficult-to-grasp [signs], such as sandalwood and other specific signs (*nimitta*):
"Fire is known by smoke, water by the crane;
the lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known by signs."
Because of this statement. ||7||
Whatever rituals, such as those of the maṇḍala, those with artificial intentions perform—all that is good, and not bad, even though it is clearly undertaken for that purpose. (8)

Just as the Jinas have taught that the Tantra, which proceeds through action, is for the sake of the cognition of reality, so too do the Sages compose that scripture for the sake of verbal knowledge. (9)

In this context, enlightenment (*bodhi*) is simply the thorough knowledge of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). One might suspect that even that which is being cultivated, though unreal, becomes manifest; thus, both the manifest and the unmanifest become causes of enlightenment. Anticipating this, he says: "That which, beginning with the mandala... and so forth. Those of artificial disposition—imagined yogins—who perform the previously mentioned mandalas and so forth either by drawing them or by means of the mind, whether all that be good or bad, when it is being cultivated, it first becomes manifest. The ellipsis of the sentence is: "that is the reality" (*tattvam*). "Even a frog, radiant with a mass of matted hair, grey with ashes..."
He wore a white sacred thread and carried a water-pot slung over his shoulder.
For there is this saying: "Whatever is repeatedly cultivated here by the foolish, that very thing appears before them. (8)

Fearing that the expansion of ritual activity (*karmaprasara*) might not be reality (*tattva*), just like the mandala and other such things, he says: "The expansion of ritual activity," and so forth. Although the Blessed One taught a tantra associated with the expansion of ritual activity that must be accomplished through various efforts, that was not intended as the ultimate reality; rather, it was for the sake of experiencing the innate (*sahaja*) consciousness of the true existent. For those who engage in meditation for the purpose of accomplishing the expansion of ritual activity enter the innate—which is the nature of the supreme space (*paramākāśa*) consisting of the self-established *dharmatā*—precisely by means of that [activity], because they discard its habitual tendencies (*saṃskāra*). Thus, the teaching of those various tantras has that [ultimate goal] as its intention; it is not that they are purposeless. He provides an example: "For the sake of knowledge of words. Just as the external sages compose that treatise on words (*śabdaśāstra*) merely for the thorough understanding of words, yet there is no realization of reality (*tattvāvagati*) in the act of composing it, in exactly the same way, following their karma, they perform the ritual procedures (*prakriyā*) according to the corresponding colors and shapes, like actors or singers, due to the accumulation of merit from previous lives and their spiritual lineage and friends.
In that way, according to their karma, human beings perform their activities;
indeed, having roused affliction through effort, they cause their own minds to run away. (10)
Therefore, in every respect, the ritual procedures for the mandala and so forth do not bring about liberation at all; they are merely a cause of supreme exhaustion.

Due to the absence of correct vows (*samyak-praṇidhāna*), those who have attained the state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) do not become [realizers]; however, those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and other factors would indeed be direct realizers of it. As it has been said:
"Through hearing the sublime Dharma, through attending upon virtuous friends, and due to their spiritual lineage, there is here an eligibility for those who have performed merit in the past."

Not only do they fail to attain reality, but even that which is cultivated through the application of physical exhaustion—being artificial because of the distraction of their own minds—they do not achieve; thus, having fallen away from both, being deluded in their practice, they fall into confusion. For it is said: "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated; with a concentrated mind, one understands suchness as it is. Also, in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*:
"Through the application of the mantra-form, there is neither awakening nor cultivation."
Having reflected, he spoke in brief regarding the characteristics of body, speech, and mind;
one should meditate upon the union with awakening, the samādhi fashioned by mantra.
Regarding such [objections], he says in anticipation of them: "Having roused affliction through effort," and so forth. This is easy to understand.
Buddhahood does not arise from the absence of conceptualization, nor likewise from that which possesses conceptualization;
it occurs for the seekers through perfectly pure thorough knowledge. (12)

Some say: "Buddhahood is attained by resorting to non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), just like the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); for in that state, there is an absence of conceptualizations regarding the defiled and the purified, and Buddhahood consists precisely of that. To this it is replied: "Buddhahood does not arise from the non-conceptual. For such emptiness belongs to the position that eliminates the nature of appearances (*pratibhāsa-maya-rūpa*). Yet Buddhahood is that which abandons both positions; thus, there is a contradiction. Now, if it is argued that the form of a deity produced through the sequence of the Moon-Vajra and so forth, accompanied by the specific conceptualization of the Tathāgata-ego (*ahaṃkāra*), will be the cause for attaining Buddhahood—the author says the following to refute that: "Nor would it arise from that which possesses conceptualization. Even from the cultivation of such a specific mental image, Buddhahood does not result, because there is no difference between a specific and a non-specific conceptualization insofar as both are causes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). And it has been said:
For what difference is there in conceptual construction, whether it be toward the auspicious or the inauspicious?
There is no difference in its nature based on the difference of its substratum, just as there is no difference in the burning power of fire.

And so forth. To the question, "From what, then, would that arise? he says: "By the thorough purity," and so on. That [state] arises from the complete knowledge of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the rest. Since these aggregates and so forth are by their very nature primordially pure as the innate (*sahaja*), which is a synonym for great bliss (*mahāsukha*), therefore neither their separation from nor their conjunction with any phenomenon can be effected—just as space cannot be affected by crows and the like. And it is stated that the mere thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature is the primary cause of that, and nothing else. Furthermore, that [knowledge] depends upon a teacher who provides instruction; everything else is merely a conventional agreement (*samaya*). (12)

Now, one might object: "Since thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) cannot exist without a knower (*parijñātṛ*), how can reality (*tattva*) be non-dual when both are present? To refute this relationship of action and agent, he says: "In its own nature, there is no action," and so forth. "In their own nature, entities possess no action, nor do they possess an agent.
An entity, when divested of the relationship of action and agent, exists in its own nature. (13)

Regarding the action characterized by going, coming, and so forth, there are two positions: is it non-different from the agent who goes, or is it different? In the first case, the agent alone exists, and action does not obtain. In the second case, what belongs to the agent? Since [action] is non-different [from the agent], [the agent would be reduced to nothing]. If their relation exists when that identity is present, then because there is no difference in that identity, the previously mentioned fault remains. If [the relation] were through origination (tadutpatti)—that is, upon the production of the effect—then since the instrument (the agent) has perished, whose is the action? Furthermore, action is held to possess an agent. Among momentary entities, what relation can exist between whom and what? And a relation based on a continuum (*santāna*) is merely imagined, not real, because that continuum lacks existence in the past and other such states.
If cognition exists prior to the object of knowledge, upon what basis could it arise?
If the object of knowledge exists prior to cognition, upon what basis could it arise?
If cognition were simultaneous with the object of knowledge, upon what could it depend for its arising?

Because of this statement, even a relationship established by the nature of cause and effect is not tenable, since the relationship between cause and fruit is unestablished due to its dependence [on other factors]; thus, all this reality is devoid of the relationship of action and agent. Consequently, because of the absence of both a knower and the act of knowing, non-duality alone is established as the ultimate reality (*tattva*). This is demonstrated through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), for even the thorough knowledge of the manifestation of one's own nature (*svarūpa-prakāśa*) sets within that very state—like the breath-wind vanishing when a mirror filled with oil is cast away. It is like the application of a mass of flames to fire when there is no fuel to be burned. That which is non-different from something has that as its essence, just as sweetness is the essence of molasses. And action is invariably connected to an agent. (13)
The essential nature of all distinctions is established within the letter A, like the ocean containing jewels of every form, both inferior and superior.
In the world, conventional practice always prevails; however, in that which is beyond the world, it is the opposite:
one cannot even conceive of its essential nature as either "it exists" or "it does not exist. (15)
For by this very [realization] one attains Buddhahood; by this very [realization] one is liberated. Relying upon the path of intrinsic nature, one is liberated while performing all activities. ||16||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Explanation of One’s Own Nature Preceded by the Worship of the Linga," which consists of the ritual procedures for the artificial mandala, fire-offerings, sacrifice, recitation, and meditative cultivation, as well as the exclusion of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper, within the *Śrī Vasantatilakā*. 1.
The second exposition:

Now, I shall describe the form of one's own deity according to the nature of the body of embodied beings—which consists of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, and is composed of the continuum of form and so forth—by means of another teaching and explanation. (1)
Form is the Buddha Vairocana, while sensation is Vajrasūrya;
perception is Padmanarteśvara, and likewise, mental formations are Vajrarāja. (2)

These formations (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the wholesome, which consist of the diverse emanations of sentient beings produced by the impelling of two individuals, are themselves the King of Vajras (*vajrarāj*) among the Tathāgatas because he rules over them. At the end of the *virama* [joy], he is the Supreme Horse (*paramāśva*), whose intrinsic nature is the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), and not the dark-blue one. (1–2)
Consciousness is Vajrasattva, while the form of sound is Heruka;
the eye is called Mohavajrā, and the ear is designated as Dveṣavajrā. (3)

This consciousness (*vijñāna*) which discerns objects is itself the "indestructible being" (*sattva*) that is indivisible like a diamond; thus he is Vajrasattva. He is Akṣobhya, the Mind-Vajra, characterized by the unification of the two—sentient beings (*sattva*) and passion (*rajas*)—and has the nature of the perfectly pure wisdom of the sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*); he is not, however, an external blue-colored form. Likewise, the form of all five previously mentioned [deities] exists within the one whose essence is the Innate (*sahaja*); he who is the pervasive "possessor of all forms" (*sarvarūpī*) is the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka, the sixth Mahāvajradhara. He should be understood as having the nature of *dharmatā*. As it is said in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*:
In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed as the five Buddhas.
Also, in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa*:
"The aggregates themselves are indeed the Perfectly Awakened Ones, arising from conditions for the sake of enlightenment."
"Those indeed are known as Tathāgatas because of their union with non-dual suchness.
"Let this entire world, whose nature is the five Buddhas, behold the wondrous divine drama,
wherein that one named Great Bliss dances alone with manifold moods."

Also in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*: "Akṣobhya alone is not named; he is devoid of all passion. He is declared to be joined with Śāśvata, a hundred million times over, by the Vajra-holder marked with the vajra."
"It is called Amita and Amitāyu, as far as the limit of space," and so forth.
Likewise, in the *Saṃpuṭa*:
"The three [factors] born of the mother, and likewise the three born of the father."
"This aggregate of the sixty-four thousand consists of the forms of the six Tathāgatas," and so forth.
"The nose is Īrṣyāvajra, and the mouth is known as Rāgavajra;
the body is Mātsaryavajra—these five are the gross deities. (4)
The supreme lord Heruka is indeed all the sense-bases and elements;
the earth element is known as Pātanī, and the water element as Māraṇī. (5)

In order to direct the sense bases (*āyatana*) through the heroes, he says: "The two eyes are called Mohavajra," and so forth. The pair of eyes is Mohavajra; because of its lack of attachment to the object of form (*rūpa*), it brings about other objects by withdrawing from them. Its delusion (*moha*) consists in the cessation of engagement with [ordinary] objects, and therein lies the Vajra—the indivisible, great power arising from the Body Wheel (*kāyacakra*). The faculty of hearing (*śruti*) is the organ of the ear; it is Dveṣavajra, Khaṇḍakapālin, arising from the Mind Wheel (*cittacakra*), because of its capacity for grasping sound and its aversion to other conceptual constructions due to its state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*). (3)

The olfactory faculty is Īrṣyāvajra; from the wheel of speech comes Virūpākṣa. "I alone am the enjoyer of all odors through my entire self; there is no other whatsoever," because of my pervasiveness. The mouth is situated in the mouth; the gustatory faculty is Rāgavajra; from the wheel of speech comes the primordial Aṅkurika. "Touch" refers to the tactile faculty, which is Mātsaryavajra; from the end of the wheel of body comes the hero Vajrasattva, because of his pervasiveness. "All the pleasure of touching the lotuses of the mudrās has been experienced by me alone and not by another"—this is possessiveness (mātsarya). ||4||

The mind-faculty (*manas*) is the sense-base of all [faculties]. Heruka, who is the Vajra-body, should be known as pervading all the faculties from the end of the Mind-wheel (*cittacakra*). Some say there are six universal monarchs:
Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Khagarbha, Lokeśvara, Viṣkambhin, and the glorious Samantabhadra; these are designated by the names of the eye and the other [senses].
The element fire is considered to be Ākarṣaṇī, while Vāyu is regarded as Narteśvarī; the element space is said to be Ruk, and Padmajvālinī is Anākulā.

Because of this statement, these [senses] receive the designation of "heroes" (*vīra*) primarily because they are permeated by great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and not because they are holders of the vajra and vajra-bell, since those are merely conceptual constructs. In the *Śrīsamāja* as well, it is said:
"The sense bases themselves are the maṇḍala of the supreme Bodhisattvas."
Because of this statement.

He speaks of the reality of the elements (*dhātutattva*), beginning with "the one who causes falling" (*pātanī*) and so forth. This earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), which consists of the formation of bones, flesh, and so on, or the wheel of phenomena (*dharmacakra*), or the sensation of solidity during meditative absorption (*samāpatti*)—that is to be known as *Pātanī*, the *Ḍākinī*, the destroyer of conceptual attachment to that [element], whose nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), bliss (*ānanda*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and skillful means (*upāya*). This water element (*abdhātu*), consisting of fluids, blood, and so on, or the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*), or the sensation of fluidity during absorption, or the flame of the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*)—that is to be known as *Māraṇī*, the *Lāmā*, the one who brings about the exhaustion of attachment to that [element], whose nature is signlessness (*animitta*), supreme compassion (*paramakaruṇā*), and aspiration (*praṇidhi*). This fire element (*tejodhātu*), which is the heat in the limbs, or the wheel of enjoyment (*saṃbhogacakra*), or the sensation of lightness during absorption, or the blazing of the fire of gnosis—that is to be known as *Ākarṣaṇī*, the *Khaṇḍarohā*, the shatterer of attachment to that [element], whose nature is wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), the joy of cessation (*viramamuditā*), and power (*bala*). Likewise, this wind element (*vāyudhātu*), characterized by coming and going, contraction and expansion, or the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), or the radiation during absorption, or the entering and exiting, the entering, remaining, and arising, or the movement of the two hundred and sixteen breaths day and night—that is to be known as *Narteśvarī*, the mistress of dance, the mistress of all bodily actions to be accomplished, the embodied one, whose nature is formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*), innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and gnosis (*jñāna*).
These very ones—the action-seal (karmamudrā), the dharma-seal (dharmamudrā), and the pledge-seal (samayamudrā)—are to be understood by me as being designated [by these names]. And it has been said:
"The earth element is called Locanā; the water element is known as Māraṇī;
fire is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; and wind is proclaimed to be Tārā."
Thus, in the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa* as well:
"The letter E is to be known as the earth, while Locanā is the action-seal (*karmamudrā*)," and so forth.
Likewise:
"By the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, the earth is born there"—
in this way, the body of embodied beings consists of the deities of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth.

Having understood pleasure, suffering, as well as karma, the afflictions, and so forth, and by relying on [the nature of] arising and ceasing, one shall attain both cyclic existence and nirvana. ||7||

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Description of the Forms of the Deities Vairocana and Others as They Truly Exist, Which is the Body of the Tathāgata Consisting of the Aggregates, Elements, and Sense-Bases," in the *Śrīvasantatilakā*.
Thus it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:

Likewise, this element of space (*ākāśadhātu*)—whether it be the vacuity of all the channels (*nāḍī*), the vacuity of the doors of the sense organs, or the space of the pores of the skin—is to be known as the one named Padmajvālinī Vārāhī, the mistress of the network of channels within the lotus. She is untainted by the stains of attachment to that [lotus], transcends the conceptual constructions of subject and object, and pervades the four aforementioned elements. And it is said:
"Abiding in the form of the element of space, she is remembered as Khecarī."
Also in the *Vajrapañjara*: "By means of the interior of all elements," so it is said.
And from the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa*: "In this [reality] whose sole intrinsic nature is space, the Great Sage dwelt. (5–6)

He states the conclusion with the words "In this way," and so forth. By this principle, the body of all embodied beings dwelling within the three realms—the aggregates (*skandhas*) and the rest—should be understood as being of the nature of the deity, not as something external possessed of a face, arms, and so on. Therefore, whatever exists within the basket of the aggregates—such as pleasure, pain, afflictions, karma, arising, and cessation—all these are of the very nature of the deity because they are non-different from it. For this very reason, that which is *saṃsāra* is itself *nirvāṇa*; there is no difference whatsoever between the two. ||7||
Thus concludes the detailed commentary on the second instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, the manual for the means of accomplishment of the *Niṣpannakrama* within the *Vasantatilakā*. 2.
The third exposition:

Now, I shall explain the classification of the gateways according to the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior [states] pertaining to the body, speech, and mind of a certain Tathāgata’s body. ||1||

Furthermore, it is said: "The body is the palace, the self is the deity, the mind is the image, and the breath is the wind. By means of these four, one should worship the Lord of the Mandala. The meaning is that one should worship the Lord of the Mandala by means of these four. Also, it is said: "The body is the palace, the self is the deity, the mind is the image, and the breath is the wind. By means of these four, one should worship the Lord of the Mandala. The meaning is that one should worship the Lord of the Mandala by means of these four. Moreover, it is said: "The body is the palace, the self is the deity, the mind is the image, and the breath is the wind. By means of these four, one should worship the
Having become twelve times doubled, he is surrounded on all sides by a host of hero-yoginīs, with threads on both flanks.
"This skeleton in the form of a staff is Heruka, the supreme support;
it is called the stūpa of the Buddhas of the aggregates, elements, and so forth.
Thus, the inferior bodily door is gross and fashioned by the deity.
Furthermore, another fourfold gate is known as the intermediate vocal [gate]. ||3||
Also in the *Śrīvajraḍāka*:
"Just as a house is supported effortlessly by a great pillar,
so too this body with its nine gates is supported by the skeletons alone."

Alternatively: The *avadhūtī* is like a single pillar (*ekastambha*) because it supports the entire network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*); thus, by virtue of being joined with this, it is "single-pillared. In the center of the navel is the great wheel (*mahācakra*), woven with sixteen threads;
it is joined with the letter *A* through the application of the *saṃpuṭīkāra* method.
"Established there in the center as the very nature of the support of all, that great queen, acting as a pillar, is celebrated as the *adhūtī*.

Thus [ends the verse]. "The nine gates," etc., is the brief enumeration (*uddeśa*). He states the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*): "Furthermore, what is it like? It has nine streams," and so forth. That which possesses nine streams—namely, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the secret place, and the anus—is described as such. Furthermore, each individual gate is proclaimed to be ninefold. For instance, regarding the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), [there are the elements of] earth, water, fire, air, and space...

There are nine divisions because [the body] is endowed with consciousness and mental factors that are wholesome, unwholesome, or both. This should be inferred in other cases as well. Furthermore, these possess the nature of the five Buddhas and the four Yoginīs. Thus, it should be understood that each door is joined with a maṇḍala wheel consisting of nine aspects. In this way, although there are ninety-nine doors, the body arises with eighty-one doors. It should be realized that those which are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) from these are also indeed Tathāgatas. ||2||

To that end, he says: "The inferior bodily door is gross and created by the deity. This very bodily door, which is ninefold along with its equipment, is *adharma* because it appears as a reflected image (*pratibhāsa*); and it is *adharma* because it manifests in an external form. Furthermore, it is not [inferior] due to being base, but rather because it carries its own natural outflow (*svaniṣpanda*). Therefore:
"The fiery, the airy, the Māhendra, and likewise the Vāruṇa [doors], situated above, on the sides, across, and below, exist through the movement of the mind within the wheel. (4)

Thus, the gross [door] is possessed of form in relation to the other doors. Because it has the nature of the previously mentioned ninefold assembly of Tathāgatas and goddesses, it is "created by the deities" (*daivatanirmita*).
He speaks of the door of speech: "another," and so forth, is the enumeration. Because it exists between body and mind, the middle door of speech should be known as fourfold. ||3||

He states the explanation, beginning with "āgneyam" (pertaining to fire), and so forth. Here, there exist four channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*)—known as those of Fire, Wind, Mahendra, and Varuṇa—which reside respectively in the throat, the navel, the secret place, and the heart. They have the forms of Padmanarteśvara, Paramāśva, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Akṣobhya; they are of the nature of Khaṇḍarohā, Rūpiṇī, Lāmā, and Ḍākinī; they move slowly through the right, left, and both [channels]; they are red, green, yellow, and white in color according to the distinction of the primary qualities (*guṇa*); they are mutually fourfold in number; they carry two thousand one hundred and sixty breaths through twenty-four movements of entry and so forth day and night; they are self-evident to all embodied beings; and within them, the movement, activity, and the process of coming and going of consciousness (*vijñāna*), which rides upon the wind, is experienced at every moment. These alone are the gates of speech. From these very channels, which are joined by the openings of the left, right, and middle channels, the Blessed Lady, the Mother of Syllables (*varṇamātṛkā*), arises. Because cause and effect are non-different, her "mouth" is simply the locus of her manifestation. And those entries and so forth belong to Fire and the others. How so? He says: "ūrdhva" (upward), and so forth. In order: the circle of Fire proceeds upward, because the eaters of oblations (*havirbhuj*) blaze upward. The gate of the circle of Wind flows from the two sides, because the wind moves in a curved path. The [circle] of Mahendra flows straight and clear, because of its evenness. The [circle] of Varuṇa flows downward, because water moves only downward. And it has been said:
The ray emerging from the south is that mandala of the fire-god;
it is clearly red in color, and its presiding deity is Padmanātha.
The third door is mental, distinguished by the moon and the sun; through entering and exiting, this indeed becomes the supreme door. (5)
The primary supreme door is proclaimed to be both below and above;
through the lower door comes discernment, and through the upper door, the elements.
"Stable, with slow movement, and resembling a white kunda flower or the moon—this is indeed the mandala of Varuṇa; Vajranātha is the deity here.
Thus it is said regarding each of the four directions. Furthermore, concerning the four [other] directions:
"The four directions are upward, sideways, straight, and downward.
Also in the *Sampuṭa*:
"In the southeast, the northwest, the northeast, and likewise the southwest."
"By the movement of the mind, there is upward, lateral, straight, and downward motion. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa*:
"In the south-eastern, the north-western, the eastern (Māhendra), and likewise the western (Vāruṇa) [directions]..."
By means of the movement of the mind, one effects upward, lateral, straight, and downward motion.
Among them, the fourth yoga is their mutual deity. Thus [ends verse 4].

He speaks of the door of the mind (*cittadvāra*): it is the third, in relation to the doors of body and speech. "Mental" means accessible by the mind alone. How so? "By the distinction of moon and sun. The moon and sun flow through the two channels, the left and the right, by way of two distinct paths. They flow upward by the sequence of the winds and downward by the sequence of substances, due to the carrying of the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, semen, and blood. Therefore, because it is accessible only through subtle yoga, it is the supreme door. Thus he says: "by entry and exit. This refers to the entry and exit of *prāṇa* and *apāna* upward, and of the two substances downward. Alternatively, "downward" is from entry, and "upward" is from exit. This is the supreme door. He states by which door the activity of each occurs: "by the lower door," and so forth.
The Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, abide moving within the upper gate;
their establishment is below, while their departure is by way of the upper [gate]. (7)

Through the lower gate, by way of the path called *lalana*, distinguished gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), known as great bliss (*mahāsukha*), proceeds; for when the two [channels] proceed below, there is the arising of the innate (*sahaja*) due to the manifestation of the spring season. Through the upper gate, known as *rasanā*, the elements whose nature is earth and so forth—the impurities such as the eyes—manifest, because they have the form of a cremation ground with its moist odors and so on. Alternatively, through the lower gate, the pentad of aggregates beginning with consciousness manifests within the bodies of embodied beings, because the pentad of aggregates is inward-facing. Through the upper gate, the elements beginning with earth—the five great elements—are born, because they are outward-facing. ||5-6||

Likewise, these six bodies of active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñānakāya*), such as the visual consciousness and so forth, which have the Buddhas Vairocana and others as their intrinsic nature, move and proceed through the upper gate in order to grasp the six objects, such as form and so forth. The entry and abiding of their respective object-deities—whose desires are fully satisfied—is experienced through the lower gate. Once they have entered within, they are emitted again through the upper gate for the sake of enjoying their own deities; this is the remaining sense. Alternatively, the consciousness, endowed with distinguished gnosis (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), proceeds from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) through the lower gate by way of the *lalanā* and other channels to reach the calyx of the lotus. Drawn back upward by the power of yoga, that very [consciousness] generates the twenty-four elements, which cause the extreme nourishment of the elements, within the four primary seats (*pīṭha*). And it has been said:
[She is] beautiful with a brilliance like that of the sun in full bloom,
marked by the rays of the newly risen, perfectly full moon upon the summit of the peak [of Mount Meru], which has a pericarp formed by a dense mass of filaments.

Though the bee is conversant with the essences of various flower-nectars, it approaches during the great festival of midnight and, with its mind fixed solely on that [lute], drinks its sound; this is indeed a marvel! For its resonance flows in fast, slow, and medium tempos.
The moon rises and again goes to its setting; from there it once more reaches the crest of the mountain of sunrise.
Yet, when one gazes upon both its ends, neither the moon nor the sun truly shines.
The sun rises within the heart of a lotus petal, and the moon dissolves even from its mountain peak;
the fire of universal dissolution ascends upward, while Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun from below.
Through the movements of coming and going in the form of invocation and so forth, the perfectly awakened ones of the three times are the ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga. (8)
In both engagement and withdrawal, by virtue of their inherent nature as qualities and defects, pleasure and pain are established as having the nature of co-nascence. (9)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Explanation of the Different Doors of the Tathāgata’s Body Consisting of the Aggregates, Elements, and Bases," in the *Śrīvasantatilakā*. ॥३॥
The closing of the eyes, which are like lotuses upon a bed of water-lilies, comes first;
then follows the closing of the two lotuses that are the thunderbolt and the water-born flower.
Instantly, through the friction of the seed-syllable of the practitioner, the triad reaches the fourth sky—
a state that consumes time by means of the series of digits of the imperishable abode, which is innate.

If the realization obtained from the mouth of a well-trained Vajravilāsinī guru has been attained, then he who possesses that [realization] reaches the definitive certainty regarding the superior, middling, and inferior; he is a knower of reality. Thus [ends verse 7].

Therefore, he says: "Invoking," and so forth. By means of this distinction between the upper and lower gates, there are the summoning (*āhvāna*) and dismissal (*visarjana*) in the form of going and coming. In that form, all the Buddhas of the three times reside in the three wheels; they are the twenty-four heroes (*vīra*) who are the nature of the *dhātu*, with Śrī Heruka as the twenty-fifth. Likewise, there are the twenty-eight Ḍākinīs residing in the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body; they are the Yoginīs within the channels (*nāḍī*) such as Abhedyā and so on, whose nature is the channels by way of the doors of the eyes and other senses. These are the accomplished heroes (*siddhavīra*).

The Sahajayoginīs are established. Alternatively, he shows the distinction that these are established as "innately accomplished" (*sahajasiddhāḥ*), meaning they are established by their very nature (*svabhāvasiddhāḥ*) and are not merely conceptual constructs. How so? Activity and cessation, arising and destruction, emergence and entry, concentration and non-concentration, qualities and defects, the auspicious and inauspicious, affliction and purification, and pleasure and pain—which consists of the nature of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) such as the agreeable and disagreeable—all this, proceeding through the three gateways, is to be known as the innately accomplished nature of the Vīras and Yoginīs. (8–9)

Thus concludes the detailed commentary on the third instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment through the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 3.
The Fourth Exposition:
Now, I shall demonstrate the ten stages, beginning with the Pīṭha, of a certain Tathāgata-body. ||1||
The channels leading to the nine streams are situated at the nine gates;
the tenth, however, is located in the middle of the *bhaga*, and it is the most excellent among them. (2)
Beginning from the location of the forehead, there is the determination of the wheel of the syllable *haṃ*;
thirty-two streams of bodhicitta flow there day and night. (3)

Having established the circle of deities residing at the three gates, he says "Now," and so forth, in order to demonstrate their abiding according to the sequence of the ten stages beginning with the *pīṭhas*. The meaning stated is that this occurs immediately after the designation of the gates. "Of any one" means of whichever body of a Tathāgata it may be, which is common to all sentient beings, and not merely my own. The connection is: "I shall show the locations beginning with the *pīṭhas*. (1)

Thus it is said: "The nine channels of the streams," and so forth. Those channels which reside within the nine streams—the previously mentioned gateways of the body—and which consist of the nine deities, as well as the tenth, the *avadhūtī* located in the center of the *bhaga* starting from the head; these very ones are called the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. The sense is: when that experience is seen within oneself through the vision of truth (*satyadarśana*), what then is the use of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth, which must be accomplished through great effort? ||2||

Having described the *bhūmis*, he speaks of the locations situated within those *bhūmis*—beginning with "the forehead" and so forth. Here, in this body, starting from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) at the forehead, the determination—that is, the ascertainment—of the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) is to be known. Likewise, those [channels] located therein are remembered as existing both externally and internally in the form of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so on;
namely, the eight yoginīs beginning with Khecarī, as well as others who are Bhūcarīs. (4)
And all those who dwell in the subterranean realms (pātāla) are likewise established within them, according to the distinctions of their various locations in the wheels of body, speech, and mind. 5.
The ten stages, beginning with the *pīṭhas*, are divided into twenty-four types;
though they abide as the innate (*sahaja*), they are differentiated according to their respective locations and essential natures.

These thirty-two [channels] extend from the enjoyment [wheel] and so forth, because the crown wheel (*uṣṇīṣacakra*) is the root of the body-tree; for this very reason, the body-tree has its branches below. Furthermore, there are four downward-facing [channels] in the four limbs—hands and feet; three on the sides and the back; and six in the heart wheel. There are three chains of binding channels for the stūpa of the four wheels. Thus is the determination of the channel-wheels starting from the forehead and so forth. These thirty-two are the Yoginīs, who carry the drops of bodhicitta equal in number to them. They themselves are the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapāla and others, the great heroes such as Vajracaṇḍa and others, and Śrī Heruka as the vajra-maṇḍala. To that end, he says: "They flow," and so forth. (3)

These [energies] reside in the external bodily gateways—namely, the regions such as Jālandhara and so forth—which correspond to the various states of putrid odor and the like, as well as in the internal twenty-four *pīṭhas* such as Śrī and others. He explains their division with the words "the sky-farers" (*khecarya*) and so on: starting from Pullīra and ending at Mālava, those channels (*nāḍīs*) are the sky-farers; starting from Kāmarūpa and ending at the Himalayas, they are the earth-farers (*bhūcarya*); starting from Pretapurī and ending at Kulatā, they are the dwellers of the underworld (*pātālavāsinī*). Due to the divisions of the upper, middle, and lower parts of the body, these twenty-four, beginning with the sky-farers, are established upon the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Furthermore, within their constituent parts and at the gateways, the channels whose intrinsic nature is that of Kākāsyā and the others are situated. (4–412)
These very stages beginning with Muditā have been fully described;
they are the abode of the Bodhisattvas whose nature consists of the faculties and so forth. (7)
The ālaya is the foundation of all Buddhas, specifically of the aggregates and so forth; it is the supreme bringer of Buddhahood for both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. (8)

This is what he says: "Body, speech, and mind," and so forth. "Based on the distinctions of other locations" means based on the distinctions of the head and so on; the ellipsis of the sentence is "they abide. Therefore, these twenty-four [sites] beginning with the *pīṭhas*, which are the channels (*nāḍīs*) in the form of the supported (*ādheya*), as well as the ten channels that serve as their support and are of the nature of the ground (*bhūmi*), exist according to the nature of their respective locations. "According to the nature of the location" (*yathāsthāna-svarūpeṇa*) means not transgressing the location. Whichever location belongs to whichever yoginī, in that very location there is for her an innate abiding (*sahaja-sthiti*), not an imagined one. (5–6)

These very ten stages, beginning with the Joyful (*pramuditā*), have been taught by me. Among them: the head, the crown-lock (*śikhā*), the right ear, and the back constitute the *pīṭha*, which is the seat of the *bodhicitta*. That itself is the Joyful stage, because it generates the three joys through the sequence of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth. The left ear, the space between the eyebrows, the eyes, and the roots of the arms constitute the *upapīṭha* (near-seat), being close to the *pīṭha*. That itself is the Stainless (*vimalā*), because the stains of conceptualization are burned away by the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*). The armpits and breasts are the *kṣetra* (field), because the *bodhicitta* is sprinkled there under the guise of one’s own milk. That itself is the Luminous (*prabhākarī*), because from beholding that, the light of joy arises in the mind. The navel and the tip of the nose are the *upakṣetra* (near-field), because the *bindu* and *siṅghāṇa* are conveyed there. That itself is the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*), because it illuminates the fire of gnosis. The mouth and throat are the *chandoha*, because the inclination (*chanda*) toward enjoyment resides there. That itself is the Very Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), because it is impossible to turn back from the flavors. The heart and the genitals are the *upachandoha*, because they are averse to the digestion of food and the comprehension of meaning. That itself is the Facing (*abhimukhī*), because it faces toward that limit and toward digestion. The secret organ and the anus are the *melāpaka* (meeting-place), because of the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), the merging therein, and the unification of the channels (*nāḍī*). That itself is the Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgamā*), because of the remoteness resulting from the refinement of those channels. The thighs and shanks are the *upamelāpaka*, because of the merging of even the two previously mentioned [locations]. That itself is the Immovable (*acalā*), because that yoga is irreversible. The fingers and the backs of the feet are the *śmaśāna* (cemetery), because they consist of all the *pīṭhas* and because of the experience of the state beyond conceptualization. That itself is the Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), because the "excellent" (*sādhu*), namely selflessness (*nairātmya*), is present there.
When the thirty-two types of bodhicitta reach fullness here, then Buddhahood will be near for the Buddhas together with their spiritual sons. ||9||
Buddhahood resides within one's own body alone, and nowhere else;
those obscured by ignorance believe that Buddhahood exists apart from the body. (10)

The thumbs and knees are the *upaśmaśāna*, as before. That very [stage] is the *dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma), because it rains like a cloud through the upward flow (*ūrdhvasrotas*) of the stable marrow that supports the Dharma; or it is the end of the application of rain, being free from disease. Thus are the twenty-four seats (*pīṭha*) comprised within the ten stages (*bhūmi*). These very [seats] are the ten stages themselves, through the sequence of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth, as knowledge increases in its successive stages.

To whom do those ten stages belong? He says: "The *ālaya*, etc. Those Bodhisattvas who have the nature of the six faculties, such as the eye, and likewise those Buddhas previously explained who have the form of the aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with form—those stages belong to them. They are called "stages" (*bhūmi*) because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas exist within them by way of their own nature. For this very reason, they bring about Buddhahood not only for the Noble Ones (*ārya*), but even for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); for those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have the nature of the aggregates and the faculties also bring about Buddhahood for them, since in reality there is no difference between the Tathāgata and an ordinary person. (7–8)

One might object: "Since enlightenment is attained only after three incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), how can the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth be fully awakened? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The thirty-two," and so on. When the fullness of the thirty-two [deities of] the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is experienced within the mouth of the thunderbolt (*dambholi*) or in the lap of the lotus-born (*payoja-kroḍa*), then Buddhahood is present—meaning near—to them. The distinction is that it does not depend upon time. ||9||

Now, one might raise the objection: "We exist in the human state, whereas the Buddhas abide in Buddha-fields such as Abhirati in the form of the mandala of gnosis; how then can enlightenment be near? To dispel this doubt, he says: "In one's own body alone," and so forth. Because of the realization of one's own nature, one is a Buddha (*buddha*); the state of being that is *buddhatva*. That is established and situated in one's own body alone. For this very reason, that [body] itself is the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*), because the innate Buddha (*sahaja-buddha*), which is established by nature, abides right here. It is not elsewhere, such as in Abhirati and other realms. Therefore, for ordinary people (*prākṛta*)—those who exist in nature (*prakṛtau bhavāḥ*)—Buddhahood is not found elsewhere, in external places.
The pīṭha, the upapīṭha, the kṣetra, and the upakṣetra, as well as the chandoha and likewise the upacchandoha. ||11||
Likewise, there are the *melāpaka* and the *upamelāpaka*, as well as the *śmaśāna* and *upaśmaśāna*; these, along with the *pīṭhas* and so forth, constitute the ten stages (*bhūmis*). ||12||

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Description of the Nature of the Grounds, such as the Ten Seats and the Channels Located within the Center of the Nine Orifices of the Tathāgata’s Body," in the *Śrī-Vasantatilakā*. 4.

Just as they were born, so too do they remain; however, those of developed intellect do not hold this view. Rather, by those who know the realization of the *niṣpannakrama* (completion stage), Buddhahood is held to be established by its very nature (*svabhāvasiddhatvena*), because of the scriptural statement: "This entire world has the five Buddhas as its essence. Furthermore, the indeterminate speculations such as "Does the Tathāgata exist after death? are rejected, because of the *Hevajra* statement: "There is not a single being who is unenlightened; there is a perfectly enlightened one for each and every one" (2473). Master Vajrapāṇi also said: "Men have the form of Vajradhara, and women are Vajrayoṣits. In the *Tathāgataguhya-sūtra* as well, it is said: "The activities of body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings are the secret of the three families. Jñānapāda also stated: "Whatever actions of body, speech, and mind in such a state of mind are expressed by all the Buddhas take the form of mudrās and mantras. (10)
He states the names of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) previously mentioned—beginning with *pīṭha* and *upapīṭha*—and their etymologies have been explained previously. (11–12)

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the fourth instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment through the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 4.
The Fifth Exposition:

Now, I shall describe the division of locations according to the distinctions between various sites situated within the wheels of body, speech, and mind—corresponding to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and perfections (*pāramitā*)—within the nature of the channels located in the midst of the nine openings of a certain Tathāgata’s body. (1)
The head is the land of Malaya, while the crest-lock is Jālandhara;
likewise, Oḍiyāna is said to be the right ear. (2)

Now, with the words "Then of another... and so forth, he states—following the sequence of brief mention (*uddeśa*) and detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*)—the names of the previously mentioned twenty-four seats (*pīṭha*) in grammatical apposition with the directions beginning with the head, as well as the nature of the channels (*nāḍī*) situated therein as being *khecarī* and so on. From "Then" up to "I shall explain," the brief mention is easy to understand. ||1||

He provides the description beginning with "The head is the Malaya region," and so forth. In this context, *malaya* refers to that in which the *bodhicitta*—the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the non-duality of the conventional and ultimate truths—is dissolved (*liyate*); such a place is the *malayadeśa*. The head is the *malayadeśa*, because that [bliss] exists precisely there. The root of the network of channels (*nāḍījāla*) is *jālandhara*; it is the crest-lock (*śikhā*) because it is the gate for its restraint. *Uḍḍiyāna* is the right ear, because through the path of the left ear, the *caṇḍālī* travels by way of the *khecarī* movement into that which is called *oḍa*, which is the external departure; thus, it is *uḍḍiyāna*. Through these two—the female messengers (*dūtī*) of vowels and consonants—and by means of the union with the three seals (*mudrā*), one experiences non-conceptual bliss due to the piercing of the staff of the Lord of the Karmic Winds (*karmamāruteśvara*). This is *arbuda*, the back of the head; the substitution of *da* for *ha* occurs according to the rule for words beginning with *pṛṣodara*.
Arbuda is in the region of the back; these four are known as the *pīṭhas*.
Likewise, Godāvarī should be understood as having the form of the left ear. (3)
Rāmeśvara is likewise renowned in the space between the eyebrows, while Devīkoṭṭa is in the eyes; and Mālava is at the base of the arms. ||4||
Thus, these upapīṭhas are established within the citta-cakra;
they are declared to be the specific locations of the khecarīs. (5)

By the logic previously stated, these four should be known as the *pīṭhas*. They are the spheres (*gocara*), that is, the objects, of the four *khecarīs*—the channels located therein named Pracaṇḍā and so forth—and they are of four kinds by virtue of their nature as supports (*ādhāra*) through their similarity to the *ūṣmas* and other [factors]. Furthermore, they are the stage of *muditā* (joy), characterized by the experience of a special delight through the experience of the bliss of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). ||2-212||

*Gāṃ* refers to the *bhuvana-bhū-svabhāva*, the *nirmāṇacakra*. Because it is chosen (*vriyate*) or covered (*cchādyate*) by that [channel], it is *godā*; thus *godā* is *avadhūtī*. Because it is pervaded by her, the left ear is *godāvarī*. Both *rāmā* and *rāmā* are the two *rāme*s—the eyebrows, which have the nature of the *lalanā* and *rasanā*. That which possesses lordship (*īśvaratva*) over the flame of knowledge between those two is the *bhrūmadhya*, the *ūrṇākoṣa*. The fortress (*koṭṭa*) of that very goddess is here the *devīkoṭṭa*; because one attains that, the two eyes are its locus. Likewise, the two roots and the two shoulders within the arms—that is, the two upper arms—is precisely *mālava*. It is called *mālava* because of the cutting (*lavana*) or severing of the "garlands" (*mālā*), which are the heterogeneous conceptual constructions; such is the experience. These are the secondary sites (*upapīṭhas*). They should be known as the spheres of activity (*gocara*)—the objects—of the sky-faring goddesses (*khecarīs*) residing there, whose natures are Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā. Thus ends the *cittacakra*. (3–5)
The two armpits are considered Kāmarūpa, and the two breasts are proclaimed as Odra;
these are designated as the fields (kṣetra), while the navel is considered Triśakuni.
Kośala is the tip of the nose, and that is called its *upakṣetra*; Kaliṅga is said to be the mouth, while Lampāka is in the middle of the throat. (7)
The place renowned as Chandoha is said to be the heart; Kāñcī is called the genitals, and Himālaya is likewise the Upacchandoha.

The two armpits and the two breasts are, respectively, *kāmarūpa*—that which possesses desirable form and appearance—and *oḍra*. Because it causes [the winds] to ascend (*ūrdhvagamana*) and receives (*rāti*) them, it is called *caṇḍālī*; thus, the two breasts are *oḍra*. These two, by the previously stated method, are the *kṣetra* (field). The navel and the tip of the nose are the two *triśakunikośala*. Where there are three birds (*triśakuni*)—meaning the channels of body, speech, and mind which resemble birds and have the shape of bird-beaks—that is the navel-center, because it has the nature of a vajra-knot (*vajragranthi*). Likewise, because it flows (*salati*) with the *siṅghāṇa* (nasal mucus), it is *kośala*, the tip of the nose. These should be understood as the *upakṣetra* (subsidiary field) according to the sequence mentioned before. (6–612)

The face and throat are Kaliṅga and Lampāka. It is called Kaliṅga because it "marks" (liṅgayati) or brings about bliss (kaṃ); for at the time of service, bliss arises simply from the sight of it. Likewise, the tongue is Lampāka because it is "greedy" (lampaṭā) for tasting the nectar of the uvula (lambikā), and thus, through that connection, the throat is Lampāka. By the previously mentioned explanation, these two are called a *cchandoha*. The heart and the genitals—thus all the locations are established within the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*).
These are declared to be the specific sites of the Bhūcarīs. (9)
The Pretādhivāsinī is at the linga, while the Gṛhadevatā is at the anus;
these two are declared to be the Melāpaka, and the thighs are said to be Saurāṣṭra.

Kāñcī and Himālaya. To explain: *kaṃ* (the letter *ka*) signifies that which attains (*añcati*), goes to, or rushes toward happiness (*sukha*). It is like the flower of the plantain tree (*kadali*) because it is endowed with a tube (*nālīkā*) for the daughters of Māra, which has the form of the syllable *hūṃ*, from which drops of nectar flow downward while hanging. *Hima-varṇa* (snow-colored) refers to the *bodhicitta*; because it is the abode (*āspada*) of that, the *meḍhra* (penis) is called *Himālaya*. *Upachandoha* is as before. By the words "in this way" (*ity evam*) and so forth, these places are to be known as the locations of the terrestrial goddesses (*bhūcarī*) residing there—namely Airāvatī, Mahābhairavā, Vāyuvegā, Surābhakṣī, Śyāmādevī, Subhadrā, Hayakarṇā, and Khagānanā. They are called "terrestrial" (*bhūcarī*) because they reside within the center of the body. (7–9)

Likewise, the *liṅga* is twofold: feminine (*strīliṅga*) and masculine (*pulliṅga*). It is the same in the case of the anus as well. These two should be known respectively as the city of the *pretas* (*pretapurī*) and the house-deity (*gṛhadevatā*). To explain: the city of the five *pretas*, which are the [five] spaces, is like a city; that pair of banners is the *pretapurī*. The deity of the house—that is, the body—is Vairocana, the house-deity, who is the fecal constituent (*viḍdhātu*); because it is the support for that, the anus is the house-deity. These two should be known respectively as being designated "the meeting place" (*melāpaka*), due to their union at the time of *samāpatti* between the pair of banners and the path of downward breath (*apānamārga*).

Likewise, the two thighs and the two shanks should be understood as Saurāṣṭra and Suvarṇadvīpa respectively. To explain: the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*) of bliss (*saukhya*) is the pair of thighs, which are mutually [connected] during the vision of the distinguished time. Similarly, the island (*dvīpa*) of the mind—which possesses a very white luster like gold—is the pair of shanks; this should be understood as a meeting point (*upamelāpaka*), as before.

Likewise, the eight toes and the back of the foot are to be known as the City (nagara) and the River (sindhu). Because they do not move, the toes are "non-movers" (*naga*); hence, because there is no further extension beyond them, it is the City. From the back of the foot to the big toe, because the *bodhicitta* vibrates there, the back of the foot is the River. These two, by the logic previously stated, constitute the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
The two thighs are renowned as being called Suvarṇadvīpa.
Furthermore, the Upamelāpaka is remembered as being in the fingers, while the City is in the [toes]. (11)
Sindhu is indeed the top of the foot, which is declared to be the cremation ground (śmaśāna);
the big toe is called Maru, and Kulūtā is said to be the knee. (12)
This cremation ground is indeed the ten stages beginning with the *pīṭhas*;
all these are born from one's own body and are differentiated according to the distinction of their locations. (13)
The ten stages of the Buddhas, existing both externally and internally, are divided into twenty-four types within the wheels of body, speech, and mind. (14)

The big toe and the knees are to be known as *maru* and *kulatā*. Because of the sounding (*ravaṇa*)—that is, the roaring—of this Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is *maru*; because of the cutting away (*lavana*) of false conceptualizations, it is *kulatā*. These two are called, respectively, the *upaśmaśāna* (near-cemetery) as before. These ten stages are the *pīṭha*s and so forth; they are designated by the terms *pīṭha* and so on. (10–1212)

"Born in one's own body" (*svadehajā*) means born together with one's own body through the sequence of the ten months; they are not, however, to be attained through the sequence of the path of vision (*dṛṅmārgakrama*). Furthermore, these are differentiated according to the distinction of their locations, as has been largely stated. For this very reason, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are spoken of by combining the nine external doors with the single internal one. To whom do these stages belong? To the "Buddhas"—that is, those whose nature consists solely of gnosis (*jñāna*), having the form of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and so forth. Alternatively, the "Buddhas" are the heroes (*vīra*) who take the form of the twenty-four elements (*dhātu*); and the "Buddhas" are the twenty-four channels (*nāḍī*), beginning with Abhedya. When the single remainder is taken, the sense is that these ten stages are the innate (*sahaja*) ones of the heroes and yoginīs, and are neither conceptualized (*kalpita*) nor something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). (13–13½)

To show that these stages belong not only to the Noble Ones (āryas) but also to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), he says: “In the wheels of mind, speech, and body,” and so forth. According to the sequences previously mentioned, the twenty-four distinct locations within the wheels of the mind and other factors situated in the body have been fully described as the locations of all the channels (nāḍīs).
In these locations, the ḍākinīs reside in the form of the channels. (15)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the exposition on the distinctions of the seats and the ten stages, in the *Śrīvasantatilakā*. 5.

Even among all embodied beings—whether they be footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—these ten stages exist in the form of channels (*nāḍī*); for in reality, all sentient beings indeed possess mastery over these stages. (14–15)

Thus concludes the detailed explanation of the fifth instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, the manual for the means of accomplishment through the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 5.
The sixth exposition:
Now, I shall briefly indicate the wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*) situated according to its proper location within the body of a certain Tathāgata. (1)
Within the center of one's own heart is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
situated in its center is a channel whose nature is like a blazing fire.
Resembling a plantain flower, it hangs suspended with its face turned downward;
in its center stands the Hero, about the size of a mustard seed. (3)

Now, in order to demonstrate that the very wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) situated within one’s own body possesses the nature of all the ḍākinīs residing in the [various] wheels, and that its presiding lord has the essence of the naturally accomplished mantra, he says "atha" and so forth to introduce the sixth chapter. "Of any one" means of that which resides within the realm of all sentient beings. "Of the Tathāgata-body" is as explained previously; or, it refers to that which consists of the deities of the ninefold [mandala], by virtue of having the aggregates (skandha) and so forth as its nature. "In their respective places" means without transgressing the proper locations. "The wheel of channels itself is the host of yoginīs. "We shall indicate" means we shall explain; this is the brief statement (uddeśa). ||1||

In that regard, he describes the abiding of the Lord in the form of mantra with the words "situated in the center of the heart," and so forth. Here, within the hearts of all embodied beings, there exists a wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) consisting of eight petals, complete with filaments at the pericarp of the wheel of phenomena (*dharmacakra*), whose intrinsic nature is the purification of the eight watches of the day. In its center is the one named *Trivṛtā*, which has the nature of oil and fire, is downward-facing, and resembles the flower of the plantain tree. In the middle of that, emitting drops resembling morning dew-drops falling from a mass of sunbeams, is the syllable *HŪṂ*, the size of a minute mustard seed; it is called "unstruck" (*anāhata*) because it cannot be articulated, and it is a "hero" (*vīra*) because it has emerged from all conceptual constructions and fears. That very [syllable] is...
The syllable HŪṂ is the unstruck seed-syllable, flowing like snow;
it is renowned as Vasanta, the delighter in the hearts of embodied beings. (4)
Vārāhī, in the form of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), is known as Tilakā; shaken by Karmamātṛtanī, she blazes within the circle of the navel.
Having attained spring, she is satisfied and abides in meditative absorption;
this is the hero Śrī Heruka, known as Vasantatilakā. (6)

Because he generates joy in the hearts of all embodied beings, like the spring season, the Blessed One Śrī Heruka should be known as "Vasanta" (the Spring); however, he is not the four-faced, twelve-armed [Brahmā]. (2–4)

This fire of knowledge, resembling the submarine fire (*vāḍavāgni*), ignited by the wind of action characterized by the friction of churning, blazing from the region of the navel and ascending through the upper path, touches that Hero residing in the heart with a torrential downpour of the streams of its nectar; thus, through non-dual union and absorption, it is called *Vasantatilakā*. (5–5½)

Therefore, he says: "This Śrī," and so forth. This *hūṃ* syllable, which has been described with the characteristics previously mentioned, is indeed Śrī Heruka. Jñajvālā, moreover, is called the *tilaka* (forehead mark) of Vajravārāhī. She herself, having assumed the previously mentioned form of the Yoginī—red in color—remains within the world consisting of the moving and the unmoving (*sacarācara*), that is, the animate and the inanimate. Likewise, that very Blessed Lady (*bhagavatī*), divided by the distinctions of body and so forth, manifests through the three gates of inferior, middling, and superior, and performs the acts of going, coming, and abiding in fifteen ways. The meaning is not only that she is thus, but that she is established within every body. (6–7½)

In order to demonstrate the pervasion of the four wheels (*cakra*) by the Lord of the Mandala Sovereign, he says, beginning with "At the navel" and ending with "He sports here as he pleases. Therein, at the navel in the *nirmāṇacakra*, that very [syllable] is the spring season, the letter *a* in its short form. At the heart in the *dharmacakra*, it has the form of the syllable *hūṃ* joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*. At the throat in the *saṃbhogacakra*, that same [syllable] is of three morae (*trimātra*), protracted (*pluta*), and remains assuming the form of the Yoginīs throughout the moving and the unmoving.
Through the division of body, speech, and mind, there is a threefold exit through the gates. (7)
Established within all bodies, this [prāṇa] performs the coming and going;
it is proclaimed as short (hrasva) by way of its form as the letter 'ha'. ||8||
For in the heart, the syllable *hūṃ* is remembered as having two long morae;
at the throat, in the form of the syllable *oṃ*, it is said to have three morae and is called protracted (*pluta*).

He is of the nature of the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). Because of the curvature of the channels (*nāḍī*), he has three revolutions due to the entry and exit through the *caṇḍālī*. In the forehead, at the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), is the unstruck syllable (*anāhatākṣara*) *haṃ*, adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*. That very same [syllable], in reverse order, takes the form of the head, throat, heart, and navel as Śrī Heruka, whose form is the mantra. He states his support: those four wheels which have the nature of earth and the other elements are his Buddha-field. The four junctions (*sandhyā*) of day and night—characterized by midday, afternoon, midnight, and dawn—are the "wheel-carriers" (*cakravāhinī*) numbering one hundred and fifty-four breaths; these indeed are the four faces of him who has Prajñā as his consort. These are the four, beginning with *vicitra*, which serve as the indicators of the joys (*ānanda*).

On the forehead is that syllable *haṃ*, which is the unstruck sound (*nāda*) and the point (*bindu*), [manifesting] through the differentiation of the four wheels within the great elements beginning with earth. (10)
Presiding over the four junctions (saṃdhyās), arising from the four moments (kṣaṇas), he is the embodiment of the four joys (ānandas) and is devoted to the four yogas. ||11||
In the form of the supreme bliss, through the relationship of action and agent, he sports here at ease in the form of Śrī Vajrasattva. (12)
Furthermore, situated upon the four petals located in the four directions are the four channels of the elements, which abide in the state of the mind-vajra. (13)

The four moments (*kṣaṇa*), beginning with *ānanda*, and the four yogas—namely *tvarita*, *bāṣpa*, *vibandha*, and *viśvastaka*—are rejected; these very [moments] are his twelve arms, these same [yogas] are his twelve upward-turned eyes, and these same [moments] are the twelve weapons situated in the center. Therefore, through the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between the agent and the action, which are respectively the burning and the nourishing, he is the illustrious *tilakā*; Vajrasattva is the spring (*vasanta*), and his form is such that, by resorting to the nature of the four joys (*caturānanda*) according to his pleasure, he plays; the meaning is that he delights within the bodies of all embodied beings. (8–12)

Having thus revealed the central leader together with his consort—including their faces, arms, colors, postures, hand-symbols, and internal forms—he speaks in order to establish the Wisdom-Wheel (*jñānacakra*), the *ḍākinīs*, and the four offering vases, beginning with the passage starting from "the four petals" and ending with "the five channels are established. Therein, the four located in the eastern, northern, western, and southern directions of the Dharma-Wheel (*dharmacakra*)—characterized by holding, flowing, inflaming, and impelling—are themselves the *ḍākinī* of the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*), as well as Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī.
The four channels situated in the intermediate directions are also located therein.
Those [channels] carrying the five nectars have attained the nature of its worship;
they are renowned as the "fourfold worship," for they are indeed of that very form through their essential being. (15)
Thus, within the center of the heart of the body, five channels are established;
they are declared to be twenty-four in the wheels of body, speech, and mind. (16)

Those who abide in the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) at the station of Śrī Heruka are to be understood as the Ḍākinīs and so forth—namely, Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī. Among these, she is called *Ḍākinī* because of moving (*ḍayana*) in the space of the earth element; *Lāmā* because of shining (*lasana*) in the space of the water element (the change in the vowel is Vedic); *Khaṇḍarohā* because she moves through (*khaṇḍayati*) the space of fire (*tejas*) and rises (*rohati*) therein through its purification; and *Rūpiṇī* because she forms (*rūpayati*) and purifies the space of wind. Having thus described the Ḍākinīs of the cardinal directions, he speaks of the offering jars situated in the intermediate directions with the words "situated in the intermediate directions. In that very wheel of gnosis within the heart, those channels (*nāḍī*) located in the corners that carry the five nectars are themselves the four offerings, which should be known as being in the form of jars, consisting of nectar situated within a garland of skulls formed by the cavities of those elements. He provides the conclusion with the words "Thus of the body," etc. By the method thus stated, the five channels beginning with Trivṛtā within the center of the body, together with the four offerings, are to be known as the Ḍākinīs of the wisdom-lotus; they are not external or imagined, because they consist of the nature of direct experience. (13–15½)

He speaks of the Yoginīs in the form of the channels (*nāḍī*) of the three wheels (*tricakra*), beginning with "body, speech, and mind" (*kāyavākcitta*). Although one should have said "mind, speech, and body," the reverse order of recitation is for the purpose of concealing [the teaching] from those who are unworthy. Consequently, within the wheels of mind and so forth—which consist of the twenty-four sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so on, such as the head—the twenty-four Yoginīs, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, abide in their respective places in the form of the twenty-four channels themselves. That is to say, they are established by their very nature in each location, from the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), and so forth, down to the cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*) and ending at the two knees. As it is stated in the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*): "The Yoginīs, relying upon the divisions of the sacred seats and so forth, are established in their respective places."
The channels originating from the head are known as the "hair-born" (śirasija) channels. ||17||
Among them, the leaders consist of the forms of rajas, sattva, and tamas;
in Pullīra, the one named Pracaṇḍā is known as the bearer of nails and teeth.
In Jālandhara is Caṇḍākṣī, who likewise carries away hair and body hair;
in the great seat (pīṭha) of Oḍiyāna, Prabhāvatī is established.
Residing in the right ear, wearing skin and filth,
the flesh-eating Ḍākinī Mahānāsā dwells at Arbuda.
Four are proclaimed as the Ḍākinīs who preside over the sacred seats (pīṭha).
The channel (nāḍī) which is situated in the Mahoru region is established in Godāvarī. 21.
Known as Vīramatī, she remains in a firm form;
that channel which is famous at Rāmeśvara is known as Kharvarī.

Because of the statement, "The innate ones are the accomplished ones," he says of those very [channels]: "Those channels that have arisen from the head are known as 'head-born'. Here, thirty-two channels emerge from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), like rivers from the Himavat mountain. (16–17)
For the arrangement of the bone-garland is established through its solid nature;
however, the channel in Devīkoṭa is considered to be soft, belonging to Laṅkeśvarī. (23)
She who always carries the *bukka* and dwells within the entire body is Drumacchāyā in Mālava; she is the Sovereign of Jinas residing in the heart. (24)
The Ḍākinīs known as the Upapīṭhas are the mothers of the world;
in the mind wheel (cittacakra), they are the Khecarīs situated in the Pīṭhas and Upapīṭhas. ||25||

And among them, those which perform the gathering of semen, blood, and both together—namely *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtikā*—should be understood as being the originators of all that arises within the three realms, consisting of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and having the nature of body, speech, and mind. Regarding this, the names of the thirty-two channels (*nāḍī*) are given in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"Indivisible, subtle-formed, divine, leftward, and left-moving;
born of the tortoise, the visionary, the consecrated, the fault, excrement, and the mother."
She is the night, the giver of coolness, the warm, the woman, the *avadhūtī*, and the tongue;
she is inclined toward [the goal], has a joyful face, is common to all, and is the bestower of causes.
Viyogā, Premāṇī, Siddhā, Pāvakī,
Sumanas, Trivṛtā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā.

And Kātyāyanī—these thirty-two, together with the four *sandhyā* channels, make thirty-six. Excluding the eight beginning with Trivṛttā and Avadhūtī, the remaining twenty-four beginning with Abhedya are to be known as the Pracaṇḍās and so forth.
The channel which carries the eye and is situated in Kāmarūpa—
She is renowned as Airāvatī, perfected through the manifestation of her form. ||26||
In Oḍra, the channel carrying bile is known as Mahābhairavikā;
these two Ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga, are designated as belonging to this sacred field (kṣetra). 27.
Born in Triśakuni is Vāyuvegā, who possesses lungs;
she is adorned with a garland of intestines and is divine. In Kośala, however, is Surābhakṣī.

Furthermore, the twenty-four elements of these [goddesses], such as nails and teeth, should be understood as being the fragments, skull-bones, and so forth. In that regard, the etymological derivation of the channels (*nāḍī*), seats (*pīṭha*), and *ḍākinīs* is as follows:

Because it brings forth the indestructible nails and teeth, Abhedya is in the head; because it carries the extremely subtle hair of the head and body, Sūkṣmarūpā is at the crest-lock (śikhā); because it carries the skin-moisture that shines outwardly, Divyā is in the left ear; because it carries the full flesh of Vāmana himself, Vāmā is on the back. Alternatively, she is Vāmanī because she produces the element of living beings (*sattvadhātu*) in the form of Vāmana upon its arising, or because she carries the sinews; or alternatively, she is in the left ear because she vomits up what has been eaten upon its arising. Because she carries a garland of bones as indestructible as the shell of a tortoise, Kūrmajā is between the eyebrows.
