Because she manifests the face and flows [with nectar], Bhāvikī is in the two eyes. Because she sprinkles the heart with the essence of nectar, Sekā is in the two armpits. These eight channels, which are the *khecara*s, reside in the seats (*pīṭha*) and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*) within the wheel of the mind (*cittacakra*), together with their means (*upāya*).

That which is defiled—that is, transformed—by its own object is called a *doṣa* (fault). It carries the *cakṣur-dhātu* (eye-element) to the two armpits; for, upon seeing the armpits, there is a transformation of the mind, and because hatred arises from the thought "this is mine," hatred and *doṣa* are synonyms. That which carries the waste known as *pitta* is [the channel] in the two breasts; it impels the *viḍ-dhātu* (fecal element). Because it carries the lungs upward, like a mother, the two *Ḍākinīs*, the Mothers of Yoga, are designated as the secondary fields (*upakṣetra*).
Śyāmādevī is located in Kaliṅga, while she rests at the side. (29)
Subhadrā indeed resides in the stomach and is proclaimed in Lampāka;
these two, known as Chandoha, are the Ḍākinīs, the Mothers of Yoga. (30)
Hayakarṇā, residing in Kāñcī, always carries excrement;
and Khagānanā, situated in the middle of Sīmānta on the Himālaya, does the same. (31)
The two well-known Upacchandohas are the Ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga;
they are the channels (nāḍīs) situated in the wheel of speech, and the messengers (dūtīs) who move upon the earth are established there. ||32||

In the navel, she is *Mātarā* because she generates longing for the mother (*mātṛ*) and because she gives birth to the world; she is *Antramālā* because she causes the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) to sleep within the chains of intestines; she is *Śarvarī*, meaning "night," because she generates conceptualization at the tip of the nose. Having encircled the intestines with the network of fat and sinews (*guṇavarti-medojālikā*), she remains there; she is *Śītadā* because she carries that [network], and she is in the mouth because she bestows the sensation of cold upon it. She is *Ūṣmā* in the throat because she carries the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) in the belly. She is *Pravaṇā* because she carries excrement; through the transposition of letters, she is *Praṇavā*; she is the carrier of Vairocana in the heart. She is *Sīmanta* because she carries [the essence] in the center of the *varaṭaka* (the central channel); she is in the genitals (*meḍhra*) because she is praised as joyful (*hṛṣṭa*) when touched by the hand, and because she provides the bliss of joy (*ānanda-nandana*) to Wisdom and Means. These eight channels, known as the fields (*kṣetra*), sub-fields (*upakṣetra*), meeting places (*chandoha*), and sub-meeting places (*upachandoha*), are the *Bhūcarīs* in the wheel of speech.
Residing among the hungry ghosts (pretas), she is of phlegmatic nature and swift as a wheel; established as the deity of the house, she constantly carries pus. 33.
The Ḍākinī known as Khaṇḍarohā is the Supreme Sovereign;
indeed, the two Ḍākinīs known as Melāpaka are the Mothers of Yoga. (34)
In Saurāṣṭra, the channel known as Lohitā is considered to be the Ḍākinī Śauṇḍinī; it carries perspiration and is situated in Suvarṇadvīpa. (35)

Because it carries the *śleṣman* (phlegm) that balances the bodily elements (*dhātu*), [the channel] is at the secret place; because it generally carries meat-eating or produces conceptualization, it is at the anus; because it carries blood and generates passion through the "spring flowers" (*vasantapuṣpa*), it is the "passionate one" (*premaṇī*) in the thighs; because it produces sweat during meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it is established everywhere; because it carries that [sweat], it is the "accomplished one" (*siddhā*) in the shanks, or because it has authority over the production of the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*). Fat (*medas*) alone is the cause for the nourishment of the body; because it carries that, the "cause-giver" (*hetudāyikā*) is in the toes. Because tears cause the face to burn with grief, the "fiery one" (*pāvakī*) is on the back of the foot; because spittle generates joy (*somanasya*) in yogins, the "well-minded one" (*sumanā*) is on the back of the foot; because it removes mucus (*siṅghāṇaka*), the "Kātyāyanī" is in the two knees. Thus, these eight channels—known as the meeting-place (*melāpaka*), the near-meeting-place (*upamelāpaka*), the charnel ground (*śmaśāna*), and the near-charnel ground (*upaśmaśāna*)—are the "Dwellers in the Netherworld" (*pātālavāsinī*) in the body wheel (*kāyacakra*).

Moving far away from the etymological explanation of the channels (*nāḍī*) of the *samayacakra*, he says: "In the previous [section on] speech, at the door" (6.40). Prior to the door of speech is the door of the body; therein, the eight channels beginning with the eyes—located in the right eyes, ears, and nostrils, as well as in the left ones, and in the mouth and anus—are to be known as residing in the *samayacakra* by their very names, because they perform the observance (*anuṣṭhāna*) of the *samaya* characterized by the enjoyment of sense objects. Thus is the etymology of the channels.

The etymology of the *pīṭhas* has been stated previously. Now the etymology of the *ḍākinīs* is being explained. It has been demonstrated many times that all *ḍākinīs* here are born from the family of Vārāhī; they are defined precisely by their non-difference from her. In this regard, she whose ferocity (*caṇḍatva*) is completely pacified is *Pracaṇḍā*, meaning she who has attained the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). She is *Caṇḍākṣī* because her two channels—the left and the right, which are fierce (*caṇḍa*), sharp, or burning—are [subdued] by means of the central channel (*madhyamā*), since she illuminates both through it. She is considered *Cakravarmiṇī* because her limbs are intensely radiant and filled with the color of fire.
In the assembly (upamelāpaka), the two ḍākinīs are said to be the mothers of yoga (yogamātṛ). ||36||
In the city, however, there is the river named Suvīrā, which carries fat and marrow; in the Sindhu region, she is known as Mahābalā, and she is also called Saśokā, carrying tears.
These two ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga, reside in the cremation ground:
the one who is withered carries a staff, while Cakravartinī dwells in the desert. (38)

She is *Prabhāvatī* because she is endowed with radiance (*prabhā*). She is *Mahānāsā* because her great nose (*mahā-nāsā*) is located at the secret place, the heart, and the mouth. The *pīṭha-ḍākinīs* are [named] according to their etymological meanings (*anvartha*). She is *Vīramatī* because the Hero (*vīra*) exists within her as her progenitor, according to the statement: "The Hero resides in the center of the navel. She is *Kharvarī* because she is both harsh (*khara*) due to the burning of the three wheels (*tricakra*) and excellent (*varā*) because she subsequently nourishes them. She is *Laṅkeśvarī* because she is the sovereign mistress (*īśvarī*) in Laṅkā, which is the city of the body (*śarīra-purī*). She is *Drumacchāyā* because her coolness nourishes like the shade of a tree (*druma-cchāyā*). These are the etymological meanings of the *upapīṭha-ḍākinīs*. Thus ends the *khecarīs* of the Mind Wheel (*cittacakra*).

*Airāvatī* is so called because she flows with speed like the elephant *airāvata*. *Mahābhairavā* is so called because of the piercing of the knots (*granthi*) in the third *oli*. *Vāyuvegā* is she whose speed and velocity are like the wind, both in the ten directions and in the two *olis*. *Surābhakṣī* is she who consumes the wine (*surā*), which is the nectar (*sudhā*), in the *jñāna-oli*. Thus, these *ḍākinīs* of the fields and sub-fields are named according to their respective meanings.

She is dark-complexioned (*śyāmā*) because she arises before dawn, and she is called the Goddess Śyāmādevī because she sports within all the wheels (*cakras*). She is Subhadrā because her satisfaction is beautiful, auspicious, and beneficial. She is Hayakarṇā because she emerges through the right ear like a horse.
In Kulatā, there is Mahāvīryā, who rides upon a young lion;
and there are two Ḍākinīs, mothers of yoga, residing in the vicinity of the cremation ground. (39)
In the body wheel, however, there are the external ḍākinīs who dwell in the underworld;
at the eastern gate of speech, there are likewise four kinds of ḍākinīs. ||40||

Because her face has the form of a bird’s beak, she is Khagānanā (Bird-Faced). Thus, these are the etymological names of the Ḍākinīs of the *Chandoha* and *Upachandoha*. In the Wheel of Speech (*vākcakra*) are the *Bhūcarīs* (Earth-Walkers). She whose speed of going and coming is like that of a wheel is Cakravegā (Wheel-Speed). She who first shatters, then causes to ascend again, and generates the Tathāgata-Locanā and others is Khaṇḍarohā. Because she possesses the intoxicating liquor of wine (*surāsava*), she is Śauṇḍinī. Her armor and mail consist of the wheels themselves; thus she is Cakravarmiṇī (Wheel-Armored). These are the etymological names of the Ḍākinīs of the *Melāpaka* and *Upamelāpaka*.

She is called *Suvīrā* because she originates well from the syllable *Vī*. She is *Mahābalā* because she possesses great strength in going and coming. She is *Cakravartinī* because it is her nature to move within the wheels (*cakras*). She is *Mahāvīryā* because she possesses great heroism in rising up. Thus are the etymologies of the names of the Ḍākinīs of the cremation grounds (*śmaśānas*) and the secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśānas*).

The etymological explanation of the *vīras* is as follows: he who "impels" (*kālayati*) or moves the *bodhicitta* located in the skull (*khaṇḍa*) by means of the form of nails and teeth is *Khaṇḍakapālī*. He who impels the great *kaṃ* (the vital essence) situated in the crown of the head—the deity of sentient beings—along with hair and body hair, is *Mahākaṅkāla*. Having reached the root of the ear, he impels the impurities of the skin; thus he is *Kaṅkāla*. He whose back possesses a formidable fang made of flesh is *Vikaṭadaṃṣṭra*. This is the etymological explanation of the *vīras* of the seats (*pīṭhas*).

Surāvairī (Enemy of Wine) originates from the left ear and is the adversary of the sinews (*snāyu*) of the gods. Amitābha consists of that [bone-garland], because by abiding between the eyebrows he brings forth the immeasurable garland of bones. Vajraprabha (Vajra-Luster) is so called because, possessing a luster like a diamond-jewel, he abides in the eye and brings forth the *vukka* (the palate). Vajradeha (Diamond-Body) is so called because his body is as firm as a diamond, and originating from the base of the arm, he brings forth the heart. This is the etymological explanation of the *upapīṭhas*. Furthermore, others are situated depending on the corner regions of those;
at the main gate is Kākāsyā (Crow-Faced), and at the second is Ulūkāsyā (Owl-Faced). (41)
In the third [corner] is Śvānāsyā, and in the fourth is Śūkarāsyā;
likewise, in the corners are Yamadāḍhī and Yamadūtī.

He is Aṅkurika because he generates the sprouts of the eyes from his two armpits. He is Vajrajaṭila because he generates the pitta-element in the form of a mass of vajras from his two breasts. He is Mahāvīra because he initiates the lungs, which cause fear even to great vajras, from his navel. He is Vajrahūṃkāra because he initiates the gateway of the intestines from the tip of his nose. Such is the etymology of the heroes of the fields and sub-fields.

He is Subhadra because he causes the functioning of the wick of qualities that nourishes through bliss. He is Vajrabhadra because he causes the functioning from the throat to the belly; that is, because from both the throat and the belly he causes the functioning of the wheel of Dharma consisting of vajras, which is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end. He is Vajrabhairava because from the heart he causes the functioning of the excrement that terrifies cowardly people. He is Virūpākṣa because from the penis he causes the functioning of the three-eyed Sīmānta. This is the etymological explanation of the heroes of the *chandoha* and *upachandoha*.

Because he carries the phlegm (*śleṣman*) capable of sustaining the body from the secret place (*guhya*), he is Mahābala. Because he causes the yellow-colored pus to flow from the secret place, he is Ratnavajra. Because he causes the blood of the powerful one to flow from the thighs, he is Hayagrīva. Because he causes the sweat that pervades the pores of the hair to flow from the shanks, he is Ākāśagarbha. This is the etymological explanation of the heroes (*vīra*) regarding the *melāpaka* and *upamelāpaka*.

He is Śrī Heruka because he causes the fat (*medas*), which has the form of the indestructible syllable *HŪṂ*, to flow from the toes of his feet. He is Padmanarteśvara because he causes the bodhicitta, which has the form of a secretion, to flow from the insteps of his feet. He is Vairocana because he causes the white-colored phlegm (*kheṭa*) to flow from his two big toes. He is Vajrasattva because he causes the nasal mucus (*siṅghāṇa*), which is pale-white like the moon, to flow from his knees. This is the etymological explanation of the heroes of the cremation grounds and the secondary cremation grounds. Immediately following that is the renowned Mahābhīmā Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī.
The fourth is also renowned as Bhīmā, considered to be Yamamathanī. ||43||
Thus, these Vajrayoginīs abide in the form of the channels;
they are declared to be the thirty-seven yoginīs of the Mind-Vajra.
Indeed, these are the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) established within the body. 44.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Arrangement of the Thirty-seven Channel-Wheels Situated within the Body of the Tathāgata," in the *Śrī-Vasantatilakā*.

Of these yoginīs—who flow through the left and right channels, who were previously identified as being accompanied by the Ḍākinīs, who correspond to their respective [deities], and who reside in the secondary seats (*upapīṭha*)—there are seventy-two to be known, due to their authority over dissolution (*laya*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*). This is the meaning: they have been established by the textual passage beginning with "In the wheels of body, speech, and mind, twenty-four are proclaimed" (6.16) and ending with "Having the form of the Perfection of Wisdom, they are situated within one's own body" (6.44). The application of the meaning of these terms is easy to understand. (18–44)

Thus ends the detailed explanation of the sixth instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment through the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 6.
The Seventh Exposition:
Now, I shall explain the purification of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening as the channel-wheel (*nāḍīcakra*) of a certain Tathāgata’s body. (1)

The application of mindfulness to the body is Ḍākinī; the application of mindfulness to feelings is Lāmā; the application of mindfulness to phenomena is Khaṇḍarohā; the application of mindfulness to the mind is Rūpiṇī. ||2||

Now, with the words beginning "atha," he states the seventh instruction in order to demonstrate that the yoginīs in the form of the channels possess the essential nature of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*); [the passage] beginning with "anyatamasya" is as before. 1.

It is established that these channels (*nāḍī*), which exist in the gateways of the body such as the heart, head, and so forth, and which have the *ḍākinīs* and others as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), also possess the intrinsic nature of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). This is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "The foundation of mindfulness of the body is the *ḍākinī*. In this context, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) must train accordingly in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, which are subsumed within the five paths. What are those five paths? They are: the path of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-mārga*), the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*). Among these, what is the path of accumulation? It consists of twelve factors. Which twelve? The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). What is the path of preparation? It consists of ten factors. Which ten? The five faculties (*indriya*) and the five powers (*bala*). What is the path of seeing? It consists of seven factors. Which seven? The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). What is the path of cultivation? It consists of the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*). How many limbs of the path are there? There are the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*). What is the path of no-more-learning? It is the final moment of the final cognition of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

For what purpose are these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*)? From where do these phenomena arise? What is enlightenment (*bodhi*)? He replied: "Enlightenment is that by which one realizes the entire nature of the self. Is it partial or all-pervasive? He replied:

[Enlightenment] is both pervasive and partial. Thus, the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas, characterized by the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*), is partial because they accept the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of phenomena. Likewise, those being liberated might fall into the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas; that enlightenment is called "partial" because it prioritizes only one's own interest and is therefore not pure. However, the enlightenment characterized by the selflessness of both [person and phenomena] is the perfect complete enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*); it is pervasive because of its pervasiveness, since phenomena abide in their true nature (*tattvabhāva*). The factors of that realization are the means, the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). "Limbs," "means," "wings," and "causes of manifestation" are synonyms.

And from where do these "dharmas" arise? They are called *dharmas* because they are maintained (*dhriyante*) by Bodhisattvas established on the path and fixed within their minds; thus, they are comprised within the side of the wholesome (*kuśalapakṣa*), because they are untainted (*anāśrava*) and because the being on the path is exclusively wholesome. However, due to the distinctions of the paths, they may be wholesome yet tainted (*sāśrava*) from the perspective of the practitioner. It should be understood that the inclusion of these five paths occurs through two [categories].

By which two? By the mundane path and the supramundane path. Among these, how many factors are there in the mundane path? Twenty-two factors. Which ones? Those known as the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, and the powers. Among these, how many factors are there in the supramundane path? Fifteen. Which ones? The seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path.

The foundations of mindfulness (*anusmṛtyupasthāna*) are: the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāya*), the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*citta*), and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma*). Among these, the foundation of mindfulness of the body is as follows: here, this entire body—belonging to one's own or another's continuum, and extending as far as the three realms (*traidhātuka*)—when thoroughly investigated, is first not a single entity, because a "whole" (*avayavin*) is unestablished. Its non-establishment is due to the observation of defects such as its being subject to baking and cooling, or being colored and colorless; for when unity is unestablished, multiplicity is untenable, since [the body] can be divided down to atoms (*paramāṇu*). Furthermore, an atom cannot be established as a composite, or else, if that were accepted, the entire universe would result in being nothing but atoms. Therefore, because it is devoid of both [unity and multiplicity], this body is empty. The application of the mind in proximity to such mindfulness is the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Likewise, feeling (*vedanā*), which consists of pleasure and so forth, is eighteenfold because it depends on the six groups of consciousness. That too is empty because pleasure and the rest do not exist through distinctions such as past and so forth. The application of mindfulness within one's own mind regarding this is the foundation of mindfulness of feeling. Similarly, the mind (*citta*) is empty because its existence prior to, after, or simultaneously with the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is unestablished. The application of mindfulness that [realizes] the mind is empty is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind. In the same way, because phenomena (*dharma*)—divided into categories such as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—are empty as previously stated, the application of mindfulness to them is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena, which is the path of the Bodhisattva. For the three realms consist of these five [foundations]. In that regard:

The generation of the power of aspiration is Pracaṇḍā; the generation of the power of vigor is Caṇḍākṣī; the generation of the power of investigation is Prabhāvatī; the generation of the power of mind is Mahānāsā. (3)

Through the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*), there is the correct awakening to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); through the middle two [applications], to sensation (*vedanā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*); and through the last, to perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*). This is because the term "phenomena" (*dharma*) is used here in its general sense, referring to the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*). However, in the Śrāvaka system, the distinction is that the four applications of mindfulness have the characteristics of impermanence, impurity, suffering, and selflessness, serving as the antidotes to the four perversions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self. In the Mantra system, however, the Ḍākinīs, whose nature is self-cognition, should be understood as the *dharmatā* (the true nature) of the body and so forth. To explain this, he says: "The application of mindfulness to the body is the Ḍākinī," and so on. (2)

Regarding the question of how many bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) there are, [the text], moving slightly aside, says: there are four bases of psychic power. They are: the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire (*chanda*), the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy (*vīrya*), the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation (*mīmāṁsā*), and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind (*citta*). These are: the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the abandonment of concentration of energy; the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the abandonment of concentration of investigation; and the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of the abandonment of concentration of mind.

The meaning of these sūtras is as follows: here, there are six faults for every meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Namely: "laziness, loss of the object, lethargy, and excitement due to lack of effort. By combining lethargy and excitement into one, there are five faults. For the sake of abandoning them, there are eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*). Which are the eight? Faith, aspiration, vigor, and pliancy as the fourth;
Mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity as the eighth. Thus it is said.

In this regard, the antidote to laziness (*kauśīdya*) is the engagement in wholesome action through faith (*śraddhā*). Through aspiration (*chanda*), there is the accompaniment of intention toward those [wholesome actions]. Through vigor (*vīrya*), there is the abandonment of laziness. Through pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), there is the realization of that abandonment. This very aspiration is called the "basis of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*). Through mindfulness (*smṛti*), one abandons the loss of the object of focus; through clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), one abandons lethargy and agitation. These two constitute the bases of psychic power consisting of vigor and investigation (*mīmāṃsā-ṛddhipāda*). Through volition (*cetanā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), there is the abandonment of effort when it has become dependent [on those states]; this is called the "basis of psychic power consisting of mind" (*citta-ṛddhipāda*). For this very reason, these are said to be the four types of vigor. Therefore, it is said in the *Samādhirāja Sūtra*:
The faculty of faith is Vīramatī; the faculty of energy is Kharvarī; the faculty of mindfulness is Laṅkeśvarī; the faculty of concentration is Drumacchāyā; the faculty of wisdom is Airāvatī. ||4||

“Based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment; through dissociation from conditioned things, one is endowed with the abandonment of the production of substantial entities—this is the basis of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) consisting of five factors. When combined, the four bases of psychic power comprise twenty types. [Thus it is said.]

What is called *ṛddhi*? It is the "accomplishment" (*ṛddhi*), because the root *ṛdh* is listed in the *Dhātupārāyaṇa* with the meaning "to increase. Consequently, since all the qualities of a Buddha—such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)—attain growth (*vṛddhi*) therein, it is *siddhi*, which is perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). The "bases of accomplishment" (*ṛddhipāda*) are the bases like feet, being the causes for its attainment. Although they are common means (*upāya*) to the path, these alone are designated as the two "bases of accomplishment" because they represent the excellence of the remedy against the defects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Those whose intrinsic nature is this—the fierce Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, and Mahānāsā—are the *ḍākinīs* of the seats (*pīṭha*) in the mind wheel (*cittacakra*). ||3||

In that regard, how many faculties (*indriya*) are there? Five. Which five? They are faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. In that context, on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), there are four factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*): the "heat" (*ūṣmagata*), the "summits" (*mūrdhagata*), the "patience" (*kṣāntigata*), and the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*). Therein, as the Bodhisattva brings forth untainted concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*), a "heat" arises like a precursor sign from fire; because it has arisen from the fire of knowledge of the mind, it is called "heat. That same [state], when it has reached its culmination and is accompanied by resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), is the "summit. Because that very mind endures through identity with that [object], it is "patience. Because it emerges immediately after that patience, it is the "supreme mundane dharma"; this is a designation for this associated state. Among those, regarding the meaning of the first two factors conducive to penetration, faith and the others are called the five faculties. Therein, faith is the conviction of the mind toward the future supramundane path, or toward the Three Jewels and so forth; that is the faculty of faith. One exerts oneself toward the dharmas produced by the faculty of faith; that is the faculty of vigor. And that [vigor] is of four kinds: the vigor of undertaking, the vigor of application, the vigor of investigation, and the vigor of practice. The faculty by which the dharmas produced by the faculty of vigor are repeatedly brought to presence and not forgotten is the faculty of mindfulness. The mental state which, having produced the dharmas of the faculty of mindfulness, establishes them by setting aside all other internal essences is the faculty of concentration. The investigation of the dharmas produced by the faculty of concentration through correct analytical observation (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) is wisdom.
The power of faith is Mahābhairavī; the power of vigor is Vāyuvegā; the power of mindfulness is Surābhakṣī; the power of concentration is Śyāmādevī; the power of wisdom is Subhadrā. ||5||

Hayakarṇā is the factor of awakening that is concentration; Khagānanā is the factor of awakening that is vigor; Cakravegā is the factor of awakening that is joy; Khaṇḍarohā is the factor of awakening that is pliancy; Śauṇḍinī is the factor of awakening that is investigation of phenomena; Cakravarmiṇī is the factor of awakening that is mindfulness; Suvīrā is the factor of awakening that is equanimity. (6)

The faculty. Why is it called a faculty (*indriya*)? It is a faculty because it prevails over wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*); it is that which produces delight in the defilement and purification of the five aggregates. Excluding the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the four ḍākinīs—Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā—are to be known as the purities of faith, vigor, mindfulness, and meditative concentration. ||4||

In that regard, how many powers (*balas*) are there? Five. Which ones? They are precisely those previously mentioned: faith and the rest. What is the distinction between the faculties (*indriyas*) and the powers? It is said: when faith and the others turn away [from their opposites], they receive the designation of "faculties"; when they are not turned back by their adversaries—namely, lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), which is a synonym for faulty wisdom—they become the five powers. This is the distinction. Furthermore, it should be understood that Airāvatī, Mahābhairavā, Vāyuvegā, Surābhakṣī, Śyāmādevī, and Subhadrā are purified by the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) mentioned previously, within the wheel of speech. 5.

In that regard, how many factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are there? Seven. Which seven? They are: the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharma-pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). These are the factors of enlightenment on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Enlightenment is unobstructed knowledge (*nirāvaraṇa-jñāna*). That by which the vision of the truths is concentrated in the mind is the factor of enlightenment of concentration. That by which there is enthusiasm for that very [vision] is the factor of enlightenment of vigor. That by which one makes the mind free from doubt regarding that very [vision] is the factor of enlightenment of joy. Through that very joy, because of the serviceability (*karmanya*) of body, speech, and mind, and through the abandonment of the heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it becomes exceedingly cool; that is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy. The thorough knowledge of the nature of reality as it truly is is the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena.

Right view is Mahābalā; right intention is Cakravartinī; right speech is Mahāvīryā; right action is Kākāsyā; right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā; right effort is Śvānāsyā; right mindfulness is Śūkarāsyā; and right concentration is the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka. (7)

In that very context, the non-forgetfulness of this [mindfulness] is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Equanimity toward attachment and non-attachment to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the equanimity factor of enlightenment (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Among these, Hayakarṇā and Khagānanā are to be known as having the nature of the concentration and vigor factors of enlightenment, respectively. Thus is the purification of the Heroines of the Speech Wheel. By means of the remaining five, beginning with joy (*prīti*), Cakravegā, Khaṇḍarohā, Śauṇḍinī, Cakravarmiṇī, and Suvīrā are purified. 6.

Having explained the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as the antidote to the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), he now describes the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as the antidote to the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): "And that is the noble eightfold path. Which eight? Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. In that regard, on the path of cultivation, the wisdom that [realizes] the obscuration of the knowable is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is right view, as is the view of the existence of future lives. Right intention is the mental orientation toward selflessness, even if it has not yet been directly realized through that view. Right speech is the teaching to sentient beings that elucidates the meaning one has seen for oneself. Right action is bodily conduct that is exclusively wholesome, or the intimidating of others through [powers such as] miraculous feats (*ṛddhi*) for the sake of disciplining them. Right livelihood is the seeking of robes and so forth solely by means of what is obtained through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Right effort is the application of one's own activities of body, speech, and mind to all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*). And it is said: [The verse follows:]... (as provided in the source text).

"In whatever way the Son of the Victor, engaged in his course, proceeds within the various objects of direct perception, in that very way he applies himself to the welfare of sentient beings through words of appropriate equality. Thus it is said.

On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the non-forgetting of the object of focus is right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*); the one-pointedness of mind is the immovable vajra-like samādhi. That which manifests within the interval of the stage known as Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā*) is purified there by the first three: Mahābalā, Cakravartinī, and Mahāvīryā. Thus is the purification of the body wheel (*kāyacakra*). Right action (*samyakkarmānta*) is Kākāsyā; right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) is Ulūkāsyā; right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*) is Śvānāsyā; and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) is Sūkarāsyā.

The generation of unarisen wholesome states is Yamadāḍhī; the preservation of arisen wholesome states is Yamadūtī; the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī; and the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states is Yamamathanī. ||8||
Thus, all the channels within the body, purified as the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, abide by assuming the colors, arms, and postures of the deities. (9)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrīvasantatilakā*, titled "The Explanation of the Purification of the Wheel of Channels and the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment. ||7||
Thus is the purification of the female gatekeepers. The Blessed One, Śrī Herukavajra, is perfect meditative absorption; this is the purification of the pericarp of the wisdom-lotus. ||7||

Yamadāḍhī is that which causes the arising of unarisen wholesome dharmas; Yamadūtī is the protector of arisen wholesome dharmas; Yamadaṃṣṭrī is the relinquisher of arisen unwholesome dharmas; and Yamamathanī is that which prevents the arising of unarisen unwholesome dharmas—this is the purification of the goddesses of the corners of the Samaya-maṇḍala. ||8||

These thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are thus distinguished by their classifications. In terms of substantial entities (*dravya*), however, they are comprised within ten categories: the five faculties (*indriya*) and the five powers (*bala*). The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are included within the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*) or the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are included within the power of wisdom or the power of energy (*vīrya*). The right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are included within the power of energy. The power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*) is included within the factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The power of energy is included within the factor of awakening of energy (*vīryāṅga*). The power of wisdom is included within the factor of awakening of discrimination (*pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The power of mindfulness is included within the factor of awakening of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*)...

Regarding the factor of enlightenment that is vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*): there is a subsumption of the factors of enlightenment within the Eightfold Path. Specifically, right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) are subsumed under the enlightenment factors of mindfulness and concentration. The enlightenment factor of vigor is subsumed under right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*). The enlightenment factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharma-pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is subsumed under right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these three constitute the practice of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*). Thus, by including right view, right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these five factors of enlightenment—the enlightenment factors of pliancy (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are also included, making ten items in total. These, in turn, are subsumed within the triad of the powers of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom. In this regard, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these three, which constitute the practice of pure ethical discipline—and right effort, which is the fruit of that practice of pure ethical discipline, comprise the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*). Right view, right intention, the enlightenment factor of pliancy, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity—these four comprise the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). Right mindfulness comprises the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*). Since both ethical discipline and concentration are contained within wisdom, according to the principle that wisdom alone is the awakener of phenomena, one should understand the subsumption in this way: the thirty-seven factors are subsumed by the ten, the ten by the three, and the three by the one.

This is what is meant: here, the thirty-seven channels, which are of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) as previously described and take the form of *ḍākinīs*, extend from the head down to the knees. Among them, four terminate at the navel-cakra, eight at the eight gates, and one in the center in the form of the *avadhūtī*. These nine channels, which rely upon the gateways of the body, are subsumed within the ten central channels. Those ten are further subsumed within the three, beginning with *lalanā*, and those three are, in turn, subsumed within the central channel. Thus, by means of the central channel—the *avadhūtī* whose very nature is Vajravārāhī—all this collection of channels, having manifested, returns and converges into that very place. By this, the state of the non-duality of the conventional and the ultimate is revealed; and that indeed is the accumulation of the path of union (*yuganaddha*). As it has been said:
Just as many clouds, appearing in various forms and colors, arise from the expanse of the sky and indeed dissolve back into it; so too does this [consciousness].
In the same way, all primordial natures (prakṛtis), which have the three appearances as their cause, having entered into all objects, enter into the clear light. Thus it is said.

Likewise, because of such statements as "form itself is emptiness, emptiness itself is form," and because of the statement, "What talk can there be of the ultimate apart from the conventional? by this [explanation], the proponents of other schools—such as those who maintain the doctrines of a tranquil Brahman, the *asāṃkhya* puruṣa, and so forth—as well as our own fellow Buddhists, such as the proponents of formless representation (*nirākāra-vijñapti*), are refuted, since they are characterized by dogmatic adherence to a distinction between the conventional and the ultimate. Enough of this excessive elaboration.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Thus, these exist within the self in the form of channels (*nāḍī*). Externally, however, they are established in the maṇḍala-circles and in the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) such as Pullīra, assuming the forms of weapons and so forth held in the hands, depending upon the specific dispositions of sentient beings.

Bestowing grace in the form of the *kṣetrajā* (field-born goddesses), they sport, delight, and engage in investigation. Likewise, within the internal self (*ādhyātman*), their faces and so forth exist. All the channels (*nāḍī*) emerge from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) and manifest their faces at the extremity of the *vajra* and *vārija*. Their sprouts are individually manifold; the arms possess colors due to the coloring of the elements (*dhātu*). For instance: nails and teeth are white; hair of the head and body is black; skin and impurities are blackish-red; flesh is red-colored; sinews are white; the chain of bones is white; the spleen (*bukka*) is black; the heart is whitish-red; the eyes are white and black; bile (*pitta*) is yellow; the lungs (*phuphphusa*) are red; the intestines are white like a string of beads; the stomach (*udara*) is dark; feces are yellow; the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*) is reddish-white; phlegm (*śleṣmā*) is white; pus is as pale as the moon; blood is indeed red; sweat has the color of fire; fat (*medas*) is white; tears are as white as pearls; saliva (*kheṭa*) is blackish-white; and nasal mucus (*siṅghānaka*) is yellowish-white—such is the distinction of colors. Their configuration, established by its own nature, exists in a curved form through movement to the left and right, in the manner of the *ālīḍha* posture and so forth. Their weapons, through the purification of the flaying knife (*kartikā*) and skull-cup (*kapāla*), should be understood as having the innate nature (*sahajasvabhāva*) that pierces the stains of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). On this point, there are these verses: [The verses follow.]
Having attained the nature of pure awareness through the severance of the stains of conceptual construction,
they are established in innate bliss, free from the duality of subject and object.
Bestowing the fruit of Buddhahood upon the world by mere touch,
the ten known as the Ḍākinīs and others are indeed conceptualizations situated within the wheel.
Abiding forever in the world with an indivisible nature and so forth,
they are joined with the twenty-four great heroes who are the forms of the *dhātu*.
If the channels and heroes are already within one's own body,
then why do deluded people wander through pilgrimage sites such as Pullīra and others without disillusionment?
Having completely renounced everything external as well as the darkness of mental constructs, liberation is attained by the yogi who is disciplined in the yoga of the inner self. (9)

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the seventh instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, the manual for the means of accomplishment of the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 7.
The Eighth Exposition:

Now I shall fully explain the ritual procedures for the mandala, fire-offering (homa), yoga, recitation (japa), meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), and so forth, pertaining to the body of a certain Tathāgata, in both their external and internal forms. (1)
It is perfectly established by the deities, Heruka and the rest, who take the form of the channels and possess the characteristics of the thirty-seven factors conducive to great enlightenment. ||2||
The body is a beautiful mandala with four gates as previously described;
it stands supported by eight pillars consisting of its own constituent limbs. (3)

Now, in order to reveal that the external mandala, yoga, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, are actually established within the internal self, he says "Then, of another... and so on. This is easy to understand because it has been largely explained previously. Therein, the body itself is presented as the mandala; the connection is that "the body is the mandala. ||1||

Of what kind? "Thirty-seven," and so forth. He speaks of the purity of the supported maṇḍala: these channels (*nāḍī*), which are established through the purity of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), exist as the very forms of the ḍākinīs and others who abide within the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body. For what reason? Here, the ḍākinīs are said to have a nature that is non-conceptual, objectless, and unobscured. As it is said: "The syllable *ḍe* (or *ḍai*) signifies moving through the sky; the Buddha-element is thus conceived. Those accomplished ones (*siddha*) who move through all space are called *ḍākinī*."
Because of this statement, the channels that move within the great sky of the five gnoses are called *ḍākinīs*, for through contact with them, the non-conceptual reality arises for both. ||2||

Having explained that which is to be supported (*ādheya*), he describes the supporting mandala (*ādhāramaṇḍala*) with the words "the body is the mandala," and so forth. In this context, the body itself is the mandala because it serves as the locus for the yoginīs and vīras, who consist of the forms of the channels (*nāḍī*) and elements (*dhātu*) of the mandalas of mind, speech, and body. Precisely because of this equality, it is proclaimed to be square (*caturasra*) in its totality.
By way of body, speech, and mind, it is said to consist of three wheels (*tricakra*). ||4||
In the filaments at the summit of the mountain, [the winds] such as Vairambha arise in their proper sequence;
thus, indeed, that mandala is produced through the successive stages of the Guru.
The Vairambha wind is situated at the soles of the feet, shaped like a bow;
likewise, fire is situated in the triangular region of the hips and waist.

It is "delightful" (*ramyam*) because it does not depend upon external dust, colored powders, and so forth. To show that the external maṇḍala has four gates just as the internal one does, he says: "Therein, in the maṇḍala of the body, there are four gates known as the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth; or else 'as previously stated' means those four gates exist according to their division. First, the gate of the mind (*citta-dvāra*) is in the left and right channels. Second, the gate of speech (*vāk-dvāra*) consists of the four [sites] beginning with the *ātma-pīṭha*. The gate of the body (*kāya-dvāra*), which is ninefold, is twofold through the distinction of lower and upper. Thus, there are four gates. Because it is joined with two pillars for each of the gates, it has eight pillars. Internally, it is joined with the pillars of the channels of the eyes and so forth. Just as the external maṇḍala is square, the body-maṇḍala should also be understood as square by virtue of its equal proportions. Why is it equal? Because this body possesses the same measurement from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) as it does when the arms are extended. The external maṇḍala consists of the three maṇḍalas of mind, speech, and body, possessing twenty-four [deities] at the highest; likewise, internally, it is endowed with the three internal wheels (*adhyātmika-cakra-traya*) consisting of twenty-four seats (*pīṭha*) from the head down to the knees, which serve as the supports for the channels of mind, speech, and body. (3–4)

The enumeration begins with "the filaments on the mountain peak" and so forth. This refers to what is designated as the Viśvapadma (Universal Lotus), situated upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, which rests above the four circles of wind and the other elements. Likewise, within the individual self (*adhyātman*), this lotus, marked by the circles of the body, is to be understood through the instruction of the Guru. ||5||

He states the detailed explanation: from "the wind is situated on the sole of the foot" up to "in manifest and unmanifest form," the state of being marked by mandalas is described. The wind is situated on the sole of the foot, that is, beneath the feet. Because it has the shape of a bow and because it initiates specific [movements], it is *vairambha*; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). Like a modification (*vaikṛta*), the action consisting of the movement of the feet is *vairambha*.
Indeed, Varuṇa, who is circular in form, is situated in the belly. And the earth itself is in the heart, square on all sides. (7)
For Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, has the form of a skeleton staff;
and situated upon its summit is a lotus with thirty-two petals. (8)
That which arises from vowels and consonants, consisting of the thirty-two marks of enlightenment, and resides in the center of the lotus, is called the moon mandala. (9)
That which is situated in the center of the head is called the brain;
in its center resides the syllable *haṃ*, in the form of a *bindu*, which is indeed unstruck (*anāhata*). (10)

Thus it is said. By this, the activity and arrangement of the wind-maṇḍala have been explained. Above that, in this region of the three hips—the pelvic area—there resides the fire-maṇḍala, triangular by nature, brilliant because it is joined with a red jewel. Above that, in the region of the belly, there resides the water-maṇḍala, circular by nature, due to its connection with the fluidity of the mantra-garland. Above that, at the heart (and in the eyes/chest), there is the earth-maṇḍala, square and resembling gold. That which is above this, the region of the neck known as the *kaṅkāla*, is to be understood as Meru, endowed with the eight peaks of the eyes and so forth, because its four petals consist of jewels. Regarding the head of that Meru, the thirty-two channels beginning with the *Abhedya* located in its center are to be known as the Viśva-lotus, the seat of the Blessed One. Within that, the brain itself—which is composed of the thirty-two vowels and consonants and is condensed as the essence of bodhicitta—is the moon-maṇḍala, the special seat of the Blessed One. No inherent distinction among seats is taught in the tantras, because the reality of purification (*viśuddhi-tattva*) is never intended to be expressed [as having such distinctions]. The differentiation of seats occurs solely through the influence of the inclinations of individuals. For this very reason, they explain that in some cases the heroes and yoginīs residing in the three wheels have moon-maṇḍala seats, while in others they have sun-seats. (6–9½)
That is the root of all worlds, both the stable and those of a mobile nature;
it exists in the form of their seed, manifest through its unmanifest form.
From that, the form of all embodied beings first arose;
it flows in the form of nectar and remains established day and night.
By that very [sound] which brings satisfaction to the fire, the resonance (nāda) is split;
by that, the mandala becomes complete—of this there is no doubt. ||13||

"Within that," and so forth. Within that brain is the syllable *haṃ*, the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound, which is called a "drop" (*bindu*) because it has the nature of being perceived as a drop due to its state of spreading forth flowing nectar. Because it is the causal basis for all phenomena, whether stable or moving, it is the locus of perfect establishment (*pūrṇapratiṣṭhā*). For this very reason, it is manifest in the form of a seed-syllable, yet unmanifest in the form of the ultimate bodhicitta. From that very source, the body of all embodied beings—whether footless, one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; born from eggs, sweat, a womb, or by spontaneous generation; including animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, gods, asuras, and humans—is produced from the very beginning. It remains as nothing other than that flowing nectar within the mother, by virtue of the union of the mother and father. That is the essential nature of the Blessed Lord Heruka, because the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) pervades all phenomena. This remains even whether Buddhas arise or do not arise, because all phenomena are primordially unproduced and, being dependently originated, lack any [inherent] production; therefore, cessation is likewise unestablished.
Neither is anyone born here, nor does anyone die;
it is cyclic existence itself that should be understood as abiding in the form and appearance of the mind.

Because of this statement: even when there is a conceptualization of arising and ceasing, if there is no real entity, it is without objective support (*nirālamba*). Even when there is an appearing object of support, because that [appearing object] is like an illusion, the entire collection of entities should be understood as inexpressible, unceasing, and unarisen. (10–12)

He speaks of the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and means: "By that very [bliss] residing in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), or by that which, mounted upon the mandala within one's own body, brings satisfaction through the fire of the gnosis of the nature of the mandala-deities; from the letter *KĀ* situated in the pericarp of the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*), there arises the *nāda*.
That itself is called the 'mandala'—the supreme essence of all things.
Because it grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) or takes (*lāti*) that, the body is considered the mandala. (14)
It is split apart; the meaning is that, by being intent on binding the waves of the nectar situated within its own nature, it causes the staff to break and is uprooted. And it has been said:
"Indeed, Nāda, which has attained the state of being the single cause of all phonemes that differentiate words and sentences, is established in the region of the navel."
Vāyu and Upavāyu, with respect to the activities of the wheel such as its emergence and so forth,
resort to states of activity and its opposite by means of the essential nature of exhalation (recaka) and the other breath-controls.
That very same basis is said to be tenfold in its intermediate form;
through the union of the churner and the churning, it brings about great bliss.
By means of the yoga of upward-flaming, it acts as the burner of the aggregates, sense-faculties, and so forth;
having the very form of the fire of time, it is the agent of the dissolution of all things.
The Bindu, in the form of the Moon, brings delight to the world;
in the Mahācakra of Great Bliss, it assumes the form of the unstruck syllable (Anāhata).
The droplets of the consciousness of awakening, resembling the moon in hue,
pulsating at the edge of the solar disc, remain present as if they were streaming forth.
He alone is the life-breath of living beings; He alone is the supreme imperishable. He alone is all-pervading; He alone is established within every body.
The resonance (nāda), nourished by this, shall attain the state of perfect contentment;
this is declared to be the Vasantatilakā yoga.

Therefore, by that very [means], the mandala consisting of the four seats, or the mandala of emanation and so forth, is declared to be complete. Even externally, the mandala becomes complete through the Lord of the Mandala together with his own consort; it is not otherwise. ||13||
The mandala is considered to be the wheel of the thirty-seven great channels;
the bodhicitta is the great jewel, the mandala that is the mandala of reality. (15)
Pervading the universe in both external and internal forms, it remains established;
the external form consists of sound and the other [objects], which set the six sense organs in motion. (16)
But within, the perfected substances such as semen and so forth are established; for the Vajra-holders, by means of the bodhicitta itself, both externally and internally. (17)

He states the etymological explanation of the support-maṇḍala with the words "That very [body] is the maṇḍala," and so forth. Because it encompasses the supported maṇḍala—which consists of the essence (*sāra*), the channels (*nāḍī*), the constituents (*dhātu*), and the nature of *Vasantatilakā*, *Ḍākinī*, the *Vīra* Śrī Heruka, and *Vajravārāhī*—the body itself is called the maṇḍala. This is because the suffix is applied to the root *lā* (to take) preceded by the prefix *maṇḍa*. (14)

He speaks of internal purity with the words beginning "thirty-seven" and so forth. These thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which are of the nature of consciousness, through their purification, are the very previously mentioned wheel of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*) as the maṇḍala. He speaks of the purity of the heroes (*vīra*) with the words beginning "the thought of awakening" (*bodhicitta*) and so forth. Those twenty-four pulsations of the thought of awakening which are of the nature of the elements—because they are priceless, they constitute the maṇḍala of the circle of goddesses; that which grasps their essence should be known as the maṇḍala of the heroes (*vīra-maṇḍala*). (15)

The emanated maṇḍala is twofold: the external, which is square and so forth; and the internal, which is the womb-maṇḍala (*garbhamaṇḍala*), consisting of the three wheels (*tricakra*) and so forth. Here, however, the external consists of the head and the *jālandhara* [and other centers], while the internal consists of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the elements (*dhātu*). For this very reason, this maṇḍala is not mine alone, but should be known as the maṇḍala of this entire universe of the five destinies (*pañcagati*). Therefore, it is said: "Pervading the universe, it stands established. Furthermore, the internal maṇḍala is worshipped by means of the external maṇḍala’s offerings of form, sound, and so forth. Within the interior, inside the skull-cup (*kapāla*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) exist for the sake of worship through bliss. Here, however, on the outside, the doors of the senses are worshipped by means of the five qualities of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), such as form and so forth. Internally, there abide the perfected substances—those substances that are established by their own nature, namely the five void-elements (*pañcavyomabhūta*). To that end, it says: "The external, however, is form, sound, and so forth," etc. The external is shown to the disciples in order to grant the coarse and subtle commitments (*samaya*). Here, however, the coarse and subtle—
By means of the meaning of the pledge (samaya) that has arisen [from] the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whose nature is the friend of the world, in both gross and subtle forms. ||18||
From this mandala, one attains Buddhahood in this very life, as well as the state of a Śrāvaka, a Buddha, and likewise a Pratyekabuddha. (19)
From this maṇḍala, there is the manifestation of the gods beginning with Brahmā;
[this occurs] through the internal [elements] such as semen and so forth, as well as the external [objects] such as form and so forth. (20)

By means of the bodhicitta, which is differentiated by its various aspects, and through Vajradhara—the achiever of Buddhahood for all the world—who, out of joy, desires to bestow the commitment (samaya) of both Buddhahood and the state of a Bodhisattva, that very state is attained from that very mandala. ||16-17||

To that end, he says: "By means of the distinction between gross and subtle," and so forth. In this context, the gross consists of the twenty-four elements (*dhātu*); the subtle is the *bodhicitta*. Alternatively, the gross refers to the impurities (*mala*) issuing from the nine apertures which are to be dissolved; the subtle is the heart of enlightenment (*bodhihṛdaya*), the dissolver. And it has been said: "Having attained a twofold state through the distinction between gross and subtle—the gross being the ninefold substance, and the subtle being the nature of enlightenment."
"These substances are perfected (*siddha*) through the differentiation of liquefying substances.

Thus, the central leader within the external mandala performs emanations as Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Samyaksambuddhas, Brahmā, and so forth, for the sake of sentient beings. Internally, however, they "flow" (*śravanti*), thus [the channels] are the Śrāvakas, which are the nine gates. The visual and other consciousnesses are the Pratyekabuddhas, because of their unconditioned nature. Ānanda and the others are the Samyaksambuddhas. Body, speech, and mind are Brahmā and the others. All these are produced from this very mandala; such is the determination of the mandala. (18–19½)

He describes the external and internal *homa*: "By means of the internal [substances], semen and so forth," and so on. Here, externally, the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*) is satisfied by the masters with offerings of sesame seeds through the mouth of the pledge-fire (*samayāgni*). In the same way, the maṇḍala of the Buddhas and their Sons, consisting of the five aggregates and so forth, is satisfied by the objects of the senses such as form, by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), and by semen and the other [elements] produced through meditative union (*samāpatti*). This *homa* should be understood as blazing with the heat of burning, due to the intensity of the flaming Caṇḍālī within the fire of wisdom (*prajñāgni*). (20–20½)
An oblation is performed with sacrificial offerings in the greatly blazing fire of wisdom, specifically for the six sense-bases, the elements, and the aggregates. (21)
In that same way, the yoga of those ḍākinīs who possess the forms of deities is declared to be worship; for by means of it, they are worshipped. ||22||
This skull of the head is called the vessel for the oblation;
the tongue is said to be the *śruva* ladle, and the heart is the moon, consisting of the *lalanā*. (23)
The vessel (pātrī) is designated as the mouth, and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as the circle of the navel;
the fire of Brahmā, fanned by the wind of karma, resides in the triple-junction (trikaṭa). ||24||

He describes the worship with the words "of the six sense-bases and elements," and so forth. Here, according to the principle previously stated, the five aggregates are the five *ḍākas*; the six sense-bases are the six Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*), beginning with Khaṇḍakapāla; the [four] elements are the four Wisdom Goddesses; and the *ḍākinīs* are the thirty-six channels (*nāḍī*). Thus, the union that consists of the non-dual application of wisdom and means regarding these [factors] which have the form of deities and so on—that is to be understood as worship. And it has been said: "From the practice of the state of selflessness comes the meditation on the form of the deity;
that is considered the great worship, which accomplishes all Buddhas."
For it is by these alone that they are worshipped; therefore, [one should worship them]. ||21-22||

He states the ancillaries of the previously mentioned fire-offering (*āhoma*) beginning with: "This skull is the head," and so forth. This skull, which is the cranial bowl at the top of the head, is itself the vessel for the sacrificial oblation (*havirbhājana*) because it serves as the support for the lunar clarified butter oblation, and nothing else. Likewise, the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels situated on the left and right are to be known respectively as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, because they carry substances downward. At the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*), the navel region is the fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*), because the oblation is poured there. From the union of the churner and the churning stick, the fire of Brahma—which is the essence of reality (*tattvamaya*) and consists of action—is ignited; that blazing fire resides in the triangle below that, in the secret place (*guhya*) at the base of the three channels, by its very nature—this is the completion of the sentence. Furthermore, the fire of Brahma is recommended externally for rites of pacification (*śāntika*); and it arises from the friction of the two kindling sticks (*araṇi*). (23–24)

The resonance (*nāda*) is said to be the mantra; its repetition is the recitation (*japa*). The manifestation of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), however, arises from the non-dual yoga of the mandala. ||25||
This mandala and so forth of the Victors is of the nature of the innate (*sahaja*).

Having explained the fire-oblation (*homa*), he speaks of the recitation (*jāpa*): "The sound (*nāda*) is said to be the mantra," and so on. This vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*), which was previously mentioned as being articulated from the region of the navel, is called "mantra" because it is the cause of all mantras. Its revolving by way of the sequence of entry and so forth is called "recitation. By this, this "natural recitation" common to all the world has been described:
"Those beings indeed within the three realms who rely upon the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*)."
"The ignorant, devoid of meditation and study, merely mutter the king of mantras.

Having thus described the recitation (*jāpa*), he speaks of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): "The manifestation of cultivation," and so forth. To the yogins, there appears an external manifestation based upon body, speech, and mind. Internally, within the four mandalas of emanation and so forth, the very manifestation of the assembly of mudrās and the rest is cultivation. Alternatively, cultivation is the non-dual yoga of the mandala, which has the lack of intrinsic nature as its object.
"In the absence [of an object], cultivation is existence; cultivation is not the cultivation of existence."
Thus, existence would not be existence; it is not found through contemplation. ||25||

He states the conclusion: "This very nature of coemergence (*sahaja*) is the mandala and so forth of the Victors. This mandala and so forth—consisting of what is known as the mandala, fire-oblation (*homa*), sacrifice (*yāga*), recitation (*jāpa*), and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—is the nature of coemergence for all beings, the Victors; it abides as their own intrinsic being (*svabhāva*) and is not artificial. However, that which is artificial was taught solely for the sake of engaging with the coemergent. Thus, all beings are indeed Vajradharas. Anticipating the question, "While these mandalas have an external [form] presided over by a master (*ācārya*), who is the master within the internal [self]? he says: "The master is the King of Mind, in the form of the presiding deity of the mandala. This one who is the Mind-Vajradhara exists as the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedya*).

But the teacher is the king of the mind in the form of the presiding master of the mandala; everything here, such as the mandala and so forth, should be understood exactly as it has been described. (26)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, the instruction on the determination of the ritual procedures for the mandala, fire-offerings, yoga, recitation, meditative cultivation, and so forth, in the *Śrīvasantatilakā*. 8.

He alone is the *ācārya* who understands the previously mentioned mandalas without distinction. He is called an *ācārya* because of his practice (*ācaraṇa*) of that [knowledge] along with its specific details (*saviśeṣa*). For this very reason, he says: "in the form of the presiding deity of the mandala. Here, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) should be understood as elided. He states the extension [of the rule] (*atideśa*): "Everything here, beginning with the mandala, is to be understood exactly as it has been described. This refers to those mandalas and so forth not mentioned here [in this context]. The mandala...

The ritual actions (*karaṇas*)—namely, the drawing of the thread (*sūtra*), the scattering of colored powders (*rajas*), the seizing of the ground (*bhūparigraha*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation (*sthāpana*), the dismissal (*visarjana*), the accomplishment of the mandala (*maṇḍalasādhana*), the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the bathing (*snāna*), the offering (*bali*), and so forth—are to be understood, that is, known, as occurring within that very body-mandala (*dehamaṇḍala*). To explain: the central channel (*madhyamanāḍī*) is the thread; the blood, semen, feces, urine, and so forth are the colored powders of the mandala; the ten channels that sustain the twenty-four sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) are the grounds; the seizing [of the ground] is the grasping of those [channels] through the process of their dissolution and so on; the invocation and other rites are performed through the process of entry and so on; the accomplishment of the mandala is by means of the "wisdom-rod" (*jñānolī*); the consecration here is the showering of the circle of goddesses and deities seated upon the lotus throne from the vase of the vajra-jewel; and the "offering" (*bali*) is the tasting of the *rasanā* (the tongue) which is the outflow of this [consecration]. (26)

Thus ends the detailed commentary on the eighth chapter of the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 8.
The Ninth Explanation:
Now I shall describe the extraction of the mantra-circle from the body of a certain Tathāgata. ||1||
The delightful triangular mandala, emerged from the *vajrāralli*, is renowned as the *dharmodayā* and is also called the *bhaga* of women. (2)
In its center is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
there, the eight classes [of consonants], mixed with the vowels (ali and kāli), are situated. (3)

Regarding the previously mentioned recitation of mantras (*mantrajāpa*), as to what that mantra is, he provides the ninth instruction beginning with "Now" (*atha*) in order to explain its extraction (*uddhāra*), stating: "of any one [mantra] whatsoever. This establishes that the extraction of whatever mantra is naturally established for any given sentient being is the source of all mantras. ||1||

In that regard, having drawn a triangular mandala on the outside and painted an eight-petaled lotus within it, one should arrange the vowels (*ālikā*) and consonants (*āli*) in the central pericarp and upon the petals according to their eightfold divisions. Then, by means of the detailed sequence beginning with "the fifth of the fourth" and continuing with "the fifth of the fifth," one should extract the root mantra and the others. As for the internal [practice]: this triangle is the primary seat (*mūlapīṭha*) together with the eight channels (*nāḍī*). Therein resides the Blessed One *A* (the letter *A*), situated in the midst of the vowels and consonants accompanied by the eight groups (*varga*). He exists in the form of all phonemes, words, sentences, great sentences (*mahāvākya*), and so forth; from him alone these phonemes manifest. They produce words, those in turn produce sentences, and those produce great sentences, extending as far as the infinite distinctions of worldly phenomena—the eighty-four thousand aggregates of teachings (*dharmaskandha*). Thus, all this originates from the phonemes and the rest. And because the relationship of support and supported between the navel and the secret place is intended here, the Nirmāṇacakra itself is called the "support of the mantra. (2–3)

Thus, mantras whose lineage is the letter *a* and which originate from the letter *a* perform and set in motion the collection of rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth in their appropriate manner; it is not otherwise, for mantras whose true nature is not fully understood do not act.
They perform the collection of rites for embodied beings in the form of mantras;
indeed, the fifty syllables themselves are established in the Vedas and other scriptures.
"The intrinsic nature of the class of mantras is the single, supreme syllable.
By the mere thorough knowledge of that, mantras become performers of ritual actions. Thus it is said. Furthermore:
For this very reason, we do not accept that mantras consist of the nature of phonemes;
for they are not capable of being the cause for even bending a blade of grass. Thus it is said.

Therefore, it is said: "They produce for embodied beings a collection of actions in the form of mantras. By the words "the fifty syllables" and so forth, he states the number. Because the vowels (*ālī*) exist as a pair in the form of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), they become sixty-four. Therein, by dividing the class of vowels (*ālivarga*) into two, thirty-two syllables arise. Through the placement of the two *rakṣas* above and below, there are likewise thirty-two *kālas*. However, from the root perspective, there are directly fifty syllables. By means of those syllables, he abides relying upon the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) according to the tradition of other schools (*paranikāya*), but according to the tradition of his own school (*svanikāya*), he abides relying upon the five branches of knowledge. And it has been said: *akāraḥ sarvavarṇāgryo mahārthaḥ paramākṣaraḥ | mahāprāṇo hyanutpādo vāgudāhāravarjitaḥ ||* The letter *a* is the foremost of all letters, of great significance, the supreme syllable, the great vital breath, the unarisen, and devoid of verbal expression.
But he who is not bound by the ten [qualities] within the range of one to nine—know him to be unbound; he knows the supreme state.
"He who knows the vowels and consonants following the number nine, unbound by mutual conjunction—he is the teacher of the world. Thus it is said.
"The limbs [of knowledge] are the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive Nyāya."
The Purāṇas and the treatises on Dharma—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.

Thus ends the position of other schools. Furthermore, the sciences (*vidyā*) are five fields of knowledge: the science of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vidyā*), the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*), the inner science (*adhyātmika-vidyā*), the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), and the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-vidyā*).

Since all these [mantras] are extracted from the letter *a* alone, there is no utterance of them without that Lord of All Mantras; therefore, he says: "or those established at the beginning of the Vedas. (4)
Of mantras, tantras, and external treatises—these alone are their true natures; there is nothing else whatsoever.
These fifty [letters], belonging to the groups beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*, are considered equal;
they reside within the vajra and lotus, having emerged from every petal in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (6)
In the midst of these, within the pericarp, resides the Supreme Lord,
the supreme syllable, encircled by the eight groups [of letters].

It should be understood that for peaceful, fierce, and terrifying mantras such as *Pratyaṅgirā* and others, for protective wheels (*rakṣācakra*), for external treatises, and for the aforementioned fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), these very letters serve as the cause. There is nothing else here whatsoever. Therefore, this extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*) should be understood everywhere—in the *Yoginītantras* and elsewhere—as being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). To that end, he says: "There is nothing else, nor anything other. (5)

Anticipating the questions—what is this mantra, what is its retinue, where is it situated, and how many [syllables] does it have—he says, beginning with the passage: "situated within *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*," and so forth. By taking the first letter from each group (*varga*), there are eight groups which are the cause of all speech, namely *Ālikāli*. These very fifty letters become sixty-four through the equalization of *Ālikāli*, because one meditates upon one letter for each channel (*nāḍī*). Therefore, it should be understood that in the *Nirmāṇacakra*, the fifty syllables are established by their own nature as consisting of the sixty-four deities of the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara* maṇḍala—which is divided into eight groups of eight—and are situated in the eight cardinal and intermediate directions. ||6||

He speaks of the central leader with the words "In their midst," and so forth. In the midst of those channels (*nāḍī*) consisting of the *āli* and *kali*, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is the sovereign (*cakravartin*) of those phonemes (*varṇa*), whose nature is that of the supreme heroes and yoginīs. For instance, excluding the four neuter seed-syllables (*napuṃsaka-bīja*), the twelve phonemes beginning with *a* are the twelve-armed Blessed One. The four burnt seed-syllables are Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī. The consonants from *ka* to *ha*, marked by the bindu of the letter *ma*, are the heroes and heroines of the three wheels. Those from *ya* to *ha* are Kākāsyā and the others. The syllable *kṣa* is Kṣayaḍāka. In the center is the vowel *a*, which is Vajravārāhī. Therefore, this supreme syllable *a*, surrounded by these eight groups (*varga*), is the cause of all mantras; thus, by means of this, the mantras are extracted. (7)
The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the leader of the classes [of consonants].
Indeed, from it alone have all the mantras of embodied beings arisen. (8)

Those accomplishments (siddhis) that follow from ritual action— such as the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, pills, the underworld, yakṣa maidens, and those moving within the belly of the three worlds, as well as those residing in mercury—
and all those great supernatural powers (maharddhi) present in their own abodes, endowed with the five true objects of desire;
The excellent vowels emerge from the midst of the eight classes, which consist of those very classes. ||9||

He states its benefit, beginning with "the letter A" and so forth. It is "of great significance" because it indicates the reality that is primordially unarisen. It is the "leader of the classes" because by means of it alone they are animated. And whatever mantras or utterances of embodied beings—or of practitioners—there may be, such as the *praṇava* and others, they are all born and produced from that very source. Thus, it is established that all sentient beings are by their very nature devoted to mantra. (8)

To state that the accomplishments (*siddhi*) resulting from the expansion of karma arise from this very thorough knowledge alone and not from anything else, he says: "The sword, collyrium," and so forth. There are five accomplishments: the sword, the wheel, the jewel, the vajra, and the *vidyādhara* (accomplishment of the knowledge-holders); the sword is mentioned as a representative example. The second is the accomplishment of collyrium, by which one becomes invisible. The third is the accomplishment of foot-ointment, by which one traverses hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* in a mere instant.
