The fourth is the accomplishment of the subterranean realm (*pātāla*), by which one perceives treasures hidden underground, enters the openings of caves, or attracts the daughters of the *asuras*. The fifth is the accomplishment of the yakṣa women, by which one enjoys yakṣiṇīs with beautiful bodies. The sixth is the accomplishment of the pill (*guṭikā*), by which, having cast it into the mouth and traveled through all the Buddha-fields, one hears the Dharma from the Buddhas. The seventh is the accomplishment existing within the belly of the three worlds, by which one accomplishes the eight activities such as pacification (*śānti*). The eighth is the accomplishment of mercury (*sūtaka*), by which one transforms stone, copper, and so forth into gold. These are the eight great accomplishments. Furthermore, there are other mundane and supramundane accomplishments—characterized by the divine eye and so forth, or the powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*), or the mastery over effects—all of which belong to the group of eight.
Whatever range of speech any living being may attain,
all that is indeed of the nature of mantra, for it is born from that very source.
For sound is said to be the mantra for all embodied beings;
from the great seat of the universal knot, it issues forth from the center of the dharma-wheel.
No mantra whatsoever is fixed; rather, it is established as having its purpose accomplished.
For the mantra is of an unarisen nature, the supreme Lord of the Classes. 12.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Narration of the Extraction of Mantras," in the *Śrī Vasantatilakā*. 9.
It is thus stated that since these [syllables] are adorned and arise from the very first vowel, no further effort need be made through elaborate explanation to establish them. ||9||

Demonstrating its pervasiveness by virtue of being included within all sentient beings, he says, "Whosoever," and so forth: Whatever flow of speech arises for embodied beings—whether articulate, inarticulate, or both—that is entirely of the nature of mantra, because it is included within that which constitutes its source of origin. (10)

The mantra is indeed the sound (*nāda*), whether it be the resonance of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) or another, arising from the region of the navel; for it protects the mind (*manas*) by means of secret speech. During sexual union (*samāpatti*), this entire class of beings—both female and male—speaks that very sound and finds joy therein; through the piercing of the "staff" (*daṇḍa*), they faint, and by that very means, the differentiation of the seminal drop (*bindu*) is also attained. Thus, from the *nirmāṇacakra*, the great locus of the universal knot for all embodied beings created by the aggregate of such activities, there issues forth and prevails the *dharmāralli*—which pervades the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*), including all phonemes, words, sentences, and great sentences. It emerges and becomes manifest.
That which women utter when the time for sexual union has arisen—
possessing both manifest and unmanifest natures— is known as the *nāda* (sound) or *mantra*.
That very same sound is heard during joy, anger, and serenity; in dreams, at the moment of fainting, and at the time of death; and upon awakening and at the time of sexual union. (11)

He states the conclusion: regarding the previously mentioned accomplishment of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*), there exists no fixed rule for the mantra by which it brings about the accomplishment of an activity. Because it possesses excellence through the intensity of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), that very excellence is its pervasion by the syllable of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatākṣara*). When that [pervasion] exists, they become performers of various and manifold activities. To that end, he says: "For the mantra, whose intrinsic nature is unarisen, is the supreme Lord of the Classes (*vargeśvara*). This letter *A* indicates the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as being primordially unarisen. It is precisely by virtue of this vision that these mantras, when applied to their respective functions, become fruitful. For this very reason, he is called the "Lord of the Classes" because he exercises sovereignty over them; it is not, however, that they are his lords. (12)

Thus ends the detailed explanation of the ninth instruction in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, the manual for the means of accomplishment through the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 9.
The Tenth Exposition:
Now, I shall explain the gnosis of great bliss in the form of the three bodies—the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation—of a certain Tathāgata’s body. (1)
The wheel located at the head and navel is established in the form of the letter E;
the wheel reaching the heart and throat is considered to resemble the letter Vaṃ.

Now, in order to explain the nature of the four wheels (*cakra*)—which are the essence of the three bodies beginning with the Dharma-body—and the four matrices (*yoni* or *dyauli*) consisting of the five vowels and so forth, as well as the inexpressible innate (*sahaja*) [nature] through the definitions of mantras and other means, he speaks the tenth instruction beginning with "Now" (*atha*). The word "now" (*atha*) signifies immediate succession in relation to the preceding instruction. "Of any one whatsoever" refers to any particular [being]. "In the form of the Dharma and so forth" means in the form of the three bodies (*kāya*). "I shall proclaim the innate great bliss-gnosis" (*mahāsukhajñāna*) is the brief statement (*uddeśa*). This is what is meant: all sentient beings indeed consist of the innate nature of the three bodies, because they are joined with the three. (1)

He states their locations with the words "the wheel situated at the head and the navel," and so forth. These two wheels situated between the head and the navel are of the form of the letter *e*; this is because they are equal to the *dharmodaya* below and share the same nature as the earth element. Likewise, the pericarp of the lotus at the *uṣṇīṣa* above is also triangular in form, because it has the *dharmodaya* as its intrinsic nature. Similarly, the two wheels located at the heart and the throat are also of the form of the letter *vaṃ*. Because the letter *vaṃ* is arranged in reverse order, it is likewise triangular. This is what is meant: although the *nirmāṇacakra* and the *mahāsukhacakra* have the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*) respectively, both take the form of wisdom; and likewise, although the heart and throat wheels have the nature of method and wisdom respectively, they also take the form of wisdom, because all of them are pervaded by the *avadhūtī*. (2)
A lotus with sixty-four petals is situated in the center of the navel;
a lotus with thirty-two petals is established in the center of the head. (3)
Furthermore, there is a sixteen-petaled lotus situated in the middle of the throat,
and likewise in the heart, there is a lotus endowed with eight petals.
The sixty-four-petaled [lotus] is proclaimed as the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya);
within the great eight-petaled lotus, the dharma body (dharmakāya) proceeds. ||5||
In the sixteen-spoked [wheel] is the sambhogakāya, and likewise in the thirty-two-petaled [wheel], the great bliss and great gnosis are established all around. (6)

Beginning with "in the center of the navel" and ending with "the eight-petaled lotus is remembered," the four wheels—Nirmāṇa and so forth—are established in their respective order as having sixty-four, thirty-two, sixteen, and eight petals, because they consist of the nature of the staffs (*daṇḍa*), the channels (*nāḍī*), the transits (*saṃkrānti*), and the watches (*prahara*). Just as there is a division of staffs and so forth externally through the movement of the sun, so too internally it occurs through the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, it is demonstrated that these are the wheels of Kālacakra, for that [breath] is indeed dependent upon the wheels. (3–4)

By the passage beginning with "sixty-four petals" and ending with "situated all around," it is demonstrated that these four [cakras] are not only of the nature of the specific times of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), but also possess the nature of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth. In this regard, the navel-cakra is the emanation body, because it is the source of the arising of all sentient beings—the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—in the form of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. The heart-cakra is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), because it withdraws the forms of the aggregates and elements, such as the syllable *HŪṂ*. The throat-cakra is the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), because it bestows the enjoyment of the nectar of the Dharma and because it is the supreme delight. The head-cakra is great primordial wisdom, the essential body (*svabhāvakāya*), because its intrinsic nature is the ultimate bodhicitta. And it is said:
"The three bodies (trikāya) are situated within the body in the form of wheels (cakra).
The thorough knowledge of the three bodies is known as the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukha).
Within the center of the emanation wheel (nirmāṇacakra), it is encircled by the eight classes [of consonants]."
This letter 'va' is the foremost form among all letters; it is the supreme syllable.
In the wheel of dharma (the throat), the syllable HŪṂ is renowned; it is considered the unstruck sound (anāhata), joined with the five vowels and adorned with ya, ra, la, and va. ||8||
In the center of the saṃbhoga-cakra, however, is the syllable Oṃ, the illuminator of colors, completely surrounded on all sides by four digits (kalās). ||9||
In the great wheel of great bliss, the syllable *haṃ* takes the form of a drop (*bindu*);
the moon and sun are renowned as being on the left and right sides respectively. (10)
Likewise: by him,
for the sake of the welfare of the world, bodies were assumed,
as well as families, goddesses, and family leaders.
"May Vajradhara, whose essential nature is conformed to the mantras of his own form, be served for the sake of auspiciousness. Thus [ends verses 5–6].

In order to establish that all sentient beings possess the nature of the mantra-body of the *cakrādheya* [the one to be established in the wheel], he says, beginning with the passage "In the center of the *nirmāṇacakra*" and ending with "the syllable *haṃ* is the illuminator. In that regard, when the *nirmāṇacakra* is reached, according to the stated method, the syllable *a* is in the center and the vowels (*ālikāli*) are on the petals. In the *dharmacakra*, there are the five *hūṃ*s, which are the seed-syllables of the five *ḍākas*, including the neuter ones. In the throat, there is Brahmā, surrounded by the sixteen vowels and the four long *praṇavas*. On the head, there is the syllable *haṃ*, facing downward and encircled twice by the consonants (*āli*). It is thus established that these wheels, having sequentially entered the Great Maṇḍala, take the form of the Heruka maṇḍala consisting of the four channels—the peaceful and most peaceful—of the Wisdom Maṇḍala that has been entered. (7–9½)

Thus, he speaks of the two channels that serve as the support for the wheels, beginning with the words "The Moon and Sun are renowned," and so forth. One should know that the Moon and Sun of the left and right wheels are the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, which, situated above and below the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, flow with the elements of semen and blood. By this, it is stated that the external manifestation of the Moon and Sun is indeed internal (*ādhyātmika*). ||10||
Starting from the throat, the channel on the left belongs to the Saṃbhogakāya;
it rests in the center of the navel, facing downward, and brings about intoxication. (11)
The channel that rises upward from above the navel likewise rests in the middle of the throat and is proclaimed as the carrier of blood.
The one known as Mada is Candra (the Moon), and the one remembered as Rakta is Sūrya (the Sun);
they are mounted upon two gates, situated respectively below and above. 13.
These two channels, known as Candra and Sūrya, are proclaimed to be the basis for the coming and going of the heroes and ḍākinīs. (14)

In order to reveal the substance-carrying nature, the gateway, and the location of these two, he says, beginning with "starting from the throat": This channel called *lalanā* on the left side flows downward, starting from the throat and reaching the center of the navel, carrying *mada* (intoxication). Likewise, this channel called *rasanā* on the right side flows upward, starting from the navel and reaching the throat, carrying *rakta* (blood). (11–12)

He states the synonym for *mada* (intoxication) and *rakta* (blood) with the words beginning, "Intoxication is known as the moon," and so forth. That which is *mada*, the moon, semen, and the downward-moving wind (*apānavāyu*)—it has been said: "That is the sun and the upward-moving wind (*prāṇavāyu*). The ellipsis to be supplied is "by way of color and by way of function. These two, the moon and the sun, relying upon the gate of the mind—which is divided into two parts consisting of the southern and northern solstices—and flowing through the modes of upward and downward movement, are to be known as having the nature of Lokeśa and Ākāśagarbha, and taking the form of Amitābha and Ratnasaṃbhava, according to the statement: "The two, Vajrasūrya and Amitābha, are the root in the accomplishment of cyclic existence. Furthermore, externally, when the sun goes down from the sunset mountain, the moon rises and goes up; and likewise by the reverse process. Those very same moon and sun that rely upon the gate of the mind are to be understood as the basis for the activity of the coming and going of the heroes and ḍākinīs. Likewise, the heroes are the twenty-four elements, and they are the feet of the moon. Thus, it is to be known that this applies to all sentient beings in their entirety. (13–14)
The twelve vowels are situated on the left and right sides, corresponding respectively to the states of sleep and awakening, which signify the meanings of setting and rising. 15.
They are declared to be facing upwards, surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka*;
they are joined with those facing downwards situated at the sides, beginning with the letter *ya*. ||16||
Joined with the syllable *kṣa* and encircled at its lower part, when the moon is situated in the throat in the form of great passion (*mahārāga*). (17)

To show that [the two movements] proceed in this manner externally from sunrise until sunset—at midday precisely—he says, beginning with "The purposes of setting and rising," and so forth. In that regard, when the prāṇa wind rises through the right nostril, then the apāna wind sets through the left nostril. Thus, the movement of the moon and sun for all sentient beings is established throughout the day and night. Sleep and waking should also be understood in the same way: sleep is the lunar portion, and waking is the solar portion. In this way, the states of sleep and waking should be known as having the nature of Amitābha and Ratnasambhava, who are the very forms of the moon and sun. (14½)

In order to explain the inner stūpa and the deception of timely death (*kālamṛtyuvañcana*), he says, beginning with the words “on the left and right sides” and ending with “is situated in the lower part. The twelve vowels, excluding the neuter seeds (*napuṃsakabīja*), reside in the left and right channels (*nāḍī*) respectively, facing downward and upward, surrounded by the twenty-four consonants from *ka* onwards, which also face downward and upward. By their very nature, they are established in the form of the resonance of the channels. For this reason, he says: “having made them central, they are joined. Below, on the path of the *apāna*, the letter *kṣa*—the protector of the *apāna*—resides in the conch-seal (*śaṅkhamudrā*), while above is the letter *ra*. By means of the rays of the syllable *hūṃ* located in the center of the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*), the vowels and consonants of the left and right are drawn in and enter the center. At that time, through the power of the worship of the *kulikā*, the yogin deceives timely death and attains the great breath of Vajradhara. (15–16½)

Now, in order to demonstrate that the *bodhicitta* assumes the nature of the three bodies (*trikāya*) through the power of its movement from one location to another, he says, beginning with "When at the throat": "When at the throat, the moon—which consists of the sixteen digits or has the nature of supreme flavor—is then called the *saṃbhoga*, the supreme body of the Buddhas.
But when it is situated at the tip of the nose, and then at the tip of the *vajra*... (18)
But when that enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) has set, it becomes situated in the center of the bhaga, renowned as the "mustard seed" (sarṣapa). ||19||
That which is designated as having the form of the sun is called the *nirmāṇakāya*; by means of it, the emanation of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas arises. (20)
King Padmanarteśvara, who possessed the yoga of Padmaprakāśa,
[remained] in the form of a manifested body when the sun had set.

When [the moon] remains thus at the tip of the nose, at the heart, at the navel, and at the tip of the vajra, then, because of its state of complete bliss, that moon is called the *saṃbhogakāya*. That very same [moon] is to be understood as the supreme body of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedya*) of the Buddhas' aggregates (*skandha*). When that very moon, from the tip of the vajra, has set and fallen into the center of the *bhaga*, having entered the center of the sun which has itself set to the size of a mustard seed, then it receives the designation of the *nirmāṇakāya*. He states the reason with the words "of the Buddhas" and so forth. Then, from the conjunction of the moon and the sun, the emanation (*spharaṇa*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the form of the aggregates and so on arises; therefore, that is the *nirmāṇakāya*. Because it is invisible to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the *saṃbhogakāya* has set, and the *nirmāṇakāya* performs the welfare of sentient beings—such is the established system. (17–20)

For this very reason, in order to demonstrate that even though he is situated in the center of the sun, his essential nature (*svarūpa*) known as Padmanarteśvara remains unmanifested, he says: "(He is) Padmanarteśvara, the King. *Padmanartana* means "lotus-dance"; one who is sovereign (*īśvara*) there, possessing power like a lord, is *Padmanarteśvara*. He is the "King" (*rājā*) because he shines (*rājate*), glowing like vermilion powder due to its conjunction with the sun. To explain that meaning, he says: "[Possessing the union of lotus-light]" (*padmaprakāśayogavān*). That which shines and is beautiful within the lotus (*padme*) is the self-arisen (*svayambhū*) lotus-light; because of its union—that is, its state of oneness—with that, the moon is called "possessing the union of lotus-light. (20½)
It is known as the manifest bodhicitta, condensed and stainless;
it cuts off the path of saṃsāra, is the cessation of conceptual proliferation, and is auspicious. (22)
Free from duality, supremely pure, the form of Śrī Vajrasattva is known as Śrī Heruka; the tantra, however, is the form of the wood-worm. ||23||
Established in the system of the three tantras through laughter, vision, and the attainment of the hand,
he remains like a wood-worm, having abandoned both passion and dispassion.

The *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* have been described; now he speaks of the *dharmakāya* with the words "When that sun has set," and so forth. When that sun known as the *nirmāṇakāya* has set—having entered therein when the two manifestations have attained a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*)—that which is the mass of the moon and the sun, the undisturbed [state] free from the stains of dualistic conceptualization, is the *dharmakāya*; this is the connection with what follows. Of what nature is it? It is that in which there is the severance of the path of cyclic existence consisting of the equilibrium of the two manifestations, as well as their conceptualization; likewise, it is where there is the subsiding of the two elaborations (*prapañca*), namely the *saṃbhoga* and *nirmāṇa* bodies. Thus, it is a compound of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). It is *śiva* because it is innate (*sahaja*). It is *nirdvandva* (beyond duality) because it is free from the two mutually opposed sides. It is *parama* (supreme) because it is self-cognizable. It is *śuddha* (pure) because it is free from afflictions (*kleśa*). *Vajra* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and *sattva* is compassion (*karuṇā*); because it rests upon these, its nature is that of *Vajrasattva*. Because it is the form of the goal—the liberation-gate of natural luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*)—which is the means for the three gates of liberation, it is *Śrī Heruka*. That very one is called the *dharmakāya*. Because it protects the mind, it is *mantra*. Because it devours the net of afflictions such as passion like chaff, it is the *ghuṇa* (woodworm). (21–23)

If it is asked: "Is it not the case that in the *Yoginītantras* only the *ghuṇa* [the 'woodworm' union] is specified, and not [the others] such as *kriyā* and so forth? Therefore, how can the *dharmakāya* be non-pervasive? It is said: "By laughing," and so forth. In the *Kriyā* and *Caryātantras*, there is mutual laughter between wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*); in the *Yogatantra*, however, it is looking; in the *Yogacaryā* and *Ubhayatantras*, it is taking hands. This is an illustration; in the *Mahāyogatantra*, it is embracing, and in the *Yoginītantras*, it is the couple (*dvandva*). And it is said: "The *Saṃvara* of the *Ḍākinījāla*, which is the union of all channels."
The secret [is found] in the element of earth, and likewise even in supreme water. ||25||
In the secret [element] called fire, and in wind, this which is established as the self of all is said to be eternally present; it is the Samvara that is the essence of all Buddhas. 26.
Alternatively, [it is taught] in the form of a mirror, likewise in equanimity, in the awakening of discernment, and similarly in the performance of duties. ||27||
"Or [it is taught] by means of smiles and glances, or likewise through embraces and pairs;
it is taught even in the four tantras by means of intentional language (*sandhābhāṣā*).

Thus, having excluded the three [states] of passion and dispassion, the wood-worm (*ghuṇa*) is established everywhere in all the tantras. Therefore, there is no fault, as this is the pervasiveness of the *dharmakāya*. ||24||

In order to demonstrate that the *dharmakāya* has the form of the maṇḍala wheel, he says, beginning with "all channels" (*sarvanāḍī*). Those elements which possess union with all the channels are the "union with all channels," namely the twenty-four heroes; the *saṃvara*—the reality—is that which is characterized by them, these *ḍākinīs*, and it is their "net," meaning their assembly. Its meaning is that it is the nature of *bodhicitta*. Showing that the *dharmakāya* possesses all aspects, he says "secret" (*rahasya*) and so forth. This statement in the King of Tantras beginning with "secret" is spoken in intentional language (*sandhābhāṣā*): the *saṃvara* whose essence is all Buddhas, whose nature is great bliss, is established within the external and internal elements of earth, water, fire, and air, and within the four wheels (*cakras*), because its nature is *dharmatā*. (25–26)

With the words beginning with "Alternatively" (*athavā*) and ending with "the perfectly pure dharmadhātu" (*suviśuddhadharmadhātukam*), he explains that this very [wisdom] has the nature of the five Buddhas, such as Ādarśa (Mirror-like Wisdom) and the others. For it is so: because it reflects the manifold wheel of objects of knowledge, it is indeed the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). It is said to be always present as one among these [five], having a perfectly pure nature:
either as Vairocana, or as Ratnasambhava. (28)
Alternatively, it is the nature of Amitābha, or that which always abides in the cloudless sky—the mass consisting of the five nectars, in the form of a drop, and composed of mind. (29)
The utterly pure great gnosis, whose very nature is that of all goddesses, is renowned as Vajrasattva and is declared to be supreme bliss. (30)
This very form of the Self-Existent is proclaimed as the Dharmakāya;
his innate wisdom (sahajā prajñā) abides as that which assumes its form. //31//

Because it is [the nature of] suchness, that very [wisdom] is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). Because it discerns and analyzes [phenomena], that very [wisdom] is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Because the welfare of the world proceeds from that alone, that very [wisdom] is the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). And because its form is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), this is the wisdom of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātujñāna*). || 27–27½ ||

With the words beginning "Vairocana," he explains that this very [deity] has the nature of the five Buddhas. For, because he shines (*rocana*) by way of being self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*), he is Vairocana. Because he is unshakeable (*akṣobhya*) by passion (*rāga*) and the other afflictions, he is Akṣobhya. Because the manifestation (*saṃbhava*) of the two jewels—the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*)—occurs from him, he is Ratnasaṃbhava. He whose immeasurable radiance consists of gnosis (*jñāna*) is Amitābha. Since his accomplishment (*siddhi*) is fruitful in the performance of the welfare of sentient beings, he is Amoghasiddhi. Having explained the manifest form (*vivṛti-rūpa*), he speaks of the conventional form (*saṃvṛta-rūpa*): "consisting of the five nectars," and so forth. The remainder of the sentence is: "The Buddhas say that even the conventional mass, which consists of the five nectars through the five [secrets] such as the secret place, which is in the form of a drop (*bindu*) and has attained a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) in the midst of the five voids, is the utterly pure gnosis of the sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddha-dharmadhātu-jñāna*) abiding within one’s own body. He provides a further qualification of that very [deity]: "Vajrasattva. That which was previously determined to have the nature of supreme bliss, independent of causes and conditions, is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). By this, his nature as the manifest form is once again established. (27–30½)
Blazing in the circle of the navel, driven by the winds of karma, she is well-known as Vārāhī and is remembered as the Vasantatilakā. (32)
With a body possessing hundreds of thousands of hair-tips and a radiance equal to a hundred flashes of lightning, [he abides] within the pores, tips, and joints during the times of deity yoga. //33//

The Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka, whose nature consists of the three bodies (kāyas), has been described. To demonstrate the Blessed Lady Vārāhī, who is non-different from him, he says: Within the navel-mandala of this very Śrī Heruka, whose nature is the co-emergent (sahaja), there is a consciousness in the form of fire—blazing, born from the union of the churner and the churning, and fanned by the winds of karma. That itself is his innate wisdom (prajñā), established by its own nature like the moon and its moonlight. She alone is Vārāhī. She is called Vārāhī because she impels (*īrayati*) and causes to flow (*srāvayati*) by means of the two syllables *vā* and *ra*, which signify wind (*mātariśvan*) and fire (*hutabhuj*). She is not, however, one with a sow's face. She is the "tilaka" because she is like a forehead-mark (*tilaka*) for the spring-like *HŪṂ* and other syllables; for it was previously explained that she is satisfied upon attaining that [spring]. (31–32)

He states her measure with the words beginning "bālāgra" (the tip of a hair): she whose limb—that is, her essential form—is like a hundred-thousandth part, a portion measuring one lakh, of the tip of a hair; by this, her extreme subtlety is established, because she is accessible only to the knowledge of yogins. And it has been said:
"Her form is equal to an extremely subtle lotus fiber, [extending] up to the abode of great bliss preceded by the fire of the eon."
"That wisdom which abides pervading [all], perceivable by the Great Being (mahāpuruṣa), is declared to belong to Varaheruka.
Regarding the phrase "having a radiance like a flash of lightning," it means having a luster resembling a streak of lightning, shining with light. He describes its function:

Regarding the passage beginning with "the time of deity-yoga" (*devatāyogakāla*): deity-yoga is the non-dual yoga of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*). At that time, at that occasion, that very flame of the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgnijvālā*) issues forth from all the pores and joints of the yogin’s body. Having terrified the gods and asuras—the conceptualizations of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*)—and having burned the fuel of the conceptualizations of the aggregates and elements, which exist in the form of knots within the *dharma-cakra* and *saṃbhoga-cakra*, it exits through the right nostril. Entering the aperture located in the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-treasure between the brows), it enters the crest-aperture (*śikhārandhra*) of those [beings] situated in the ten directions. Having burned their four wheels (*cakra*), it exits again through the left nostril and enters through the crest-aperture.
Emerging toward all directions and threatening the gods and asuras, she burns [them] within the heart-dharmacakra from the sambhogacakra. (34)
Having emerged through the right nostril on all sides,
it likewise enters the aperture located in the circle of hair between the brows and indeed pervades the ten directions.
Having entered through the left nostril of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should emerge after kindling the wheel at the crown of the head.
And again, through the previously mentioned aperture, she enters the crest-lock (śikhā);
having produced bliss for the Buddhas who have been incinerated, she returns to the navel-center and remains there as before. (37)

Thus, in the *Śrī-Vasantatilakā*, the tenth chapter is concluded: the description of the Tathāgatas residing in each respective object, whose nature consists of the thirty-four syllables and the twelve vowel-morae, situated within the four lotuses of the wheels of Great Bliss—namely the Emanation, Enjoyment, Dharma, and Secret wheels—which are the knowledge of the mantras and the movement of the Tantras, preceded by the embrace of the three bodies: the Dharmakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya; this is remembered as the *Śrī-Heruka-Vasanta-Vajravārāhī-Tilakā*.

As before, it causes the replenishment of the burnt Tathāgatas and becomes stable, then dissolves into the navel-mandala. And it is said: "Through the union of the churning-stick and the churning-vessel, the fire of gnosis, impelled here by the wind of karma, dissolves into the navel-mandala and blazes with radiant flames. Having burnt the Sugatas residing in the *samaya*-cakra, it [reaches] the Means (*upāya*) residing in the *saṃbhoga*-cakra three times.

The sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, pills, the subterranean realm, the yakṣa women, and the accomplishments (*siddhis*) that follow from karma—all those existing within the belly of the three worlds, situated in the mercury—[are attained]."

"Having circumambulated [the body], one enters the Tathāgatas residing in the ten directions through the door that reveals the vital points (*marmodghāṭana*) known as Oḍḍiyāna, located within the *ūrṇā*-cavity; then, having entered through the golden door known as Jālandhara, one burns their four previous wheels (*cakras*), exits through the aforementioned door, reaches the stream of milk, and generates bliss for the Tathāgatas who were previously burned. Thus are the *tantrali*, *jñānoli*, and *mantroli* explained. By the statement, "The twelve vowels are situated on the left and right sides" (10.15), the *mantroli* is indicated; however, in the investigation of the *dharmakāya*, it is the *guhyoli*. (33–37)

He states the conclusion: therein, by describing the four wheels (*cakras*) in the embrace of the three bodies (*kāyas*), and by describing the two manifestations and establishing their state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*), [the meaning] has been stated. By describing the union of *nāda* and *bindu*, the meaning of the *Vasantatilaka* for Heruka and Vajravārāhī has been stated. By the term "going and coming," their conjunction is stated; this is the description of the secret of the knowledge of mantra and tantra. By the external statement, "The twelve vowels are situated on the left and right sides" (10.15), and by the statements beginning with "Her innate wisdom (*sahajā prajñā*) is this very one" (10.31) and ending with "having incinerated the wheel, she should emerge" (10.36), as well as by "she should again produce bliss for the Buddhas who have been incinerated" (10.37) and "having reached the navel-mandala, she remains as before" (10.38), the four *olīs* known as the secret of the knowledge of mantra and tantra have been described. Likewise, regarding the arrangement of the five vowels and so forth in the four wheels beginning with the *nirmāṇa*-wheel, there is—in brief—the arrangement of the doubled *āli* and *kāli*, the five seed-syllables beginning with *HŪṂ*, the neuter seed-syllables, the arrangement of long *brahmans*, and the arrangement of the unstruck syllable (*anāhatākṣara*) encircled by the thirty-two *ālis*. This is stated in the passage beginning with: "In the center of the *nirmāṇa*-wheel, encircled by the eight classes [of consonants], the letter *A* is the supreme syllable, the foremost form of all letters" (10.7). The detailed exposition follows the summary. For a summary is a presentation in brief, while a detailed exposition is in detail—this is the implication. This "detailed exposition" means the specific section. As for the eight great accomplishments (*mahāsiddhis*) previously mentioned, such as the sword, collyrium, and so forth, they are clear in meaning. It is established that these arise from understanding the previously mentioned ritual manual (*sādhanopāyikā*) of the *Vasantatilaka*.

This [teaching] concerns individuals of sharp faculties, excluding those of dull faculties; showing this, he says, beginning with "from the brief statement" (*uddeśāt*). From the brief statement, by the grace of the Guru’s feet, through the jewels of the pollen from his lotus-like feet, and through the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the teaching Guru—indeed, all great supernatural powers (*maharddhi*), together with the five objects of desire, exist in one's own abode;
all these are attained when they arise through the power of the *Vasantatilaka* yoga.

Thus, having received the instruction of the guru and having ascertained [the teaching] while in a dream through the command of the venerable Lord Heruka, this *Vasantatilakā* has been clearly elucidated by the practitioner of the observance, the illustrious Kṛṣṇācārya, according to the tradition of the venerable Cakrasaṃvara, both externally and internally, and through meditation on its own nature; it is indicated for the awakening of those of dull intellect. And because the goddess Vajravārāhī, by the command of the spring-like Heruka, is called "Vasantatilakā," that is also the title of this treatise.
Thus ends the *Vasantatilakā*.

Those who are adorned and graced by the crowns (*paṭṭa*) that distinguish the jewels of realized reality; and likewise those others who, through the instruction known as *prajñā*, have been inspired and led toward enthusiasm by the preeminent Jinas, the Blessed Tathāgatas, through words that illuminate the syllables of reality—words consisting of successive steps and counter-arguments experienced through faith up to the level of the masters:
"Certainty indeed comes from scripture, and likewise certainty from the guru;
certainty from oneself, and likewise certainty from another."

For it is stated in the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa*: "It is to be grasped by means of four conditions," and so forth; for this very reason, as in the passage beginning, "those who [engage] through the appropriation of the external and internal."

They receive instruction through the similarity between the external and the internal, according to the statement: "As it is internally, so it is externally; thus has restraint been fully revealed. Thus, for those who possess the Vajra-Ḍākas within their own hearts alone and not externally, this *Vasantatilakā* was composed by me. Since they grasp the object of knowledge with firm faith, the author demonstrates the completion of the work by showing his own nature to one who grasps with firm faith, beginning with the words: "Thus, by the venerable Guru-Buddha... etc. By me, Kṛṣṇa—the observer of the *caryā-vrata*, established in the body of the Tathāgata, and having received the command of my own Vajra-Guru and Buddhas—this work titled *Vasantatilakā*, consisting of ten instructions, has been completed. This means that because it is a compendium of the meaning of all Tantras, there is no dependence on anything else.

Thus ends the detailed explanation in the tenth instruction of the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilakā*, which is a manual for the means of accomplishment in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). 10.
Thus ends the commentary on the Vasantatilaka.
